Cognitive status and capacity to understand: PT has a much better understanding of his diagnosis and treatment plan than he did back in 01/10/2014 when he began dialysis.MOC also has a basic understanding of condition but refers back to PT for decision making as he is "the man of the house." MOC does not read or write.     2. Ability to meet basic needs: Family is extremely low income. MOC does not receive any support for her four kids from FOC and is getting by on about $700 a month. MOC utilizes family support as well as foodstamps to make it work. MOC has begun to receive SSDI benefits for PT which has been a tremendous financial help. MOC has started working as a house cleaner which she notes is hard work but has been helpful for her finances. PT worked this summer at Bly  and has since stopped. PT is interested in finding more part time work and swer showed him tools to job searching using the Internet.    3. Ability to follow the treatment prescription: PT reports following a renal diet and taking his supplements and multivitamins and trying protein shakes. Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He "will do what he needs to do" but team fearful given high risk nature of transplant in teens, lack of support at home, and attitude of PT. He has made progress and done a good job of taking more  responsibility in his medical condition. Family working on identifying people to provide consistent transportation. PT has made a lot of progress and become more communicative with the team.    4. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the need for counseling. Dutt and medical team explained that all teenagers are encouraged to see a counselor and referrals were given to him last month. MOC reports that she has not found any providers. Swer will reiterate importance of therapuetic support.    5. Substance abuse history: none reported.    6. Current ability to cope with and adjust to dialysis:PT has been dialyzing at an outpatient clinic and appears to be attending, however he has not talked to any of his friends about this.PT works with social worker at Davita, Elkadry. PT has a tough demeanor but will answer questions politely when asked, and appears to appreciate opportunities to vent. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally.    7. Expectations for the future and living with kidney failure and treatment: PT had a kidney transplant evaluation many months ago and was not re. PT was overwhelmed by the meeting and he and family were not prepared for the referral. Now that he is dialyzing on a regular schedule he would benefit from more information regarding transplant and the transplant process. MOC has mentioned in passing that they have many extended family members who are interested in donating but is somewhat resistant to ask again. He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He is active on txp list and swer discussed the unavailability of RMH for the next 15 months and family's likely need to stay in a local hotel post txp.    8. Educational and employment status,  concerns and goals: PT will be a senior this fall in high school and reports doing well in school but being on the cusp of graduation in June. PT does not have a lot of wiggle room in terms of losing credit as he is just barely staying on track. PT reports he does not have a school counselor or an IEP. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation. Swer encouraged PT to let her know if he needs help navigating the school system.    9. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 16-4.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Damien Deol for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but appears somewhat uninterested at this point.     13. Eligibility for federal, state and/or local resources: SSI, medi-cal and CCS.

Patient: Goodale: 01/06/1997   MRN: [000000]   Date of Service: 02/08/2015   Date of First Dialysis Treatment:    Primary Nephrology Fellow:    Primary HD Nurse:      Lucile Packard Children's Hospital  Pediatric Dialysis  Interdisciplinary Comprehensive Patient Assessment and Plan of Care     Brief Identification:  Yehuda Nicolas Pi is a 18-year old male who was diagnosed with ANCA negative pauci-immune glomerulonephritis in 02/10/2013. Briefly, he has had a history of persistent microscopic hematuria since age 6 to 7 and presented in 10/11/2012 with elevated creatinine of 3.1, rinalysis showing proteinuria and hematuria. Workup revealed a negative c-ANCA, negative p-ANCA, negative MPO, negative PR3, negative ANA, normal complement levels and a slightly elevated ESR. Further workup during his initial hospitalization at Santa Clara  at Conneaut Lake  in 03/13/2013 included a pulmonary consult, chest CT which revealed scattered pulmonary nodules which were nonspecific, but with normal spirometry. He has no evidence of pulmonary hemorrhage. He has seen ophthalmology in 03/13/2013 and had no signs of uveitis. A kidney biopsy was performed 02/11/2013 at Children's Hospital Oakland, which revealed 11/15 globally or near globally sclerosed glomeruli. Immunofluorescence was positive for 2+ C3 segmental sclerosis pattern, but otherwise negative. EM showed no evidence of Alport syndrome with podocytes showing mild patchy foot process effacement and therefore, the biopsy was consistent with chronic and subacute crescentic process with severe tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis more compatible with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. Rheumatology team had recommended immunosuppression, but he declined. He eventually progressed to ESRD and was started on hemodialysis in 06/10/2013. He was started started on CellCept in 07/11/2013. He is currently being dialyzed thrice weekly at  Davita center in Kuna . Yehuda returns to the clinic for his monthly comprehensive dialysis visit. SOCIAL SERVICES MONTHLY ASSESSMENT          NAME: Tremaine Nicolas Turman  MRN: [000000]  DOB: 01/06/1997LOC:     Seen by SW this month: yes     Plan for next Psychosocial Assessment: Reassess monthly     Referrals to outside agencies/resources: yes     Outside agencies/resources Details: Send HEAL/IEP packet     Age appropriate recreation/activities: yes     Seen by counselor/psychologist/asychiatrist: no     KDQOL-36 completed (Pt> 18 yrs old): no     HRQOL completed (Pt <18 yrs old): yes     Patient plans to maintain health insurance (If >17 yrs old): yes     1. Cognitive status and capacity to understand: PT has a much better understanding of his diagnosis and treatment plan than he did back in 01/10/2014 when he began dialysis.MOC also has a basic understanding of condition but refers back to PT for decision making as he is "the man of the house." MOC does not read or write.     2. Ability to meet basic needs: Family is low income. MOC does not receive any support for her four kids from FOC and is getting by on about $700 a month. MOC utilizes family support as well as foodstamps to make it work. MOC has begun to receive SSDI benefits for PT which has been a tremendous financial help. MOC has started working as a house cleaner which she notes is hard work but has been helpful for her finances. PT works part-time.    3. Ability to follow the treatment prescription: PT reports following a renal diet and taking his supplements and multivitamins and trying protein shakes. Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He "will do what he needs to do" but team fearful given high risk nature of transplant in teens, lack of support at home, and attitude of PT. He has made progress and done a good job of taking more responsibility in his medical condition. Family working on identifying people to provide consistent transportation. PT has made a lot of progress and become  more communicative with the team.    4. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the need for counseling. Lowry and medical team explained that all teenagers are encouraged to see a counselor and referrals were given to him last month. MOC reports that she has not found any providers. Swer will reiterate importance of therapuetic support.    5. Substance abuse history: none reported.    6. Current ability to cope with and adjust to dialysis:PT has been dialyzing at an outpatient clinic and appears to be attending, however he has not talked to any of his friends about this.PT works with social worker at Davita, Heinz. PT has a tough demeanor but will answer questions politely when asked, and appears to appreciate opportunities to vent. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally.    7. Expectations for the future and living with kidney failure and treatment: PT had a kidney transplant evaluation many months ago and was not re. PT was overwhelmed by the meeting and he and family were not prepared for the referral. Now that he is dialyzing on a regular schedule he would benefit from more information regarding transplant and the transplant process. MOC has mentioned in passing that they have many extended family members who are interested in donating but is somewhat resistant to ask again. He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He is active on txp list and swer discussed the unavailability of RMH until late 02/10/2015 and family's likely need to stay in a local hotel post txp.    8. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT will be a senior this fall in high school and reports doing well in school but being on the cusp of graduation in June. PT does not have  a lot of wiggle room in terms of losing credit as he is just barely staying on track. PT reports he does not have a school counselor or an IEP. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation. Swer encouraged PT to let her know if he needs help navigating the school system.    9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Windham . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 16-4.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Coty Hibma for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but appears somewhat uninterested at this point.     13. Eligibility for federal, state and/or local resources: SSI, medi-cal and CCS.

Cognitive status and capacity to understand: PT has a much better understanding of his diagnosis and treatment plan than he did back in 01/10/2014 when he began dialysis.MOC also has a basic understanding of condition but refers back to PT for decision making as he is "the man of the house." MOC does not read or write.     2. Ability to meet basic needs: Family is low income. MOC does not receive any support for her four kids from FOC and is getting by on about $700 a month. MOC utilizes family support as well as foodstamps to make it work. MOC receives SSDI benefits for PT which has been a tremendous financial help. MOC has started working as a house cleaner which she notes is hard work but has been helpful for her finances.    3. Ability to follow the treatment prescription: PT reports following a renal diet and taking his supplements and multivitamins and trying protein shakes. Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He has made tremendous progress. He has made progress and done a good job of taking more responsibility in his medical condition. Family working on identifying people to provide consistent transportation. PT has made a lot of progress and become more communicative with the team.    4. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the  need for counseling. Bahadur and medical team explained that all teenagers are encouraged to see a counselor and referrals were given to him last month. MOC reports that she has not found any providers. Swer will reiterate importance of therapuetic support.    5. Substance abuse history: none reported.    6. Current ability to cope with and adjust to dialysis:PT has been dialyzing at an outpatient clinic and appears to be attending, however he has not talked to any of his friends about this.PT works with social worker at Davita, Babu. PT has a tough demeanor but will answer questions politely when asked, and appears to appreciate opportunities to vent. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally.    7. Expectations for the future and living with kidney failure and treatment: PT had a kidney transplant evaluation many months ago and was not re. PT was overwhelmed by the meeting and he and family were not prepared for the referral. Now that he is dialyzing on a regular schedule he would benefit from more information regarding transplant and the transplant process. MOC has mentioned in passing that they have many extended family members who are interested in donating but is somewhat resistant to ask again. He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He is active on txp list and swer discussed the unavailability of RMH until late 02/10/2015 and family's likely need to stay in a local hotel post txp.    8. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT will be a senior this fall in high school and reports doing well in school but being on the cusp of graduation in June. PT does not have a lot of wiggle room in terms of losing credit as he is just barely staying on track. PT reports he does not have a school counselor or an  IEP. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation. Swer encouraged PT to let her know if he needs help navigating the school system.    9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Espanola . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 18-6.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Ori Raval for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but appears somewhat uninterested at this point.     13. Eligibility for federal, state and/or local resources: SSI, medi-cal and CCS.

Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He has made tremendous progress. PT has made a lot of progress and become more communicative with the team.    4. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the need for counseling. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally.    7. PT has yet to pass either CAHSEE exam. Swer spoke with PT this month regarding meeting with his principal once school commences to talk about earning credits via alternative methods. Ciaccio will also work with PT on creating a resume.    9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Mather . He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He received an offer in summer 2015, which he declined, stating that he felt very scared and overwhelmed. However, after time to think about his choice he stated in clinic today that he is ready and open to transplant. Patient will be represented for activation on 11/14/2015. Whereas two months ago Zalenski denied a kidney offer, today he states he is ready. He attributes his previous denial to timing, having just d/c from hospital and feeling that "everything was happening too fast" If asked today, Khristopher states that he would accept the transplant.    8. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT  is technically a senior at his high school (continuation) Inez Nadel, though he has only 127/210 credits currently and will likely not graduate. PT reports he does not have a school counselor or an IEP. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation and ability to advocate for PT (re: role reversal). Swer spoke to principal Grey Craddock and came up with unique ideas for earning credits for PT by utilizing his time spent on dialysis towards earning credits. PT would benefit from a tutor as he endorses feeling unable to concentrate and complete tasks at home. As a student on independent study, it may be challenging to build in accommodations to help him. PT has yet to pass either CAHSEE exam. Swer spoke with PT this month regarding meeting with his principal once school commences to talk about earning credits via alternative methods.     9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Kennebec . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 18-6.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Levar Cipriano for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but was not interested, and now is 18 and no longer qualifies.     13. Eligibility for federal, state and/or local resources: SSI, medi-cal and CCS.

SOCIAL SERVICES MONTHLY ASSESSMENT          NAME: Yetta Nicolas West  MRN: [000000]  DOB: 01/06/1997LOC:     Seen by SW this month: yes     Plan for next Psychosocial Assessment: Reassess monthly     Referrals to outside agencies/resources: no    Outside agencies/resources Details:     Age appropriate recreation/activities: yes     Seen by counselor/psychologist/asychiatrist: no     KDQOL-36 completed (Pt> 18 yrs old): yes    HRQOL completed (Pt <18 yrs old): no    Patient plans to maintain health insurance (If >17 yrs old): yes     1. Cognitive status and capacity to understand: PT has a much better understanding of his diagnosis and treatment plan than he did back in 01/10/2014 when he began dialysis.Presents as an adult in charge of his treatment and able to manage and navigate care. He has expressed that he is ready for transplant, he is aware of what is required of him.     2. Ability to meet basic needs: Family is low income. MOC does not receive any support for her four kids from FOC and is getting by on about $700 a month. MOC utilizes family support as well as foodstamps to make it work. MOC receives SSDI benefits for PT which has been a tremendous financial help. MOC has works a house cleaner which she notes is hard work but has been helpful for her finances. Pt is now working at the movie theater he states it is full time. He is now driving and more independent with his treatments. He drives himself to HD and is now able to drive himself to all of his appointments.     3. Ability to follow the treatment prescription: PT reports following a renal diet and taking his supplements and multivitamins and trying protein shakes. Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He has made tremendous progress. He has made progress and done a good job of taking more responsibility in his medical condition. CCS transportation helps to get Yetta to monthly  visits.    4. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the need for counseling, presents as age appropriate. SSwer worries that PT does not have support at home and that he has not shared much of his experience with his family members. Whereas two months ago Yetta denied a kidney offer, today he states he is ready. He attributes his previous denial to timing, having just d/c from hospital and feeling that "everything was happening too fast" If asked today, Yetta states that he would accept the transplant and is looking forward to it.     5. Substance abuse history: none reported.    6. Current ability to cope with and adjust to dialysis:PT has been dialyzing at an outpatient clinic and appears to be attending, however he does not talk to his friends about this. PT works with social worker at Davita, Giller. PT has a tough demeanor but will answer questions politely when asked, and appears to appreciate opportunities to vent. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally. He keeps his dialysis a secret from his peers, always wearing long sleeves to cover his fistula. His extended family however is aware of his condition.     7. Expectations for the future and living with kidney failure and treatment: Now that he is dialyzing on a regular schedule he would benefit from more information regarding transplant and the transplant process. He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He received an offer in summer 2015, which he declined, stating that he felt very scared and overwhelmed. However, after time to think about his choice he stated in clinic today that he is ready and open to transplant. He attributes his previous denial to timing, having just d/c from hospital and feeling that  "everything was happening too fast" If asked today, Yetta states that he would accept the transplant.    8. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT is technically a senior at his high school (continuation) Konnor Macy, though he has only 127/210 credits currently and will likely not graduate. PT reports he does not have a school counselor or an IEP. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation and ability to advocate for PT (re: role reversal). Swer spoke to principal Jude Khair and came up with unique ideas for earning credits for PT by utilizing his time spent on dialysis towards earning credits. PT would benefit from a tutor as he endorses feeling unable to concentrate and complete tasks at home. As a student on independent study, it may be challenging to build in accommodations to help him. PT has yet to pass either CAHSEE exam. Swer spoke with PT this month regarding meeting with his principal once school commences to talk about earning credits via alternative methods.     9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Muncy . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 18-6. Pt has started working at the movie theater, he states that he works full time hours and is able to meet all of his medical regimen.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Naim Weintraub for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but was not interested, and now is 18 and no longer qualifies.     13. Eligibility for federal, state and/or local  resources: SSI, medi-cal and CCS.     Howard Dejong, MSW   Pgr: 18743

Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He has made tremendous progress. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the need for counseling, presents as age appropriate. Whereas two months ago Keefe denied a kidney offer, today he states he is ready. Substance abuse history: none reported.    6. Current ability to cope with and adjust to dialysis:PT has been dialyzing at an outpatient clinic and appears to be attending, however he does not talk to his friends about this. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally. He keeps his dialysis a secret from his peers, always wearing long sleeves to cover his fistula. His extended family however is aware of his condition.     7. Expectations for the future and living with kidney failure and treatment: Now that he is dialyzing on a regular schedule he would benefit from more information regarding transplant and the transplant process. He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He received an offer in summer 2015, which he declined, stating that he felt very scared and overwhelmed. However, after time to think about his choice he stated in clinic today that he is ready and open to transplant. He attributes his previous denial to timing, having just d/c from hospital and feeling that  "everything was happening too fast" If asked today, Olsen states that he would accept the transplant.    8. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT is technically a senior at his high school (continuation) Fernando Kuehne, though he has only 127/210 credits currently and will likely not graduate. PT reports he does not have a school counselor or an IEP. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation and ability to advocate for PT (re: role reversal). Swer spoke to principal Konnor Tao and came up with unique ideas for earning credits for PT by utilizing his time spent on dialysis towards earning credits. PT would benefit from a tutor as he endorses feeling unable to concentrate and complete tasks at home. As a student on independent study, it may be challenging to build in accommodations to help him. PT has yet to pass either CAHSEE exam. Swer spoke with PT this month regarding meeting with his principal once school commences to talk about earning credits via alternative methods.     9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Meeteetse . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 18-6. Pt has started working at the movie theater, he states that he works full time hours and is able to meet all of his medical regimen.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Drew Mahmud for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT is technically a senior at his high school (continuation) Yaakov Plate, though he has only 127/210 credits currently and dropped out before graduation. Pt is currently employed full time and SWer provided information on GED completion. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation and ability to advocate for PT (re: role reversal). Swer spoke to principal Jonah Gearhart and came up with unique ideas for earning credits for PT by utilizing his time spent on dialysis towards earning credits. PT would benefit from a tutor as he endorses feeling unable to concentrate and complete tasks at home. As a student on independent study, it may be challenging to build in accommodations to help him. PT has yet to pass either CAHSEE exam. Swer spoke with PT this month regarding meeting with his principal once school commences to talk about earning credits via alternative methods.     9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Acton . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 18-6. Pt has started working at the movie theater, he states that he works full time hours and is able to meet all of his medical regimen.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Asher Jeng for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but was not interested, and now is 18 and no longer qualifies.     13. Eligibility for  federal, state and/or local resources: SSI, medi-cal and CCS.     Osbaldo Mullinix, MSW   Pgr: 18743

Cognitive status and capacity to understand: PT has a much better understanding of his diagnosis and treatment plan than he did back in 01/10/2014 when he began dialysis.Presents as an adult in charge of his treatment and able to manage and navigate care. He has expressed that he is ready for transplant, he is aware of what is required of him.     2. Ability to meet basic needs: Family is low income. MOC does not receive any support for her four kids from FOC and is getting by on about $700 a month. MOC utilizes family support as well as foodstamps to make it work. MOC receives SSDI benefits for PT which has been a tremendous financial help. MOC has works a house cleaner which she notes is hard work but has been helpful for her finances. Pt is now working at the movie theater he states it is full time. He is now driving and more independent with his treatments. He drives himself to HD and is now able to drive himself to all of his appointments.     3. Ability to follow the treatment prescription: PT reports following a renal diet and taking his supplements and multivitamins and trying protein shakes. Since he has begun dialyzing, PT has been on time and very compliant in terms of making his apts. He has made tremendous progress. He has made progress and done a good job of taking more responsibility in his medical condition. CCS transportation helps to get Theresa to monthly  visits.    4. Mental health history, capacities, and needs for counseling: PT is somewhat stoic but negates the need for counseling, presents as age appropriate. SSwer worries that PT does not have support at home and that he has not shared much of his experience with his family members. Whereas two months ago Theresa denied a kidney offer, today he states he is ready. He attributes his previous denial to timing, having just d/c from hospital and feeling that "everything was happening too fast" If asked today, Vosbikian states that he would accept the transplant and is looking forward to it.     5. Substance abuse history: none reported.    6. Current ability to cope with and adjust to dialysis:PT has been dialyzing at an outpatient clinic and appears to be attending, however he does not talk to his friends about this. PT works with social worker at Davita, Elston. PT has a tough demeanor but will answer questions politely when asked, and appears to appreciate opportunities to vent. His attitude has greatly improved. Team would like him to participate in post-txp psych protocol once transplanted during the time when he was living locally. He keeps his dialysis a secret from his peers, always wearing long sleeves to cover his fistula. His extended family however is aware of his condition.     7. Expectations for the future and living with kidney failure and treatment: Now that he is dialyzing on a regular schedule he would benefit from more information regarding transplant and the transplant process. He is blood type B and therefore may wait awhile if receiving a deceased donor txp, which swer discussed with PT today. He received an offer in summer 2015, which he declined, stating that he felt very scared and overwhelmed. However, after time to think about his choice he stated in clinic today that he is ready and open to transplant. He attributes his previous denial to timing, having just d/c from hospital and feeling that  "everything was happening too fast" If asked today, Theresa states that he would accept the transplant.    8. Educational and employment status, concerns and goals: PT is technically a senior at his high school (continuation) Olan Watt, though he has only 127/210 credits currently and dropped out before graduation. Pt is currently employed full time and SWer provided information on GED completion. MOC somewhat limited in her understanding of PT's school situation and ability to advocate for PT (re: role reversal). Swer spoke to principal Tyrel Fraley and came up with unique ideas for earning credits for PT by utilizing his time spent on dialysis towards earning credits. PT would benefit from a tutor as he endorses feeling unable to concentrate and complete tasks at home. As a student on independent study, it may be challenging to build in accommodations to help him. PT has yet to pass either CAHSEE exam. Swer spoke with PT this month regarding meeting with his principal once school commences to talk about earning credits via alternative methods.     9. Home environment including current living situation: Pt lives with MOC and three younger siblings in an apt in Oakland . Many extended family members live in the area and in their apt complex.    10. Legal issues: none known.     11. Financial capabilities and resources: MOC receives $700 dollars a month and relies on extended family for support. MOC is has begun part-time work and has her hands full as a single mom of four children ages 18-6. Pt has started working at the movie theater, he states that he works full time hours and is able to meet all of his medical regimen.     12. Access to available community resources: Swer connected PT and MOC to Nathanial Kern for CCS reimbursement for transportation and helped the family fill out logs this month. He has been referred to MAW but was not interested, and now is 18 and no longer qualifies.     13. Patient: Plonk: 01/06/1997   MRN: [000000]   Date of Service: 12/04/2016   Date of First Dialysis Treatment: 06/17/2013     Primary Nephrology Fellow:    Primary HD Nurse:      Lucile Packard Children's Hospital  Pediatric Dialysis  Interdisciplinary Comprehensive Patient Assessment and Plan of Care     Brief Identification  Quinn N Sims is a 19-year old male diagnosed with ANCA negative pauci-immune glomerulonephritis in 02/10/2013. Briefly, he had a history of persistent microscopic hematuria since age 6 to 7 and presented in 10/11/2012 with elevated creatinine of 3.1 with urinalysis showing proteinuria and hematuria. Workup revealed negative c-ANCA, negative p-ANCA, negative MPO, negative PR3, negative ANA, normal complement levels and a slightly elevated ESR. Further workup during his initial hospitalization at Lakewood  at Port Jefferson  in 03/13/2013 included a pulmonary consult, chest CT which revealed scattered pulmonary nodules which were nonspecific, but with normal spirometry. He has no evidence of pulmonary hemorrhage. He has seen ophthalmology in 03/13/2013 and had no signs of uveitis. A kidney biopsy was performed in 02/10/2013 at Children's Hospital Oakland, which showed 11/15 globally or near globally sclerosed glomeruli. Immunofluorescence was positive for 2+ C3 segmental sclerosis pattern, but otherwise negative. EM showed no evidence of Alport syndrome with podocytes showing mild patchy foot process effacement and therefore, the biopsy was consistent with chronic and subacute crescentic process with severe tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis more compatible with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.      In the past, rheumatology team recommended immunosuppression for systemic disease involving kidneys and lungs. He refused steroid treatment because of side effects. He was observed and managed only on antihypertensives and eventually progressed to  endstage renal disease and was started on hemodialysis in 06/10/2013. He was started on CellCept in 06/10/2013, which was self- discontinued in early 2016.     Quinn receives thrice weekly hemodialysis at DaVita in Akron  under the supervision of Dr. Ila Culpepper. Tiu returns to our clinic for monthly visit.      Patient Active Problem List   Diagnosis   • ESRD (end stage renal disease)   • Hypertension   • Hyperphosphatemia   • Anemia in CKD (chronic kidney disease)   • ROD (renal osteodystrophy)      Interval History:  Quinn was last seen in our Dialysis clinic in 10/11/2016. Since that time, he reports being healthy without any major intercurrent illnesses. He works from 1am - 9 am filling vending machines. He's been having sleeping difficulties after work and more recently on non-working days.         Quinn thinks he last saw Rheumatology at LPCH about 1 year ago; he last saw them in 05/11/2014. He stopped taking cellcept about 4 months ago. He hasn't had any other new symptoms such as gross hematuria, coughing, hemoptysis.     He has no complaints about dialysis today. He's had issues with HTN due to fluid overload, which has improved but still hypertensive requiring 4 anti-hypertensive agents. Our SW has been in communication with his DaVita center and has learned that Quinn has been asking for his HD time to be shortened or has been skipping scheduled HD intermittently. His dialysis MD has discussed this with him. We established a contract for transplant activation with the following requirements: he must go to dialysis and not miss any visits, come to this clinic every month and call our team back within less than 24 hours when we call him. He agreed that he would need to demonstrate this 5 out of 6 months in order for him to be activated for transplant. However, he has not been able to meet these activities consistently. One of his current barriers is his work schedule, which requires him to work from 1am - 9 am, but he enjoys his work. We discussed transferring his kidney transplant plan to Adult Kidney Transplant team at Stanford and he agrees with this. We will also completely transfer his ESRD/HD care to his adult nephrologist, therefore he does not need to return to our clinic at this time. He agrees with this.     It's been a great pleasure working with Salahuddin. Please do not hesitate to contact us with additional concerns/questions. In addition, a NT-proBNP < 300 pg/mL effectively rules out acute congestive heart failure, with a 98% negative predictive value.  In guiding  heart failure therapy, a rise or fall in NT-proBNP of 25% implies a biologically significant change in physiology.  The greatest prognostic value for NT-proBNP levels is observed 2 weeks after a therapy change. CT of the chest without any IV contrast revealed stable  large partially loculated right pleural effusion, right middle lobe and right  lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms.  The patient was started on  moxifloxacin and admitted for further care.  Potassium was elevated at 5.7.  Of note, the patient has been inconsistent with his dialysis as an  outpatient, occasionally has been losing weight.  Dry weight has been dropped  down from 70 to 65 kilograms.  Blood pressures have been elevated and his  clonidine dose has been recently increased.    PAST MEDICAL HISTORY  1.  End-stage kidney disease, status post kidney biopsy at age 12 at  Cullowhee . Was on the  transplant list, initially at the pediatric kidney  center now has been transferred to adult kidney transplant.  2.  Hypertension with recent elevation in his blood pressures.  3.  Anemia.  On erythropoietin stimulating agents.    FAMILY HISTORY  Unremarkable.    SOCIAL HISTORY  The patient was working previously.  No history of any tobacco or alcohol  use.    ALLERGIES  None.    MEDICATIONS  AT HOME  He is on;  1.  Clonidine 0.4 mg twice a day.  2.  Metoprolol 50 mg b.i.d.  3.  Lisinopril 20 p.o. b.i.d.  4.  Amlodipine 10 mg b.i.d.  5.  Renvela 800 mg 4 tablets with each meal.  6.  Cinacalcet 30 mg daily.  7.  He is also on Avelox now at 400 mg daily. PHYSICAL EXAMINATION  GENERAL:  Well-developed, young male.  VITAL SIGNS:  Blood pressures are 150-160/70.  NECK:  There is some adenopathy.  LUNGS:  Decreased breath sounds at the right bases.  HEART:  Regular rate rhythm, S1, S2 was normal.  ABDOMEN:  Soft.  EXTREMITIES:  No edema.  He has a left upper arm fistula with a good bruit  and thrill.    LABORATORIES  His potassium was 5.7, BUN 61, creatinine 8.4, sodium 129.  Albumin 3.4.  Troponin 0.04.  Influenza A and B were negative.  White count was 12,000. End-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis, currently with mild  hyperkalemia.  2.  Right pleural effusion with a right middle and lower lobe infiltrate  consistent with pneumonia. Anemia secondary to end-stage renal  disease.  5.  Hyperphosphatemia.    PLAN  1.  IV antibiotic therapy per her primary M.D.  2.  Pulmonary evaluation for thoracentesis.  3. DATE OF ADMISSION:    02/03/2017   PT. NAME:  Tuan, Tierra N    DATE OF CONSULTATION:     02/04/2017   99999999    CONSULTING PHYSICIAN:     Ayden Levinson, MD  ATTENDING PHYSICIAN:  Izaya Oliver, MD    REASON FOR CONSULTATION  Viral upper respiratory infection symptoms in a patient with end-stage renal  disease on hemodialysis with chronic right pleural effusion, question  pneumonia.    HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS  Mr. Tuan is a very pleasant 20-year-old male patient with a longstanding  history of end-stage renal disease (diagnosed at age 12, on hemodialysis via  left AV fistula for the past 2 years), history of hypertension, longstanding  history of chronic right-sided pleural effusion (present for at least 2  years), who was in his usual state of health until approximately 1 week ago  when he first developed mild sore throat, rhinorrhea, fatigue, orthopnea.  The patient denies any fevers or chills.  The patient also notes a mild cough  occasionally productive of yellow sputum.  Denies any hemoptysis.  Denies any  severe headache, trauma, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, UTI  symptoms, joint pains or rashes.    EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT COURSE  The patient was afebrile on arrival with a temperature of 99.7, heart rate  88, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 161/118.  Of note, patient's oxygen  saturation was 100% on ambient air on arrival and the patient did not require  any supplemental oxygen.  Based on patient's presenting symptoms, he was  given empiric Tamiflu and Avelox.  Initial labs were notable for a markedly  elevated BNP at 70,000, abnormal electrolytes and creatinine, and a white  blood cell count mildly elevated at 12.6 with 83% neutrophils.  Influenza PCR  became negative within a few hours and a chest x-ray showed a slight increase  in a moderately-sized, right-sided, pleural effusion as well as pulmonary  edema; note, that the pleural effusion was seen as far back as 02/10/2015, at  which point, the indication for that chest x-ray was "history of  pleural effusion," so it has likely been present for at least 2 years.  The  patient then had a CT chest, which showed a large, partially loculated, right  pleural effusion as well as patchy infiltrates.  The patient was admitted to  the hospital into the hospitalist service with empiric moxifloxacin which was  then brought into IV vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and doxycycline.    HOSPITAL COURSE  The patient remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable without any hypoxia  or signs of sepsis.  The patient underwent a thoracentesis which revealed  fluid, findings consistent with a transudative pleural effusion.  The Gram  stain showed no organisms and the culture is currently pending.  MRSA nares  PCR was negative.    PAST MEDICAL HISTORY  1.  End-stage renal disease diagnosed at age 12, based on biopsy, dependent  on hemodialysis via left AV fistula for the past 2 years.  2.  Hypertension.  3.  Chronic right pleural effusion.  4.  Anemia of chronic kidney disease.    PAST SURGICAL HISTORY  Status post left AV fistula 2 years ago.    MEDICATIONS PRIOR TO ADMISSION  1.  Clonidine 0.4 mg p.o. b.i.d.  2.  Metoprolol 50 mg p.o. b.i.d.  3.  Lisinopril 20 mg p.o. b.i.d.  4.  Amlodipine 10 mg p.o. b.i.d.  5.  Renvela 800 mg 4 tablets with each meal.  6.  Cinacalcet 30 mg daily.    DRUG ALLERGIES  None known.    FAMILY HISTORY  Reviewed and noncontributory.    SOCIAL HISTORY  The patient lives with his mother in Washington .  No pets.  No recent travel  or unusual exposures.  No known sick contacts.  The patient is unemployed.  Denies any alcohol, tobacco or illicit drug use.  Denies any history of IV  drug use.  Denies any sexual activity.    REVIEW OF SYSTEMS  A complete 14-point review of systems was reviewed with the patient.  It has  been negative with the exception as per HPI above.    PHYSICAL EXAMINATION  VITAL SIGNS:  Temperature 97.6, blood  pressure 128/66, heart rate 68,  respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.  GENERAL:  Mildly ill-appearing male patient sitting upright in bed in no  acute distress, nontoxic-appearing, speaks full sentences.  HEENT:  Extraocular muscles intact, anicteric sclerae, positive conjunctival  pallor.  Nares with bilateral edematous, erythematous, boggy turbinates with  mild congestion.  No sinus tenderness to palpation.  Oropharynx clear.  NECK:  Supple, no lymphadenopathy.  CHEST:  Diminished breath sounds and rhonchi over right posterior lung fields  with dullness to percussion at the right base, no wheezing, positive  bibasilar rales.  No accessory muscle use, no cough.  CARDIOVASCULAR:  Regular rate and rhythm.  No murmurs, rubs or gallops.  ABDOMEN:  Soft, nontender, nondistended, no appreciable hepatosplenomegaly.  Normoactive bowel sounds.  GENITOURINARY:  Normal-appearing external male genitalia without Vandemark  catheter, no lesions.  EXTREMITIES:  No clubbing, cyanosis or edema.  Left AV fistula present.  SKIN:  Warm, dry.  No rashes.  CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM:  Cranial nerves II-XII grossly intact, full strength  and sensation throughout.    LABORATORY DATA  LDH 284.  HIV negative.  Cold agglutinins 1:4.  PTT 44.9, white blood cell  count 13.6, hemoglobin 8.8, platelets 286.  Sodium 131, potassium 4.7,  chloride 80, bicarbonate 27, BUN 73, creatinine 9.29.  Glucose 112, ALT 17,  AST 16, alkaline phosphatase 59, T-bilirubin 0.4.    Thoracentesis fluid studies:  Gram stain shows no organisms.  Culture:  No  growth to date.  WBC 119 (8% PMNs, 90% monocytes).  Glucose 117, LDH 127.    MRSA nares negative.  Procalcitonin pending.    IMAGING  01/08, CT chest without contrast, reviewed per radiology:  "IMPRESSION:  1.  Stable, large, partially loculated right-sided pleural effusion.  2.  Right middle lobe and right lower lobe consolidation with air  bronchograms and patchy bilateral infiltrates elsewhere,  suspicious for  multifocal pneumonia."    02/03/2017, chest x-ray (compared to 09/06/2016), per radiology:  "IMPRESSION:  1.  Progression of moderate right-sided pleural effusion with progressive  right basilar consolidation.  2.  Mild-to-moderate pulmonary edema and patchy bilateral infiltrates."    02/17/2015, chest x-ray, per radiology:  "IMPRESSION:  1.  Mild increased density is present in the right lung base.  This is  consistent with any combination of atelectasis, infiltrate, and/or pleural  effusions.  2.  A central venous catheter is present on the right with the tip near the  cavoatrial junction.  3.  Otherwise unremarkable 2 views chest."    IMPRESSION  Mr. Tuan is a very pleasant 20-year-old male patient with a history of  end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and a past medical history  significant for known right-sided chronic pleural effusion that has been  present for at least the past 2 years, who presented to the Emergency  Department yesterday with mild viral upper respiratory infection symptoms and  found to have right-sided pleural effusion with possible consolidation and  patchy infiltrates.  The patient is status post thoracentesis, which revealed  a transudative effusion based on fluid analysis.  Etiology of chronic pleural  effusion is unknown, but likely secondary to end-stage renal disease, chronic  volume overload, as well as likely secondary to atelectasis and possibly  secondary to additional unknown etiology.  The patient has no clinical signs  or symptoms of atypical bacterial pneumonia.  The patient has not had any  fevers since his arrival and has not had any hypoxia or signs of sepsis.  I  suspect that the patient may have a superimposed atypical pneumonia versus  simple viral upper respiratory infection in the setting of a chronic  right-sided pleural effusion.    PROBLEM LIST  1.  Chronic pleural effusion that is transudative, unclear etiology:  Status  post thoracentesis  with Gram stain and culture currently negative.  2.  Approximately 1 week of viral URI symptoms including sore throat,  rhinorrhea and fatigue.  3.  Multifocal infiltrates, question atypical pneumonia versus secondary to  pulmonary edema:  Note, the patient has not had any hypoxia despite clear  evidence of volume overload and large pleural effusion and that the patient  has an MRSA PCR of the nares that is negative.  4.  Orthopnea, likely secondary to volume overload:  Improved with  hemodialysis.    RECOMMENDATIONS  1.  Discontinue IV vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam and oral  doxycycline.  2.  Okay from an infectious disease standpoint to discharge the patient home  on 5 days of oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for possible atypical pneumonia.  3.  Symptomatic treatment for viral URI symptoms.  4.  Follow up pending thoracentesis studies and consider outpatient  evaluation for further investigation into etiology of chronic pleural  effusion.    Discussed with Dr. Klos, who agrees.  Thank you for this interesting  consult.  Please call me with any further questions.    _________________________________      ___________________  Stanford Tubbs, MD                             Date/Time signed    JS D: 02/04/2017  tr T: 02/04/2017  Job#: [000000]  cc:   Azriel Kottra, MD        Gordon Cutright, MD

Negative - No significant  level of detectable Parvovirus  B19 IgG antibody.  0.90 - 1.10 IV ........... Equivocal - Repeat testing in  10-14 days may be helpful.  1.11 IV or greater ....... Positive - IgG antibody to  Parvovirus B19 detected which  may indicate a current or  past infection.  The best evidence for current infection is a significant change on  two appropriately timed specimens, where both tests are done in  the same laboratory at the same time. PARVOB19 IGM:0.10 IV; Normal Range:<=0.89  INTERPRETIVE INFORMATION: Parvovirus B19 Antibody, IgM  0.89 IV or less .......... Negative - No significant  level of detectable Parvovirus  B19 IgM antibody.  0.90 - 1.10 IV ........... Equivocal - Repeat testing in  10-14 days may be helpful.  1.11 IV or greater ........ Positive - IgM antibody to  Parvovirus B19 detected which  may indicate a current or  recent infection. However, low  levels of IgM antibodies may  occasionally persist for more  than 12 months post-infection.  The best evidence for current infection is a significant change on  two appropriately timed specimens, where both tests are done in  the same laboratory at the same time.  Appearance of an IgM antibody response normally occurs 7 to 14  days after the onset of disease. Testing immediately post-exposure  is of no value without a later convalescent specimen. A residual  IgM response may be distinguished from early IgM response to  infection by testing sera from patients three to four weeks later  for changing levels of specific IgM antibodies. 04/23/2017        Earline Ning, MD   Chabot Nephrology Medical Group   5720 Menahga , Suite 61 Oconee Bell Ct, Seneca SC     RE: Turk, Tomeka N  MRN: [000000]  DOB: 01/06/1997  DOS: 04/23/2017    Dear Dr. Grewal,     I had the pleasure of meeting your patient Tomeka Turk, a 20-year-old, Hispanic male, currently listed for transplantation at the Lucile Packard Children's Hospital at the Stanford Adult Kidney Transplant Evaluation Clinic. He was unaccompanied. Tomeka additionally met with our transplant nurse coordinator and social worker, and viewed in educational video on kidney transplantation.     To review his history for our records, the patient had been incidentally noted to have microscopic hematuria on a routine physical examination when he was approximately 6-7 years of age. In 06/10/2012, he was noted to be hypertensive as well and was referred to the pediatric nephrology service at Everett , where he was first seen in 10/11/2012. At that time, he was found to have a significant degree of proteinuria and hematuria, and had a serum creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL, and BUN of 37 mg/dL. ANA and complement levels were normal. C-ANCA, T-ANCA and PR3 titers were unremarkable. MPO was less than 0.2. His PTH was a bit elevated. Renal ultrasonography showed mild increase in echogenicity of both kidneys, and the corticomedullary differentiation was slightly less than normal. There was no hydronephrosis or hydroureter. The right renal length was 10.9 cm and the left, 10.8 cm. There was a small cyst measuring 7 mm in diameter in the upper pole of the left kidney.     In 02/10/2013 the patient underwent a percutaneous native kidney biopsy at Mondovi  in Freeport  which was reviewed by the pathology department at Stanford. Light microscopy showed that 11/15 glomeruli were nearly globally sclerosed. The remaining glomeruli were normal in size without evidence of any mesangial or  endocapillary proliferation. Basement membranes were normal in thickness and contour. There were no deposits on light microscopy. Tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis was seen involving at least 70% of the sampled cortex. Immunofluorescence was largely negative. Electron microscopy showed no abnormality other than patchy mild foot process effacement. The biopsy was consistent with chronic and subacute crescentic process with severe tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis more compatible with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. The patient also developed bronchospasm at that time. A chest CT scan revealed non specific subcentimeter scattered pulmonary nodules, which the pulmonary team thought might be an indication for underlying scarring. Spirometry was normal. There was no evidence of pulmonary hemorrhage. He was seen at the Ophthalmology Clinic, but had no evidence of uveitis. Echocardiography was within normal limits. There was no evidence of pulmonary hypertension or pericardial effusion. A repeat CT scan on 07/16/2013 showed that the pulmonary nodules were stable and unchanged, and nonspecific, mostly subpleural in location. There were no areas of cavitation or  ground-glass opacification. There were no pleural effusions or pneumothorax.     He had been evaluated for kidney transplantation at the Lucile Packard Children's Hospital on 04/16/2013, however, at that time, exhibited lack of commitment for lifelong immunosuppression and demonstrated noncompliance to clinic visits and medications. It was determined that he was not a candidate for transplantation at that time. He eventually initiated maintenance hemodialysis on 06/23/2013, by means of a tunneled hemodialysis catheter. He was transitioned from Bryce  at Stanford to the DaVita dialysis unit in Placerville  which was closer to his home. Repeat echocardiography (04/21/2014) showed a normal cardiac examination, and  normal cardiac function and wall thickness. There was no pericardial effusion. He is currently dialyzed for 3 hours 3 times a week and has a dry weight of 64 kg. His 24 hour urine production is approximately 4 ounces and he is dialyzed by means of a left Birdsong AV fistula which had been constructed 2 years ago.    The patient was hospitalized at the Valley Care Medical Center in early 04/10/2017, some 3-1/2 weeks ago, with acute respiratory failure with hypoxia secondary to a drug overdose. He also had apparently experienced a cardiac arrest. He states that he had smoked some marijuana that had been laced with "something." The details of that hospitalization, however, are unavailable to me. He denies any history of cocaine use or methamphetamine use, and denies any history of intravenous drug use. He denies any history of diabetes, stroke, seizures, headaches, peptic ulcer disease, venous thrombosis, or pulmonary emboli.    Current Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg b.i.d., clonidine 0.2 mg b.i.d., vitamin D 2000 international units daily, Renvela 800 mg tablets 4 p.o. t.i.d. with meals, Pollard 30 mg daily, Toprol 25 mg b.i.d., Dialyvite 1 daily.    Allergies: None known.    Transfusion History: 2 units, 2 weeks ago.     Past Medical History:   1. Childhood asthma, resolved.  2. History of seasonal allergies.  3. Microscopic hematuria and proteinuria.  4. Biopsy documented ANCA-negative pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.  5. End-stage kidney disease.  6. Pulmonary nodules, stable.  7. Status post placement of tunneled dialysis catheters at least twice.  8. History of Staphylococcus epidermidis catheter exit site infection.  9. Status post construction of left Abate AV fistula.  10. Secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal etiology.  11. Vitamin D deficiency.  12. Anemia of chronic kidney disease.  13. History of accidental drug overdose with acute respiratory failure and cardiac arrest, 04/10/2017.    Social History: The  patient was born in San Tomeka and raised in Burlington , California. He has an 11th grade education, but plans to get his GED. He had to drop out of school secondary to illness. He lives with his mother, 2 brothers and a sister. He works for a vending service, stocking vending machines for Facebook, and drives a van. He denies any history of tobacco or alcohol use, however, has smoked marijuana since age 16. He recently was hospitalized with apparently an accidental drug overdose after smoking marijuana which had been laced with an unknown agent. Hobbies include listening to music and in the past he played soccer.    Family History: His mother is 40 years of age and in good health. He has 2 brothers and 1 sister, all younger and in good health. He has a 42-year-old father, with whom he keeps in touch with, who also lives in the San Tomeka area, who apparently is in good health.    Review Of Systems: Constitutional: Maximum weight was 170 pounds and he now weighs 150 pounds. He denies chronic fevers, chills or night sweats. HEENT: He denies hearing loss, tinnitus, double or blurry vision, epistaxis, sinusitis, odynophagia, dysphagia or hoarseness. He does have a history of seasonal allergies. Endocrine: Denies history of thyroid disease or diabetes. He has secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal etiology. Pulmonary: Denies chronic shortness of breath or cough. He did have a history of childhood asthma which has resolved, and he no longer required bronchodilators. He also has stable pulmonary nodules noted on 2 CT scans. Cardiovascular: Denies exertional chest pain or pressure, palpitations, or syncope. He apparently experienced a cardiac arrest during a hospitalization in early 04/10/2017 for an accidental drug overdose. GI: Denies chronic nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hematemesis, melena, rectal bleeding or jaundice. GU: See above. The patient has a history of end-stage kidney disease, secondary to  pauci-immune glomerulonephritis and is on maintenance hemodialysis. He denies gross hematuria, although has microscopic hematuria. He also has proteinuria. Neurological: Denies focal sensory motor loss or seizures.    Physical examination: Blood pressure 111/55 mmHg, Pulse 73 reguular, Temp 36.7, weight 64.5 kg, BMI 19. Results called to and read back by: Chowdhary P./DG. eGFR:3 mL/min  In most healthy people, the normal GFR is 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 or higher. A result of 60-89 mL/min/1.73 m2 without kidney damage may be normal in some people (such as the elderly, and infants). A result of 60-89 mL/min/1.73 m2 for three months or more, along with kidney damage, means the person has early kidney disease. When GFR is <60 for three months or more, chronic kidney disease is present. The MDRD calculated eGFR should be multiplied by 1.21 for African Americans. Procedure:                Pre-Anesthesia Assessment:                           - Prior to the procedure, a History and Physical                            was performed, and patient medications, allergies                            and sensitivities were reviewed. The patient's                            tolerance of previous anesthesia was reviewed.                           - The risks and benefits of the procedure and the                            sedation options and risks were discussed with the                            patient. After obtaining informed consent, the endoscope was                            passed under direct vision. Throughout the                            procedure, the patient's blood pressure, pulse, and                            oxygen saturations were monitored continuously. The                            GIF HQ190 [000000] was introduced through the mouth,                            with the intention of advancing to the duodenum.                            The scope was advanced to the second part of the                            duodenum before the procedure was aborted.                            Medications were not given. The patient tolerated                            the procedure fairly well. The upper GI endoscopy                            was somewhat difficult due to the patient's                            combativeness. Successful completion of the                            procedure was aided by increasing the dose of                            sedation medication. Biopsies were taken       with a cold forceps for histology.      The examined duodenum was normal. Impression:               - No specimens collected. Recommendation:           - Use Protonix (pantoprazole) 40 mg PO daily for 4                            weeks. Pre and postoperative diagnosis: Subtotal clotting of the left forearm arteriovenous fistula.    Name of the operations: #1 fistulogram #2 thrombolytic therapy.    Findings there was subtotal clotting at the midportion of an aneurysmal left forearm arteriovenous fistula.    Description of the operation the patient was placed in the angiographic suite and given moderate sedation with 50 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of Versed.  Chlorhexidine prep and sterile drapes placed.  2% lidocaine infiltrated proximally and a 7 French sheath was placed over the needle and guidewire.  5000 u of heparin were given, a fistulogram was performed mapping the pathology.  I then advanced a Enid Farnsworth catheter placed into the clot and => 2 mg of TPA in 20 cc of saline at the same time as I was massaging the clotted area there was complete resolution of the clot after the thrombolytic therapy was completed.  The procedure was terminated by placing a suture of 5-0 Prolene at the insertion site and sterile dressings applied the patient transferred to recovery stable condition no complications, blood loss 1 mL contrast given 20 mL

After Your Surgery: Hemodialysis   What to expect at home with your dialysis  Your recovery  Hemodialysis is a way to remove your body¿s wastes from the blood when your kidneys can no longer do the job. It is not a cure, but it can help you live longer and feel better. It is a lifesaving treatment when you have kidney failure.  Hemodialysis is often called dialysis. Your doctor created a place (called an access) in your arm for your blood to flow in and out of your body during your dialysis sessions.  This access site will be 1 of 2 types: a fistula or a graft. After this surgery to create the access, your arm will probably be bruised and swollen. It may hurt. The cut (incision) may bleed.  The pain and bleeding will get better over several days. You will probably need only over-the-counter (nonprescription) pain medicine. You can reduce swelling by propping your arm on 1 or 2 pillows and keeping your elbow straight.  You will have stitches. These may dissolve on their own, or your health care team will tell you when to come in to have them removed. You should also be able to return to work in a few days.  You may feel some coolness or numbness in your hand. These feelings usually go away in a few weeks.  Your health care team may suggest squeezing a soft object. This will strengthen your access and may make hemodialysis faster and easier.  You should always be able to feel blood rushing through the fistula or graft. It feels like a slight vibration when you put your fingers on the skin over the fistula or graft. This feeling is called a thrill or pulse.  This care sheet gives you a general idea about how long it will take for you to recover. But each person recovers at a different pace. Follow the steps below to get better as quickly as possible.  How can you care for yourself at home?   Activity     · Rest when you feel tired. Getting enough sleep will help you recover. Do not lie on or sleep on the arm with the  access site.  · Avoid activities such as washing windows or gardening that put stress on the arm with the access site.  · You may use your arm, but do not lift anything that weighs more than about 15 lbs. This may include a child, heavy grocery bags, a heavy briefcase or backpack, cat litter or dog food bags, or a vacuum cleaner.  · You can shower, but keep the access site dry for the first 2 days. Cover the area with a plastic bag to keep it dry when you shower.  · Do not soak or scrub the incision until it has healed. Avoid swimming or soaking in a tub for at least 6 weeks after your surgery.  · Wear an arm guard to protect the area if you play sports or work with your arms.You may drive when your doctor says it is okay. This is usually in 1 to 2 days. Avoid driving if you are taking pain medicine.  · Most people are able to return to work about 1 or 2 days after surgery.    Food     · Follow an eating plan that is good for your kidneys. A registered dietitian can help you make a meal plan that is right for you. You may need to limit protein, salt, fluids, and certain foods.    Medicines     · Your health care team will tell you if and when you can restart your medicines. Team members will also give you instructions about taking any new medicines. You can restart your prescription medicines the day after your surgery.  · If you take blood thinners such as warfarin (Coumadin), clopidogrel (Plavix), or aspirin, be sure to talk to your health care team. Team members will tell you if and when to start taking those medicines again.  · Make sure that you understand exactly what your health care team wants you to do. Restart your blood thinners the day after your surgery, unless you have a big bruise around your surgical site.  · Take pain medicines exactly as directed.  ? If the doctor gave you a prescription medicine for pain, take it as prescribed. Do not drive if you are taking pain medication.  ? If you are not  taking a prescription pain medicine, ask your doctor if you can take acetaminophen (Tylenol). Do not take ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve), or similar medicines, unless your doctor tells you to. They may make chronic kidney disease worse.  ? Do not take 2 or more pain medicines at the same time unless the doctor told you to. Many pain medicines have acetaminophen, which is Tylenol. Too much acetaminophen (Spanish Fort ) can be harmful.  · If you think your pain medicine is making you sick to your stomach:  ? Take your medicine after meals (unless your doctor has told you not to).  ? Ask your doctor for a different pain medicine.  · If your doctor prescribed antibiotics, take them as directed. Do not stop taking them just because you feel better. You need to take the full course of antibiotics.    Incision care     · Keep the area dry for 2 days. After 2 days, wash the area with soap and water every day, and always before dialysis. Pat the area dry after showering.  · Do not soak or scrub the incision until it has healed, usually at least 6 weeks after your surgery.  · If you have a bandage, change it every day or as often as your care team recommends. Your health care team will tell you when you can remove it.         Exercise     · Squeeze a soft ball or other object as often as your care team tells you. This will help blood flow through the access site and help prevent blood clots.  · Avoid lifting heavy objects more than 10 to 15 lbs with the arm that has your fistula or graft for at least 6 weeks after your surgery.  Elevation  · · Prop up the sore arm on a pillow anytime you sit or lie down during the first 3 days after surgery. Try to keep it above the level of your heart. This will help reduce swelling.    Other instructions     · Every day, check your access site for a pulse or thrill in the fistula or graft area. A thrill is a vibration.  · To feel a pulse or thrill, place the first 2 fingers of your  hand over the access site. If you don¿t feel the thrill, your fistula or graft might be clotted. If so, call the vascular clinic at (999-999-9999. We might request an ultrasound test to make sure that it is not blocked.  · If you have a fistula in place and the dialysis team has trouble using it, your dialysis nurse will call us within 72 hours. Your dialysis care team will determine if we need to fix it.  · If you are having pain from the access site, or the flow is low, your dialysis nurse will call us within 72 hours.  · If you have a graft access site and had problems using it, call our clinic at (999-999-9999 within 24 hours.  · Do not bump your arm.  · Do not wear tight clothing, jewelry, or anything else that may squeeze the access site.  · Use your other arm to have blood drawn or blood pressure taken.  · Do not put cream or lotion on or near the access site.  · Make sure all doctors you deal with know you have a dialysis access site.   Follow-up care is a key part of your treatment and safety. Be sure to make and go to all appointments, and call your health care team if you are having problems.  It's also a good idea to know your test results and keep a list of the medicines you take.  You need to have an office appointment 2 weeks after your surgery for a wound check. Also make an appointment for 6 to 8 weeks after surgery. Your team will follow up with an ultrasound test and check if your fistula or graft is ready for access.  If your fistula or graft was used during dialysis several times without problems, ask your kidney doctor if it is okay to remove the catheter on your neck. If it is ready to be pulled, your dialysis nurse will call us to schedule your catheter removal.  When should you call for help?   Call 911 anytime you think you may need emergency care. For example, call if:  · You passed out (lost consciousness).  · You have chest pain, are short of breath, or cough up blood.  Call your  health care team now at (999-999-9999 or seek immediate medical care if:  · Your hand or arm is cold or dark-colored.  · You have no pulse in your access site.  · You have nausea or you vomit.  · You have pain that does not get better after you take pain medicine.  · You have loose stitches, or your incision comes open.  · You are bleeding from the incision.  · You have signs of infection, such as:  ? Increased pain, swelling, warmth, or redness  ? Red streaks leading from the area  ? Pus draining from the area  ? A fever  · You have signs of a blood clot in your leg (called a deep vein thrombosis), such as:  ? Pain in your calf, back of the knee, thigh, or groin  ? Redness or swelling in your leg  Watch closely for changes in your health, and be sure to contact your health care team if you have any problems.   Where can you learn more?
