CANCER GENETIC COUNSELING CONSULTATION    IDENTIFICATION  Referring provider: Dr. Dudley of visit: 02/18/2017    Ms. Struble, a 45 Y of Caucasian descent, was seen in consultation for this Cancer Genetics evaluation. This visit included risk evaluation, genetic counseling and coordination of genetic testing. A total of 60 minutes was spent with the patient, all of which were spent in counseling and coordination of care.    ONCOLOGY HISTORY  Ms. Sink is a 45 Y with no personal history of cancer, who presents today because of her family history, as detailed below.    Past Medical History: No significant past medical history contributory to the hereditary cancer assessment.    Social History:    Ms. Sink is married and has three children, a son, age 16, and two daughters, ages 13 and 9. She is a physician at the VA specializing in internal medicine.     Family History:   See attached pedigree for details. Unless otherwise noted, family history is by patient and/or family report.   · Mother with lymphoma at 56, meningioma at 59, pituitary tumor causing Bianca's disease, and a hx of hyperparathyroidism; alive at 69.; total abdominal hysterectomy and oophorectomy at 45 years, which would have reduced her risk of endometrial, ovarian and breast cancer.   · Sister with adrenal tumor causing Cushing¿s syndrome, alive at 43.  · Maternal grandfather with chronic lymphocytic leukemia at 50, died at 75.   · Maternal grandmother¿s mother with lung cancer at 92, non-smoker, died at 92.   · Paternal aunt with breast cancer in her 70¿s, alive at 86.   · Paternal uncle with prostate cancer in his 70¿s, alive at 82.   · Paternal grandmother with breast cancer at 65, died at 82.     Maternal Ethnicity: Polish AJ  Paternal Ethnicity: Russian AJ  Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry: Yes  Consanguinity: No    Cancer Risk Factors   Age at Menarche 14   Age at Menopause N/A   Parity and Age at First Birth G4P3; 29   Total  Time breast feeding 36 months   Oral Contraceptives 10 years   Hysterectomy/Oophorectomy? No   Age at First Mammogram 40   Self-Breast Exam Sometimes   Breast Biopsy No   Hormone Replacement Therapy No   Colonoscopy No   Polyp number/size/histology No   Smoking Never   Alcohol (per week) No   Radiation exposure No   Exercise 3x/week; tennis       Previous germline cancer genetic testing No prior hereditary cancer genetic testing     RISK ASSESSMENT  Most cases of cancer do not have a strong hereditary basis, yet it is important to identify the relatively rare families in which there is a hereditary predisposition. Identifying such families allows for prevention and early detection strategies. Hereditary cancer risk assessment begins with review of personal and family history.  Often, genetic testing is helpful in assessing risk. There are several approaches to genetic testing, from analysis of a single gene to analyzing multiple genes, depending upon the risk assessment.     Approximately 10% of cancers are considered to have a hereditary cause.  Ms. Sink's family history is suggestive of a hereditary basis.  We discussed the most likely hereditary cancer genes in which a mutation could explain Ms. Sink's family history of cancer.      Hereditary Breast Cancer  Breast cancer is the most common cancer in American women, occurring in 12.5% of the general population. Most breast cancers are not due to strong hereditary factors. Only about 5 - 10% of breast cancers diagnosed in women have a hereditary cause. The most common cause of inherited risk for breast cancer are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Mutations in these two genes are present in 1/400-1/800 individuals in the general population and 1/40 individuals of Eastern European (Ashkenazi) Jewish descent. Women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations have significantly elevated breast and ovarian cancer risks, and men have elevated risks for prostate cancer  as well as male breast cancer. Mutations in other genes (e.g. TP53, CDH1, PTEN, STK11, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2) also predispose to breast and other cancers.        Hereditary cancer genetic testing panels are clinically available for patients and allow for the detection of mutations that could potentially explain a cancer family history. The goal of the testing is cancer prevention and early cancer detection in families.    ¿ Ms. Sink meets the guidelines of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network for BRCA1/BRCA2 genetic testing.    · Of note, we also briefly reviewed the small chance that a mutation in the MEN1 gene could be underlying her mother's history of hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumor and her sister's adrenal tumor. Therefore testing considerations for the maternal family could also include the MEN1 gene.     INHERITANCE AND FAMILIAL IMPLICATIONS  Mutations in most hereditary cancer genes follow an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.  Therefore, in most cases there is a 50% chance that the mutation would pass to a child with each pregnancy.  Identifying a mutation may mean that all other blood relatives are at-risk to carry it as well.  The gene mutation does not skip generations and typically it has been present in a family for many generations.  The gene mutation is inherited equally by males and females.  When genetic testing is negative/uninformative, we presume a higher risk of cancer for close family members based on the family history alone.      GENETIC TESTING  The potential benefits, risks and limitations of DNA testing were discussed.  There are three potential results. We discussed the possible test outcomes of a positive result (a pathogenic gene mutation is identified), a negative result (no pathogenic mutations), identifying one or more genetic variants of uncertain significance (a change is found but its effect on the gene function and cancer risk is currently unknown or  uncertain).  In addition, we discussed the possibility of identifying a gene mutation that is not consistent with Ms. Sink's personal or family history.  We discussed the benefits and limitations to multi-gene panel testing versus testing for single disorders.       It is important to note that genetic testing is always most informative when pursued by an individual with a personal history of cancer. If Ms. Sink pursued genetic testing and results were negative, we would not be able to determine if she did not inherit a mutation that is present in the family or if there is no currently identifiable mutation that explains her family history. Therefore, the most informative relatives to undergo genetic testing would be her paternal aunt and her mother. She thinks it less likely that her paternal aunt would consider testing at this time, thus testing is appropriate and medically indicated for Ms. Stanley.    After reviewing the testing options, Ms. Zeitz chose not to pursue genetic testing at the time of our consultation. She expressed that she wanted to take a few days to consider her options further and that she will contact me with her decision. If Ms. Sink decides to move forward with genetic testing, she expressed being interested in pursuing the following test:     Multi-gene cancer risk panel through Invitae Laboratories. This includes analysis of the following 44 genes: APC, ATM, AXIN2, BARD1, BMPR1A, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDH1, CDKN2A, CDK4, CHEK2, DICER1, EPCAM, GREM1, KIT, MEN1, MLH1, MRE11A, MSH2, MSH6, Chandler , NBN, NF1, PALB2, PDGFRA, PMS2, POLD1, POLE, PTEN, RAD50, RAD51C, RAD51D, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SMAD4, SMARCA4, STK11, TP53, TSC1, TSC2, VHL    We discussed that we would expect results in approximately 3-4 weeks from the release of testing. Some laboratories require patient consent to out-of-pocket amount prior to the sample being released for testing, which can delay the start of  testing.      SCREENING AND PREVENTION FOR INDIVIDUALS AT HEREDITARY CANCER RISK  We briefly reviewed that medical management options available to individuals at hereditary cancer risk may include earlier and increased surveillance, the possibility of risk-reducing surgery and/or risk-reducing medications. If genetic testing identifies a pathogenic gene mutation, specific medical management recommendations will be reviewed with the cancer genetics physician at a subsequent appointment.      CANCER RISKS AND SCREENING FOR INDIVIDUALS BASED ON FAMILY HISTORY  Some families decide not to pursue testing or undergo genetic testing and no mutations are found despite a significant family history of cancer.  In these families, the cancer risk remains genetically unexplained, but there remains a higher risk for cancer.  In this scenario, medical management is based on personal and family history.      Breast cancer screening considerations based on family history  The future breast cancer risk for Ms. Sink is estimated to be 21.7% using the Tyrer-Cuzick (IBIS) model. The American Cancer Society recommends that women who have an estimated lifetime breast cancer risk of greater than or equal to 20-25% undergo annual screening with breast MRI in addition to annual mammogram.  Breast MRI is typically recommended to start ten years prior to the earliest age of breast cancer diagnosis in the family or by age 40y, whichever is earlier. Mammograms are also recommended to begin ten years younger than the earliest diagnosis in the family, but not prior to the age of 30y.  Clinical breast exams are completed twice per year and monthly self-breast exams are encouraged. Ms. Sink can discuss this level of screening with her providers. An appointment with our cancer genetics physician is available should she be interested in a more detailed discussion.     Probability of ovarian cancer based on family history  The average risk for  a woman in the general population to develop ovarian (fallopian/primary peritoneal) cancer is 1 - 2%. If genetic testing is negative, Ms. Sink¿s risk for ovarian cancer is not expected to be higher than that of the general population as she does not have a family history of ovarian cancer. Screening and prevention options are generally not needed for women at average risk for ovarian cancer.    Other medical management considerations based on family history  Ms. Sink should report the family history of other cancer/tumor types (lymphoma, leukemia, meningioma, pituitary tumor, adrenal tumor) to her providers so she can be monitored appropriately. This additional family history does not necessarily prompt consideration for any additional screenings, given that the additional family history is not expected to confer a significantly increased empiric risk for these other cancers.     PSYCHOLOGICAL AND SOCIAL CONSIDERATIONS  Cancer risk assessment and genetic testing can provoke strong personal emotions and complex family interactions.  We encourage patients to identify people who can offer support during this process. We are available to discuss personal concerns further or to identify peer or professional counseling resources.     GENETIC INFORMATION NONDISCRIMINATION ACT (GINA) 2008  GINA is a federal law that protects Americans from discrimination by health insurance companies and employers based on their genetic information.  For more information, please visit www.ginahelp.org     SUMMARY  Ms. Sink is a 45 Y year old female with a family history of cancer that is suggestive of an inherited cancer predisposition. Ms. Sink would like to further consider the benefits, limitations, and considerations before making a decision about undergoing genetic testing to define her future cancer risks and management options. Genetic counseling was provided and all questions and concerns were answered and addressed.      PLAN:  · Ms. Sink will contact our clinic once a decision about genetic testing has been made  · If genetic testing is chosen, a time would be arranged for the patient to come back to have her blood drawn. Once collected, the sample would be sent to Invitae for testing a panel of multiple hereditary cancer genes.  · Results would become available in approximately 3-4 weeks from the release of testing.   · We would contact Ms. Sink by phone with the results  · If a gene mutation were identified, we would schedule Ms. Sink for a return visit to review medical recommendations and familial implications with one of our cancer genetics physicians  · If the results were negative or a variant of uncertain significance were identified, we would send Ms. Sink a letter reviewing the results.    Weldon Clardy, MS, LCGC,  Licensed Genetic Counselor

Only about 5 - 10% of breast cancers diagnosed in women have a hereditary cause. The most common cause of inherited risk for breast cancer are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Mutations in these two genes are present in 1/400-1/800 individuals in the general population and 1/40 individuals of Eastern European (Ashkenazi) Jewish descent. Women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations have significantly elevated breast and ovarian cancer risks, and men have elevated risks for prostate cancer as well as male breast cancer. Mutations in other genes (e.g. TP53, CDH1, PTEN, STK11, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2) also predispose to breast and other cancers.        Hereditary cancer genetic testing panels are clinically available for patients and allow for the detection of mutations that could potentially explain a cancer family history. The goal  of the testing is cancer prevention and early cancer detection in families.    ¿ Ms. Saez meets the guidelines of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network for BRCA1/BRCA2 genetic testing.    · Of note, we also briefly reviewed the small chance that a mutation in the MEN1 gene could be underlying her mother's history of hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumor and her sister's adrenal tumor. Therefore testing considerations for the maternal family could also include the MEN1 gene.     INHERITANCE AND FAMILIAL IMPLICATIONS  Mutations in most hereditary cancer genes follow an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.  Therefore, in most cases there is a 50% chance that the mutation would pass to a child with each pregnancy.  Identifying a mutation may mean that all other blood relatives are at-risk to carry it as well.  The gene mutation does not skip generations and typically it has been present in a family for many generations.  The gene mutation is inherited equally by males and females.  When genetic testing is negative/uninformative, we presume a higher risk of cancer for close family members based on the family history alone.      GENETIC TESTING  The potential benefits, risks and limitations of DNA testing were discussed.  There are three potential results. We discussed the possible test outcomes of a positive result (a pathogenic gene mutation is identified), a negative result (no pathogenic mutations), identifying one or more genetic variants of uncertain significance (a change is found but its effect on the gene function and cancer risk is currently unknown or uncertain).  In addition, we discussed the possibility of identifying a gene mutation that is not consistent with Ms. Saez's personal or family history.  We discussed the benefits and limitations to multi-gene panel testing versus testing for single disorders.       It is important to note that genetic testing is always most informative when  pursued by an individual with a personal history of cancer. If Ms. Saez pursued genetic testing and results were negative, we would not be able to determine if she did not inherit a mutation that is present in the family or if there is no currently identifiable mutation that explains her family history. Therefore, the most informative relatives to undergo genetic testing would be her paternal aunt and her mother. She thinks it less likely that her paternal aunt would consider testing at this time, thus testing is appropriate and medically indicated for Ms. Saez.    After reviewing the testing options, Ms. Saez chose not to pursue genetic testing at the time of our consultation. She expressed that she wanted to take a few days to consider her options further and that she will contact me with her decision. If Ms. Saez decides to move forward with genetic testing, she expressed being interested in pursuing the following test:     Multi-gene cancer risk panel through Invitae Laboratories. This includes analysis of the following 44 genes: APC, ATM, AXIN2, BARD1, BMPR1A, BRCA1, BRCA2, BRIP1, CDH1, CDKN2A, CDK4, CHEK2, DICER1, EPCAM, GREM1, KIT, MEN1, MLH1, MRE11A, MSH2, MSH6, Aiken , NBN, NF1, PALB2, PDGFRA, PMS2, POLD1, POLE, PTEN, RAD50, RAD51C, RAD51D, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SMAD4, SMARCA4, STK11, TP53, TSC1, TSC2, VHL    We discussed that we would expect results in approximately 3-4 weeks from the release of testing. Some laboratories require patient consent to out-of-pocket amount prior to the sample being released for testing, which can delay the start of testing.      SCREENING AND PREVENTION FOR INDIVIDUALS AT HEREDITARY CANCER RISK  We briefly reviewed that medical management options available to individuals at hereditary cancer risk may include earlier and increased surveillance, the possibility of risk-reducing surgery and/or risk-reducing medications. If genetic testing identifies a pathogenic  gene mutation, specific medical management recommendations will be reviewed with the cancer genetics physician at a subsequent appointment.      CANCER RISKS AND SCREENING FOR INDIVIDUALS BASED ON FAMILY HISTORY  Some families decide not to pursue testing or undergo genetic testing and no mutations are found despite a significant family history of cancer.  In these families, the cancer risk remains genetically unexplained, but there remains a higher risk for cancer.  In this scenario, medical management is based on personal and family history.      Breast cancer screening considerations based on family history  The future breast cancer risk for Ms. Saez is estimated to be 21.7% using the Tyrer-Cuzick (IBIS) model. The American Cancer Society recommends that women who have an estimated lifetime breast cancer risk of greater than or equal to 20-25% undergo annual screening with breast MRI in addition to annual mammogram.  Breast MRI is typically recommended to start ten years prior to the earliest age of breast cancer diagnosis in the family or by age 40y, whichever is earlier. Mammograms are also recommended to begin ten years younger than the earliest diagnosis in the family, but not prior to the age of 30y.  Clinical breast exams are completed twice per year and monthly self-breast exams are encouraged. Ms. Saez can discuss this level of screening with her providers. An appointment with our cancer genetics physician is available should she be interested in a more detailed discussion.     Probability of ovarian cancer based on family history  The average risk for a woman in the general population to develop ovarian (fallopian/primary peritoneal) cancer is 1 - 2%. If genetic testing is negative, Ms. Saez¿s risk for ovarian cancer is not expected to be higher than that of the general population as she does not have a family history of ovarian cancer. Screening and prevention options are generally not  needed for women at average risk for ovarian cancer.    Other medical management considerations based on family history  Ms. Theis should report the family history of other cancer/tumor types (lymphoma, leukemia, meningioma, pituitary tumor, adrenal tumor) to her providers so she can be monitored appropriately. This additional family history does not necessarily prompt consideration for any additional screenings, given that the additional family history is not expected to confer a significantly increased empiric risk for these other cancers.     PSYCHOLOGICAL AND SOCIAL CONSIDERATIONS  Cancer risk assessment and genetic testing can provoke strong personal emotions and complex family interactions.  We encourage patients to identify people who can offer support during this process. We are available to discuss personal concerns further or to identify peer or professional counseling resources.     GENETIC INFORMATION NONDISCRIMINATION ACT (GINA) 2008  GINA is a federal law that protects Americans from discrimination by health insurance companies and employers based on their genetic information.  For more information, please visit www.ginahelp.org     SUMMARY  Ms. Saez is a 45 Y year old female with a family history of cancer that is suggestive of an inherited cancer predisposition. Ms. Saez would like to further consider the benefits, limitations, and considerations before making a decision about undergoing genetic testing to define her future cancer risks and management options. Genetic counseling was provided and all questions and concerns were answered and addressed.     PLAN:  · Ms. Saez will contact our clinic once a decision about genetic testing has been made  · If genetic testing is chosen, a time would be arranged for the patient to come back to have her blood drawn. Once collected, the sample would be sent to Invitae for testing a panel of multiple hereditary cancer genes.  · Results would  become available in approximately 3-4 weeks from the release of testing.   · We would contact Ms. Saez by phone with the results  · If a gene mutation were identified, we would schedule Ms. Vaidya for a return visit to review medical recommendations and familial implications with one of our cancer genetics physicians  · If the results were negative or a variant of uncertain significance were identified, we would send Ms. Sundermann a letter reviewing the results.    Kushnir Nolder-Petrone, MS, LCGC,  Licensed Genetic Counselor

General recommendations:  Please sign up for myHealth portal at: www.example.com    Annual exams are recommended yearly . If you have any prescribed medication you need a yearly visit.  For women 30-65, a Pap smear can be performed every 3-5 years if the HPV test is negative. While HPV is common, cancer is RARE.  HPV websites include: www.asscp.org, www.nccc-online.org and www.healthywomen.org    Read about cancer symptoms in the pamphlet www.example.com  For additional information of gynecologic cancers: The cancer information Service;   1-800-4CANCER; www.cancer.gov/cis  National ovarian cancer coalition; 1-888-OVARIAN, www.ovarian.org  or the Women's cancer networ - 1-999-999-9999 - www.wcn.org    Breast self exam should be done monthly after cycle. If you do not have cycles the breast exam can be done at the start of every month. Mammograms should be done yearly to every other year between 40 and 50.  Mammograms are frequently read as dense. The radiologist may recommend additional magnification views or an ultrasound. If a MRI is recommended, please contact the office so that authorization for the procedure can be performed.     A normal body mass index (BMI) is 18.5 - 24.9.  Your BMI is calculated each time you are seen at StanfordHealthcare. You can also calculate it online at: www.example.com  If you are outside of normal parameters, consider dietary and nutritional help. More information is available at: www.example.com    Aerobic exercise is encouraged at least 3 times a week for 40-60 minutes or 20 minutes daily. This includes walking, biking, dancing, swimming and most sports. Time can be split up throughout the day. Consistency is the key. Flexibility and strength exercises are needed at least 2 times a week (yoga, pilates,  weights).    Stay current with vaccinations. A yearly influenza or flu shot is recommended. A complete list of immunizations is available at: www.example.com    Healthy Habits   1. Limit alcohol to less than one drink a day for women. One drink is equal to 12 oz of beer or 4 oz of wine or 1 oz of liquor.   2. Don't smoke.   3. Use sunscreen if you are in the sun. Use at least SPF15 and/or wear a hat.   4. Get regular dental care and eye care.   5. Check that your smoke alarm has fresh batteries (change it 2 times a year).   6. Wear a seatbelt at all times and wear a helmet if you ride a bike.   7. If you have firearms at home keep them under lock and key.   8. Practice safe sex to prevent unwanted pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.   9. Multivitamins are not necessary as most vitamins are available in a healthy diet. vitamin D is important for absorption of calcium from the diet into the blood stream. The recommended amount is 7-10,000 IU each week. As vitamin D is fat soluble, the vitamin D can be taken once weekly.     Get help if you are in a relationship that is causing you mental or physical harm. Resources for domestic violence:   1. Support Network for Battered Women 1-999-999-9999 (www.snbw.org)   2. Next Door Solutions to Domestic Violence 999-999-9999 (www.nextdoor.org).     How soon are my results available? STI Cultures: results are available within 3 - 5 days.  Biopsies: results are available in 10 - 14 days. You will be called with results. If you do not hear from us, please send a message. If you are recommended to have an MRI, please contact the office for a referral.     Please stay current with recommended screening tests. Some have been completed today. - Colonoscopy with miralax prep  Dr. Sell performs procedures every Tuesday and Friday.      Preparation Instructions for Colonoscopy  Using MIRALAX, Delta , and GATORADE: Split Preparation                         Read these instructions at least TWO WEEKS before your procedure so you can prepare. You may need to make changes to your daily medicines. If you take blood thinners; have a pacemaker or defibrillator device; have a history of liver, heart, or lung disease; obstructive sleep apnea, kidney disease (dialysis); diabetes; or excessive bleeding during previous surgery or dental extraction please discuss this with your gastroenterologist if you haven't already. Arrange to have an adult drive you to your test and be there to drive and/or accompany you home after you are done (no taxi or Uber).  Medicines given to help you relax during your test will affect your judgement and reflexes much of the day.  If you are taking a form of public transportation, an adult other than the driver MUST ride with you for your safety.  Bring a copy of your current medicines and doses on the day of your procedure.      Stop drinking all fluids 2 hours prior to your appointment time.  Your colon is well-prepared for this procedure when your bowel movements are either clear or clear yellow.  If you need to reschedule your procedure, please call our office.    About your procedure    You are scheduled for a colonoscopy.  This is an exam of your large intestine, or colon, using a flexible tube that will be placed into your rectum.  This tube has a light and camera at the end of it, and your gastroenterologist will check your colon for abnormal growths or other problems.  This test helps your doctor diagnose illnesses and make plans for treatment if needed.  At Stanford Health Care, we strive to perform the safest and most careful exam for every patient.  A colonoscopy may take longer for some patients than for others.  As a result,  your exam may not be performed at the exact time you were scheduled.  We ask you for your patience.  Please allow 3 to 4 hours from check-in time for your visit.    You may need to make changes to your daily medicines    If you take medicines for diabetes, call the doctor who manages your diabetes to discuss how to manage your medicines for this procedure.  You should not take your oral diabetes medication on the day of your procedure unless otherwise instructed.  If you take injectable insulin, we recommend that you hold your morning dose.  If you have an insulin pump, you¿ll need instructions on the settings of your device during this procedure, as well as your prescribed off-pump instructions.  Prevent low blood sugar by consuming chicken, beef, or vegetable broth up to 2 hours before your appointment time. Keep glucose tablets on hand for any sudden drops in blood sugar.  They are available over-the-counter at any pharmacy.    If you take blood thinners such as Plavix, Coumadin, Gettysburg , Effient, Inwood , Sour Lake , Fragmin, Placerville , Charlotte , West Columbia , Vandenberg, Lovenox, Heparin, or any other blood thinner not on this list, you will need additional instructions provided from the doctor who manages your medication.  It is very important for you to receive instructions on your blood thinner in a timely manner, as your procedure may need to be rescheduled if we don¿t receive this information in time.      If you have a Pacemaker or Internal Defibrillator please bring your device card with you on the day of your procedure.    Seven (7) days before your procedure    1) If you take a blood thinner medication and you have not been advised whether you should stop taking the medication prior to your procedure, please call our office.   2) Avoid eating seeds, corn, popcorn, or fruits and vegetables with many seeds like cucumbers, tomatoes, and strawberries.  These foods are hard to digest, do not clear out of your colon  easily, and can make it difficult for your doctor to visualize your colon.  Seeds can also clog the colonoscope, the flexible tube that will be used during your test.  For more food options that are easier to digest, please see the final page of these instructions.  3) Stop using fiber supplements like Metamucil, Citrucel or Fiberall  4) Stop taking iron pills, fish oil, vitamin E, and supplements.  You may continue to take Aspirin 81 mg, or ¿baby aspirin.¿   5) Purchase your bowel prep supplies from your pharmacy:  o One bottle of Miralax 238 grams.   o One Gatorade bottle (or any electrolyte drink) 64 ounces (no red, blue, or purple).   o Ashley Hijazi (Bisacodyl) 5 mg tablets.    6) Purchase a variety of clear liquids that you will consume the day before your procedure  o Please refer to the clear liquid options listed under, ¿One (1) day before your procedure.¿  7) Optional: Purchase any items that can help minimize anal irritation  o Petroleum jelly or diaper rash ointment to use around the anus  o Baby wipes (alcohol and fragrance-free).      AFTER YOUR PROCEDURE, YOU WILL NEED A DRIVER TO RETURN HOME. THIS CANNOT BE PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION SUCH AS UBER, LYFT, TAXI, ETC.     Three (3) days before your procedure    1) Stop taking NSAIDs such as Ibuprofen, Aleve, Naproxen, Advil, etc.     One (1) day before your procedure: CLEAR LIQUIDS ONLY & FIRST ½ OF PREP    Only follow the bowel preparation instructions on this sheet, or instructions given by your doctor.  You will receive a call from the endoscopy center to confirm your appointment time. You need to know this time because it determines when you should drink your second dose of bowel prep.  If you have not received a call by 3 pm the day before your procedure, please call the location where your procedure is scheduled.  .  1) You will be on a clear liquid diet the entire day before your procedure:  ¿ Do not consume solid food the entire day   ¿ Do not consume  alcohol  ¿ Do not consume milk/creamer with your coffee. Sugar is ok  ¿ Consume clear liquids only, (no red, blue, or purple) such as:    Chicken, beef, or vegetable broth Consommé    Sodas  Juice popsicles    Black coffee with no cream or milk Tea with no cream or milk   Fruit juices with no pulp Clear Jell-O    Sports drinks  Clear, hard candy    Lemonade and juices with no pulp       2) At 2 pm, take TWO Dulcolax 5 mg tablets with 8 ounces of clear liquids.   3) Between the hours of 5 pm - 9 pm, mix and drink half of the Sontag /Gatorade mixture:    o Mix the entire Miralax bottle into the bottle of Gatorade, and shake until dissolved. Drink 8 ounce glasses every 10-15 minutes until you have consumed half of the bottle, or 32 ounces.  It usually takes one hour to take effect.  If you develop nausea, take a 10-15-minute break until it subsides.  While you are drinking the Norfolk /Gatorade mixture, you must not drink any other clear liquids.  You may resume the clear liquid diet when you have consumed half of the Cody /Gatorade mixture.  Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of clear liquids before going to bed.    The day of your procedure: SECOND ½ OF PREP    1) Upon waking, you may continue the clear liquid diet.  Absolutely no solid foods may be consumed.    2) If applicable, take your blood pressure and heart medications with a small sip of water at least 30 minutes prior to drinking the second dose of prep.  If you are diabetic, you should not take your oral diabetes medication or injectable insulin on the day of your procedure unless otherwise instructed by your doctor.    3) Using your scheduled appointment time (not check-in time), determine when you should take the second dose of bowel prep:  o 4 hours before your appointment time, begin drinking the remaining half of your bowel preparation, and finish within the hour.  o Stop drinking all fluids 2 hours before your appointment time.  o Example: If your  scheduled appointment time is 8 am, start drinking the second dose of prep at 4 am and finish by 6 am.  Do not drink any more fluids after 6 am until your procedure is completed.  You will be able to eat and drink as soon as your procedure is completed, unless you are told otherwise by your doctor.    4) Your colon is well-prepared for this procedure when your bowel movements are either clear or clear yellow.      5) Please be sure that you will have a responsible adult with you to take you home.   o If you do not have a responsible adult with you to take you home, your procedure cannot be done and will be cancelled.  o You may take any form of transportation to and from the procedure, however you MUST have someone with you to accompany you home.      Tips while drinking the bowel preparation    1) To prevent dehydration, drink plenty of fluids while you are on the clear liquid diet and after your test is complete. Your body can lose a significant amount of fluids during the bowel preparation.   2) Common symptoms you may experience that should decrease over the course of the bowel preparation: bloating, nausea, abdominal cramps, and/or chills.    What to expect upon arrival to the endoscopy suite    1) You will meet your endoscopy nurse  o He or she will ask you questions to ensure that you understand the test and reason for it, and to ensure that you are properly prepared.    2) Your endoscopy nurse will start your intravenous (IV) line   o You will receive medications for your procedure through your IV line.  Unless your procedure is scheduled with anesthesia, you will be receiving moderate sedation.  The medications given to you for moderate sedation include a sedative, which helps you relax, and a narcotic, to help with discomfort.   o Your vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen level) will be monitored closely before, during, and after your test.     After the procedure    1) Rest for the remainder of  the day for your health and safety  o You must not drive for the remainder of the day.  Do not participate in any activities that require coordination or judgment, or sign legal documents. Do not consume alcohol. You may resume normal activities the next day after your procedure.  2) Please inform your physician if you plan to travel by air after your procedure    o There is a small risk of bleeding for up to two weeks after a polyp is removed during a colonoscopy.  We discourage booking an international flight within two weeks after your colonoscopy for your safety.  3) Bloating, gas, or mild cramping is normal after a colonoscopy and should diminish  o If you experience severe abdominal pain and/or severe bleeding, please call our office.      Frequently asked questions    1) Do I really have to drink all this prep?   o Yes, you do!  National studies have demonstrated that the most effective way to cleanse the colon is to take the entire bowel preparation split into two doses.  You want your colon to be as clean as possible so that your gastroenterologist may fully visualize your colon.  This makes a significant difference in how good the colonoscopy is at achieving its purpose, which includes colon cancer prevention.  2) Can I have other fluids that are not clear?   o No, you should not drink fluids that are not clear.  The general rule is if you can see through it, you can consume it.  You should stay well hydrated while drinking the bowel preparation.  Please feel free to drink as many clear liquids as you¿d like.  However, be sure to stop drinking all fluids 2 hours prior to your appointment time.  3) Is a colonoscopy perfect?  o A colonoscopy has been considered the ¿gold standard¿ for examination of the colon and rectum.  However, polyps and other findings can sometimes go unseen at the time of a colonoscopy.  You can minimize this risk by taking your bowel preparation as instructed.  On rare occasions, the  colonoscope cannot be advanced all the way around the colon.  In cases like this, your gastroenterologist will discuss alternatives with you.      Seven (7) days leading up to your procedure avoid Nuts and seeds. Remember, you will be on a clear liquid diet the entire day before your procedure.      For any questions about your scheduled endoscopic procedure(s), please contact our office.    Thank you,    Los Gatos Gastroenterology  999-999-9999

Yocheved Slack  156 2350th St, McLean IL       07/10/2021    Dear Sakina,    Thank you for allowing me to participate in your care recently. I'm writing to inform you of the pathology results from your recent colonoscopy and to provide recommendations.    A total of 2 polyps were removed completely.     The pathology findings were:   1 polyp with no significant abnormality  1 adenoma <1 cm.    Biopsy results of your colon polyp showed that you had an adenomatous polyp.  This is a pre-cancerous polyp that, if not removed, had the potential to turn into colon cancer.  They are very slow growing.   Fortunately, the polyp was removed in its entirety.  These are very common polyps.  To prevent future polyps,  I would recommend a high fiber diet, low red meat consumption and maintain an ideal body weight.    Based on your results, I recommend that you return for a follow up colonoscopy in 5 years. We will send you a reminder at that time.   Please let us know if you move and have changed your address.  Also, please let us know if any changes in your family history for colon polyps or colon cancer.      It is my pleasure to participate in your medical care.  Please don't hesitate to contact me with any questions.    With best wishes,    Marrazzo Pulley, MD

MR BREAST W AND WO IV CONTRAST BILATERAL 10/09/2021 INDICATION: Female, 50 years old, screening, elevated risk of breast  cancer.  High risk for breast cancer. COMPARISON: 03/13/2021 PROCEDURE COMMENTS: A 3.0 tesla examination of both breasts was performed  using a GE scanner with the patient prone on a dedicated phased array  breast coil using the following sequences: 1. 3-plane localizer 2. Axial T1-weighted 3D spoiled gradient echo images 3. Axial T2-weighted 3D fat-suppressed images (CUBE) 4. Axial Diffusion-weighted 2D EPI images with B-0 and B=600 5. Axial multiphase centrically encoded 3D T1-weighted SPGR images with  Glidewell separation into fat- and water-specific images including: * A pre-contrast high-resolution series * 14 view-shared rapid dynamic contrast enhanced series (15 sec each) with  bolus power injection of gadobutrol (Gadavist) injection 7.5 mL, Total  Given: 7 mL (1 dose) and a 20 ml saline flush starting 15 seconds after  start of the acquisition * Four high-resolution post-contrast series. MIP images and multiplanar reformats were created from the first  high-resolution post contrast "peak" series. Computer-aided evaluation  software was used for image processing and kinetic assessment. FINDINGS: Tissue Composition: The breasts have heterogeneous fibroglandular tissue. The background parenchymal enhancement is mild and symmetric. MR Breast w and wo IV Contrast Bilateral Bilateral There is debris filled duct ectasia seen in both breasts.   No suspicious enhancement or lymphadenopathy. Other Findings: Incompletely evaluated 5 mm T2 hyperintensity in the left liver best seen  on series 1 image 3 and likely represents a cyst or hemangioma. IMPRESSION: Left Breast: BI-RADS: 2 - Benign Right Breast: BI-RADS: 2 - Benign Recommend routine age- and risk-appropriate screening mammogram for both  breasts. The addition of supplemental screening breast MRI for women at elevated  breast cancer risk should be based on national guidelines including those  of the American College of Radiology, the American Cancer Society and the  National Comprehensive Cancer Network. A negative breast MRI does not obviate the need for biopsy of significant  findings on clinical examination or other breast imaging studies.  Decisions regarding management of such significant findings should be  based on their clinical and/or other imaging features.  EXAM:

MAMMO BREAST SCREENING TOMOSYNTHESIS 03/19/2022 INDICATION: Female, 50 years old. Asymptomatic. Screening Mammogram.   COMPARISON: 03/13/2021, 03/03/2020, 03/02/2019, 02/27/2018 , 01/07/2017,  05/02/2015, 03/25/2014, and 02/26/2013 PROCEDURE COMMENTS: Digital 2D (synthetic and/or full-field) and  tomosynthesis mammogram images were obtained.     FINDINGS: The breasts are heterogeneously dense, which may obscure small masses. There are no significant masses, calcifications, or other abnormalities. IMPRESSION: BI-RADS® ATLAS category (overall): 1 - Negative Recommend routine age- and risk-appropriate screening mammogram for both  breasts. If additional imaging is recommended, a Stanford Health Care Breast  Imaging Representative will contact the patient to coordinate additional  imaging. A lay letter regarding these findings will also be sent to the  patient. This report will be faxed, mailed, or sent by EPIC electronic  communication to the referring clinician upon finalization. Screening Guidelines: For asymptomatic women at average breast cancer risk, current guidelines  recommend screening mammography every 1-2 years, starting at age 40-50  years. Supplemental screening with whole breast ultrasound is not  recommended by current guidelines but is an option for those women with  mammographically heterogeneously or extremely dense breast who desire more  intensive screening. For asymptomatic women with a personal history of treated breast cancer  who have not had bilateral mastectomies, current guidelines recommend  mammography every year.  This can be a screening or diagnostic examination  based on patient/provider preference.  Stanford recommends the first  annual mammogram after lumpectomy be a diagnostic examination, which is  typically performed at 1 year after the last annual mammogram or the  lumpectomy, with modifications per the referring provider based on the  timing of systemic and/or radiation therapy.  For asymptomatic women at elevated breast cancer risk, such as with a BRCA  gene mutation, current guidelines recommend supplemental screening with  breast MRI every year. EXAM:

She is a life-long headache sufferer, runs in her family. They started when she was a teenager. She's learned to live with them. She has migraines 3-4 days per week. Usually they are responsive to Ibuprofen or Excedrin. About two months ago she started Magnesium 400 mg and headaches dropped significantly, now down to 10-14 days per month that are 3-4/10. They are frontal, behind both eyes.     She has a second headache, 7/10, ice pick in right eye that starts as her typical headache, but then becomes way more intense and lasts longer. She tends to lay in her room and lay down in her room.  She denies nausea. She's had one to two visual auras in the past, squiggly lines, lasting 20-30 minutes followed by migraine. These are generally not responsive to anything. She's tried triptans and they don't work . She takes Ibuprofen, Lyle , at night she takes 1-2 Percocet. It knocks the pain down so she can sleep but still has a headache in the morning, takes more Excedrin then it usually works. These can last a couple days. Since starting Mag, she takes an acute medication 10-14 days/month, before Mag she took something 3-4 days/week. She would take Excedrin 3 days per week. GEN: appears well, in no apparent distress, pleasant and cooperative   HEENT: EOMI, conjunctiva clear   RESP: breathing comfortably, speaking in full sentences, no tachypnea  NEURO: alert and oriented, CN grossly intact, moves upper extremities appropriately  SKIN: normal skin appearance  PSYCH: appropriate affect, intact thought and speech    Discussion and Recommendations:  The patient is a 50 Y female with a past medical history of migraine who presents today for evaluation of headaches. She started having migraines in her teenage years. She started Magnesium 400 mg two months ago and since then her migraines have  decreased in frequency. She now has moderate headache about half of the days per month. Every 6-8 weeks she has a severe migraine lasting multiple days that is refractory to her typical acute treatments. Her symptoms are consistent with chronic migraine and a couple of her migraines have been associated with visual aura. For prevention, we discussed nutraceuticals since she responded so well to Magnesium. We will also start Atogepant. We also discussed medication overuse headache. For acute treatment we will start Zomig nasal spray and Phenergan.     Diagnosis - chronic migraine with a history of visual aura    1. Treatment Plan   To prevent your headaches:  -Atogepant is a newly FDA approved gepant. It is 30mg twice per day. If you would like to try it, please fill out the first 2 sections on page 3 of the following PDF and send it back - www.example.com     To rescue your headaches, you can consider trying the following medications. Please limit the use of all rescue medications to no more than 10 days per month:  -You can try a triptan (zomig nasal spray) at the start of a severe headache. If you still have pain after 2 hours then repeat the dose. Limit the use of triptans to no more than 10 days per month  -You can try NSAIDs at the start of a severe headache. If you still have pain after 2 hours then repeat the dose. Limit the use of NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, motrin, advil) to no more than 10 days per month  -You can try phenergan 12.5mg PO PRN for a severe headache or nausea. This causes drowsiness.     -If home regimen doesn't work, you can contact me about toradol IM in the clinic or an infusion of Mg, IVF and PRN toradol, reglan, zofran.     INFUSION THERAPY CENTER INFORMATION  - you are scheduled at:    The Stanford Neuroscience Heath Center (SNHC)  213 Quarry RD 740 Q25 Rd, Cedaredge CO   Parking and Valet  available  Appointments:   999-999-9999  Hours Monday - Friday 8 AM- 5 PM    An order has been placed for your infusion.  Please allow time for the authorization department to contact your insurance company and obtain approval for this therapy.  This can often take two business days.  Please call to schedule at the most convenient infusion center listed above.     What to expect:  · Please allow a minimum of two hours for your infusion appointment, this does not include any prolonged wait time.  · Wear loose comfortable clothing.       2. Reviewed lifestyle changes that will help to reduce headache frequency and intensity   · Diet: Eat at regular times each day. Eat protein throughout the day. It is especially important to start the day with protein.  · Sleep: Keep regular hours for going to bed at night and getting up in the morning. Do not vary the hours on the weekend. Do not watch TV and read in bed. If you are unable to sleep, get up and read something boring until you feel sleepy, then go back to bed. If you are not able to sleep within 20 minutes, get up again. Even if you do not sleep well, get out of bed at the same time in the morning. Do not take naps. This will help you to regulate your sleep, and improve your sleep quality.  · Exercise: The goal is to exercise at the same time every day for at least 20 minutes at an intensity that increases your heart rate.    3. Headache diary- mark on a calendar the days you have a headache, severity of headache, medication taken, and how long headache lasted      Patient seen and discussed with Dr. Doherty.    Adebanjo, MD  Neurology Headache Fellow PGY-5    Teaching Physician Attestation  Ms. Dorothea Shriner, a very pleasant 50 Y female with a history of headaches since her teenage years. She was experiencing headaches 3-4 days per week decreased with magnesium to 10-14 days per month. Headaches are typically mild to moderate although every 6-8 weeks she has a  7/10 right retro-orbital pain lasting days per episode associated with modest migrainous features. Prior evaluations include an MRI Brain that was unremarkable. Her headaches are most consistent with migraine with visual aura, MOH.     See below for next steps.      Diagnosis - migraine with visual aura, MOH    Plan -   -For prophylaxis - atogepant, magnesium, add riboflavin and coQ10, consider mABs  -For abortives -  zomig NS, phenergan, toradol IM if ineffective - trudhesa, nurtec. If you still have pain after 2 hours then repeat the dose. Limit the use of triptans to no more than 10 days per month  -You can try NSAIDs at the start of a severe headache. If you still have pain after 2 hours then repeat the dose. Limit the use of NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, motrin, advil) to no more than 10 days per month  -You can try phenergan 12.5mg PO PRN for a severe headache or nausea. This causes drowsiness.     -If home regimen doesn't work, you can contact me about toradol IM in the clinic or an infusion of Mg, IVF and PRN toradol, reglan, zofran.     INFUSION THERAPY CENTER INFORMATION  - you are scheduled at:    The Stanford Neuroscience Heath Center (SNHC)  213 Quarry RD 738 Yellow Dawn Ct, Las Vegas NV   Parking and Valet available  Appointments:   999-999-9999  Hours Monday - Friday 8 AM- 5 PM    An order has been placed for your infusion.  Please allow time for the authorization department to contact your insurance company and obtain approval for this therapy.  This can often take two business days.  Please call to schedule at the most convenient infusion center listed above.     What to expect:  Please allow a minimum of two hours for your infusion appointment, this does not include any prolonged wait time.  Wear loose comfortable clothing.       2. Reviewed lifestyle changes that will help to reduce headache frequency and  intensity   Diet: Eat at regular times each day. Eat protein throughout the day. It is especially important to start the day with protein.  Sleep: Keep regular hours for going to bed at night and getting up in the morning. Do not vary the hours on the weekend. Do not watch TV and read in bed. If you are unable to sleep, get up and read something boring until you feel sleepy, then go back to bed. If you are not able to sleep within 20 minutes, get up again. Even if you do not sleep well, get out of bed at the same time in the morning. Do not take naps. This will help you to regulate your sleep, and improve your sleep quality.  Exercise: The goal is to exercise at the same time every day for at least 20 minutes at an intensity that increases your heart rate.    3. Headache diary- mark on a calendar the days you have a headache, severity of headache, medication taken, and how long headache lasted

The 2055del9>A mutation (c.1923_1931delinsA) causes cystic fibrosis when present in trans to an additional disease causing mutation. The two sentinel cases exhibited elevated sweat chloride, pancreatic insufficiency, and moderate/severe lung disease. Reference: Solomon et al., Hum Mutat 1997   Mutation 2 R117H R117H (c.350G>A) was first described in patients with mild CF. However, the 5T/7T/9T variant in intron 8 can influence the severity of the R117H. It can be a disease-causing allele (R117H in cis with 5T) or demonstrate no symptoms to mild manifestations in the CF spectrum (R117H in cis with 7T or 9T). Homozygous R117H was reported in a CBAVD patient. G542X/R117H (in cis with 5T) was reported in three pancreatic sufficient CF patients. References: Dean et al., Cell 1990; Quintero et al., Nature Genetics 1993; Hammersmith et al., J Med Genet 1993; Nokes et al., Pediatrics 1999   Novel Variation 1 None Detected     Poly T/TG Track: (TG)10-7T/(TG)12-7T       Additional Interpretations: This child carries one severe CF mutation and an additional mutation that is associated with clinical symptoms in the CF spectrum, such as congenital absence of the vas deferens. Parent studies would be necessary to determine whether these two mutations are present on the same or on opposite chromosomes. If present on different chromosomes, clinical follow up is recommended. The 2055del9>A mutation (c.1923_1931delinsA) causes cystic fibrosis when present in trans to an additional disease causing mutation. The two sentinel cases exhibited elevated sweat chloride, pancreatic insufficiency, and moderate/severe lung disease. Reference: Juarez et al., Hum Mutat 1997   Mutation 2 R117H R117H (c.350G>A) was first described in patients with mild CF. However, the 5T/7T/9T variant in intron 8 can influence the severity of the R117H. It can be a disease-causing allele (R117H in cis with 5T) or demonstrate no symptoms to mild manifestations in the CF spectrum (R117H in cis with 7T or 9T). Homozygous R117H was reported in a CBAVD patient. G542X/R117H (in cis with 5T) was reported in three pancreatic sufficient CF patients. References: Dean et al., Cell 1990; Mcvey et al., Nature Genetics 1993; Wolfinger et al., J Med Genet 1993; Lievano et al., Pediatrics 1999   Novel Variation 1 None Detected     Poly T/TG Track: (TG)10-7T/(TG)12-7T       Additional Interpretations: This child carries one severe CF mutation and an additional mutation that is associated with clinical symptoms in the CF spectrum, such as congenital absence of the vas deferens. Parent  studies would be necessary to determine whether these two mutations are present on the same or on opposite chromosomes. If present on different chromosomes, clinical follow up is recommended. Problem List/Past Medical History:  Cystic Fibrosis Diagnostics:    Parent Testing:  Mom: Cedeno of  2055del9>A CFTR mutation    Component   Ref Range & Units 10/11/2021 0930   Sweat Collected   >=0.075 g 0.279    Sweat Chloride   <60 mmol/L 33      Component   Ref Range & Units  10/30/2021 1151   Elastase-1, Stool   >200 (Normal) mcg/g 499            Patient Active Problem List   Diagnosis   • High immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening   • Abnormal findings on newborn screening   • Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator-related metabolic syndrome   • Other constipation   • Gastroesophageal reflux disease in infant     Birth History   • Birth     Weight: 3.43 kg   • Gestation Age: 39 wks   • Feeding: Breast Fed   • Hospital Name: Rochester    • Hospital Location: Coldwater MS      Elevated IRT on NBS 110.0 ng/mL      CFTR DNA Sequencing  Type Name Description   Mutation 1 2055del9>A This mutation is a known deleterious mutation in the CFTR gene. The 2055del9>A mutation (c.1923_1931delinsA) causes cystic fibrosis when present in trans to an additional disease causing mutation. The two sentinel cases exhibited elevated sweat chloride, pancreatic insufficiency, and moderate/severe lung disease. Reference: Powers et al., Hum Mutat 1997   Mutation 2 R117H R117H (c.350G>A) was first described in patients with mild CF. However, the 5T/7T/9T variant in intron 8 can influence the severity of the R117H. It can be a disease-causing allele (R117H in cis with 5T) or demonstrate no symptoms to mild manifestations in the CF spectrum (R117H in cis with 7T or 9T). Homozygous R117H was reported in a CBAVD patient. G542X/R117H (in cis with 5T) was reported in three pancreatic sufficient CF patients. References: Dean et al., Cell 1990; Tasch et al., Nature Genetics 1993; Allison et al., J Med Genet 1993; Gumbs et al., Pediatrics 1999   Novel Variation 1 None Detected     Poly T/TG Track: (TG)10-7T/(TG)12-7T       Additional Interpretations: This child carries one severe CF mutation and an additional mutation that is associated with clinical symptoms in the CF spectrum, such as congenital absence of the vas deferens. Parent studies would be necessary to determine  whether these two mutations are present on the same or on opposite chromosomes. If present on different chromosomes, clinical follow up is recommended. The 2055del9>A mutation (c.1923_1931delinsA) causes cystic fibrosis when present in trans to an additional disease causing mutation. The two sentinel cases exhibited elevated sweat chloride, pancreatic insufficiency, and moderate/severe lung disease. Reference: Puffer et al., Hum Mutat 1997   Mutation 2 R117H R117H (c.350G>A) was first described in patients with mild CF. However, the 5T/7T/9T variant in intron 8 can influence the severity of the R117H. It can be a disease-causing allele (R117H in cis with 5T) or demonstrate no symptoms to mild manifestations in the CF spectrum (R117H in cis with 7T or 9T). Homozygous R117H was  reported in a CBAVD patient. G542X/R117H (in cis with 5T) was reported in three pancreatic sufficient CF patients. References: Dean et al., Cell 1990; Buchanan et al., Nature Genetics 1993; Adamczyk et al., J Med Genet 1993; Murata et al., Pediatrics 1999   Novel Variation 1 None Detected     Poly T/TG Track: (TG)10-7T/(TG)12-7T       Additional Interpretations: This child carries one severe CF mutation and an additional mutation that is associated with clinical symptoms in the CF spectrum, such as congenital absence of the vas deferens. Parent studies would be necessary to determine whether these two mutations are present on the same or on opposite chromosomes. If present on different chromosomes, clinical follow up is recommended. The 2055del9>A mutation (c.1923_1931delinsA) causes cystic fibrosis when present in trans to an additional disease causing mutation. The two sentinel cases exhibited elevated sweat chloride, pancreatic insufficiency, and moderate/severe lung disease. Reference: Chugh et al., Hum Mutat 1997   Mutation 2 R117H R117H (c.350G>A) was first described in patients with mild CF. However, the 5T/7T/9T variant in intron 8 can influence the severity of the R117H. It can be a disease-causing allele (R117H in cis with 5T) or demonstrate no symptoms to mild manifestations in the CF spectrum (R117H in cis with 7T or 9T). Homozygous R117H was reported in a CBAVD  patient. G542X/R117H (in cis with 5T) was reported in three pancreatic sufficient CF patients. Clinical Notes:
US GUIDED INGUINAL LYMPH NODE BIOPSY RIGHT  09/22/2017 PROVIDED CLINICAL INDICATIONS:  R59.0: Localized enlarged lymph nodes. ADDITIONAL CLINICAL HISTORY:  None. COMPARISON:  None. TECHNIQUE:  Following a PARQ conference, written informed consent was obtained from the patient.  Prior to beginning the procedure, a standard team pause was performed. Moderate sedation achieved with intravenous fentanyl and Versed during continuous monitoring of vital signs by a trained nurse.  Total duration of sedation was approximately 30 minutes. Following a PARQ conference, written informed consent was obtained from the patient.  Prior to beginning the procedure, a standard team pause was performed. Surgical safety checklist performed. The patient was placed supine on the procedure table.  Sterile preparation of the right groin was performed; maximal sterile barrier technique followed including: cap and mask and sterile gown and sterile gloves and a large sterile sheet and hand hygiene and 2% chlorhexidine for cutaneous antisepsis. Sterile gel and sterile probe covers were utilized for ultrasound guidance.  Local anesthesia achieved with 1% lidocaine solution subcutaneously. Under CT  guidance, a 19-gauge introducer needle was advanced into the lesion.  The inner stylet was removed and a 20-gauge core biopsy device advanced.  8 core samples were collected.  Samples were submitted for surgical pathology and flow cytometry.   The introducer needle was removed and access site dressed with a sterile bandage.  Completion ultrasoundobtained.  The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complication. FINDINGS:   Initial ultrasound redemonstrates the right groin lesion.    Intraprocedural images document the access needle projecting to the lesion.     Completion images show no evidence of acute complication. IMPRESSION- Successful ultrasound-guided biopsy of dominant right groin lymph node with a total of 8 20-gauge core samples collected and submitted for surgical pathology and flow cytometry.     Dictated by: Taganas M.D. on 09/22/2017  Electronically signed by: Pla M.D. on 09/22/2017 PSR_OR

Stanford Cancer Center  Lymphoma Clinic  New Patient Visit      Date: 10/18/2017             ID: Tad Pope is a previously healthy 27 Year old male referred for treatment of newly diagnosed stage IIIA classical Burch lymphoma.    Oncologic History  06/29/2017 - initially noted a firmness in his right groin. He thought this was a tight tendon and tried icing the area. Over the following weeks, he developed an enlarging lump in the right groin that became very painful. He initially thought this could be an inguinal hernia.  08/04/2017 - he presented to a local urgent care in Portland, OR where he was working at the time with right groin pain and swelling. An ultrasound of the right groin was done and showed right inguinal adenopathy with a 3.7 x 1.1 x 2.0 cm inguinal node and another 3.4 x 2.1 x 2.7 cm inguinal node. He was tested for a number of STIs including HIV, hepatitis B & C, gonorrhea, and chlamydia, all of which were negative.  09/22/2017 - underwent core biopsy of an enlarged right inguinal node in Shawnee Mission , OR with outside pathology showing scattered Reed-Sternberg cells (CD30+ CD15+ PAX5 weakly positive) in a background of inflammatory cells and thick sclerosis consistent with classical Driggers lymphoma, nodular sclerosing vs mixed cellularity subtype. Outside pathology slides have been requested but have not yet been received. Established care with local oncologist in Spartansburg , Dr. Gage Duhaime.  10/04/2017 - outside labs notable for WBC 12.9, ANC 10.5, ALC 1.3, Hgb 15.4, Plt 421, Cr 1.0, Tbili 0.5, AST 29, ALT 26, Alk phos 97, Albumin 4.6, LDH 243, ESR 11.  10/05/2017 - CT CAP showed lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm with the following index lesions:    Anterior mediastinal mass adjacent to main pulmonary artery, 4.5 x 3.2 cm  Right hilar node, 1.1 cm  Aortocaval node, 1.2 cm  Right iliac bifurcation, 4.5 x 3.0 cm  Right external iliac node, 6.0 x 3.5 cm  Right inguinal node 2.5 cm    10/10/2017 - TTE showed  mildly reduced LVEF of 45-50%  10/11/2017 - right chest mediport placed  10/12/2017 - PFTs showed normal diffuse capacity (DLCO 85% of predicted) and no ventilatory defect. PET-CT showed hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm with the following index lesions:    Anterior mediastinal mass adjacent to main pulmonary artery, 5.4 x 3.6 cm (SUV 7.5)  Right hilar node, 1.1 cm  Aortocaval node, 1.2 cm  Right iliac nodal conglomerate, 6.1 x 4.2 cm (SUV 9.6)  Right inguinal node 2.6 cm (SUV 12.7)    Interval History  Mr. Rudd presents to clinic today with his very supportive adoptive parents. Subjectively he feels well overall with no fevers, drenching night sweats, or weight loss. He has noticed increased fatigue over the past few months, but has still been able to work as a powerline technician. He continues to have several swollen nodes in his right groin but the pain has subsided significantly. Assessment  Erna Neupane is a previously healthy 27 Year old male referred for treatment of newly diagnosed stage IIIA classical Selzer lymphoma.    Mr. Neupane's presentation is somewhat atypical for classical Winters lymphoma with the bulk of his disease being infradiaphragmatic in the right groin and pelvis with only minimal disease in the chest and no disease in the neck. In general, patients with predominantly infradiaphragmatic disease have poorer outcomes than those with supradiaphragmatic disease with a higher rate of treatment failure (hazard ratio 2) [1,2].  However, his IPI score is low at 1 (male gender), associated with a 5-year disease-free survival of 77% [3].    In general, frontline treatment for advanced stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma involves either 6 cycles of ABVD or 12 weeks of Stanford V, which are associated with a 5-year failure-free survival rate of 74% and 71%, respectively (p=0.32) [4]. A recent study of over 1000 patients also evaluated the use of interim PET-CT to omit bleomycin for patients with advanced classical Wages lymphoma with a negative PET-CT after 2 cycles of ABVD. Patients with a negative PET (Deauville 1-3) were randomized to receive 4 additional cycles of ABVD vs AVD. At a median follow up of 32 months, no difference in 3-year progression-free survival was found between the two groups (85.5% for ABVD and 84.5% for AVD) [5].    Prior to starting chemotherapy, Mr. Neupane will have a repeat TTE (given outside TTE from Oregon with borderline low LVEF 45-50%), sperm banking, and Stanford pathology review of his outside biopsy specimen. We will also review his case in detail at our Hodgkin staging conference on 10/9. Assuming his LVEF is 50% or greater, then we would plan to start treatment next week on 10/11 with ABVD followed by an interim PET-CT after 2 cycles and omission of bleomycin with subsequent cycles should he achieve a CR (Deauville 1-3). However, should his LVEF be <50%, then we would likely prefer Stanford V given the lower dose of anthracycline. We would also consider additional interventions for cardioprotection including continuous infusion of adriamycin and/or treatment with Zinecard or an ACE inhibitor. Following chemotherapy, we would also consider consolidative XRT to the right groin as this is his primary site of disease. We will discuss this further at our Hodgkin tumor board on 10/9.    References:  1. Tewell et al, Infradiaphragmatic versus supradiaphragmatic Hodgkin lymphoma: a retrospective review of 1,114  patients. Leuk Lymphoma 2005;46(12):1715-20.  2. Vassilakopoulos et al, Pure infradiaphragmatic Ragsdale's lymphoma. Clinical features, prognostic factor and comparison with supradiaphragmatic disease. Haematologica 2006;91(1):32-9.   3. Hasenclever et al, A prognostic score for advanced Kramer¿ disease. N Engl J Med 1998;339:1506-14.  4. Southall et al, Randomized Phase III Trial of ABVD Versus Stanford V With or Without Radiation Therapy in Locally Extensive and Advanced-Stage Cristina Addis: An Intergroup Study Coordinated by the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (E2496). J Clin Oncol 2013;31(6):684-91.  5. Akhtar et al, Adapted Treatment Guided by Interim PET-CT Scan in Advanced Hodgkin¿s Lymphoma. N Engl J Med 2016;374:2419-29.    Plan  - requested outside slides from Oregon, to be reviewed by Stanford pathology prior to starting chemotherapy  - ordered repeat TTE given borderline low LVEF 45-50% on outside TTE from Oregon  - sperm banking to be done prior to starting chemotherapy  - we will review his imaging and pathology at Hodgkin staging conference on 10/9  - assuming LVEF is 50% or greater, will plan to start treatment with ABVD for 6 cycles with omission of bleomycin after 2 cycles per the RATHL trial if interim PET-CT shows a CR (Deauville 1-3)  - if LVEF is <50%, then would prefer Stanford V to ABVD given lower anthracycline dose, and would also consider continuous infusion of anthracycline and/or Zinecard and ACE inhibitor for cardioprotection  - following chemotherapy, would consider consolidative XRT to the right groin, will discuss further at Hodgkin tumor board on 10/9  - RTC in 1 week with labs and plan to start treatment at that time    The patient was seen and discussed with the attending oncologist, Dr. Lum, who agrees with the assessment and plan above. Mr. Risch had no previous medical history and was otherwise healthy until earlier this year. Assessment and Plan:  AHA Stage/NYHA Class: B / I    It was a pleasure to see Mr. Novak in the cardiomyopathy clinic today for initial evaluation prior to chemotherapy administration. Based on Dr Verma's recent documentation, Stanford V will be the therapy of choice given the EF remains <50%. We, of course, agree with any  cardioprotective measures available to the patient while not jeopardizing his overall prognosis. Along these lines, we took the liberty of initiating lisinopril and would recommend repeat echocardiogram preferably halfway through his treatment but certainly upon completion. In regards to utilization of dexrazoxane, we do not feel strongly about incorporating this agent with the mildly reduced EF but would certainly recommend it should the LV function worsen. We will plan to see the patient back for follow up in 3-4 months or sooner if indicated. SPECIMEN SUBMITTED:
VP17-[000000], 8 SLIDES; VP17-2715, 6 UNSTAINED SLIDES ADDED


DIAGNOSIS:

lymph node, right inguinal, needle core biopsy
     --   classicAL hodgkin lymphoma (see comment)

Narayanan/NATKUNAM/GRATZINGER

COMMENT: Sections of the needle core biopsy show small fragments of lymph node tissue and intervening fibrous tissue. The lymphoid tissue is composed of a mix of small lymphocytes, neutrophils, plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, and histiocytes. Additionally, there are scattered atypical large cells with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, one or multiple large rounded nuclei with vesicular chromatin, and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli with perinuclear clearing; consistent with Olivieri and Port Isabel  cells. Additionally, there are occasional mummified cells with condensed cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei. Subtyping classical Gin lymphoma on a needle core biopsy is generally not done and the differential includes mixed cellularity and nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma. Given the thick band or fibrosis seen in the specimen, we favor a nodular sclerosing subtype.  On submitted immunostains the Zelig cells show membranous and Golgi pattern CD30 and CD15 staining, and are negati*

Additional immunohistochemical studies are performed at Stanford on provided unstained slides as follows:
The large cells are OCT2 positive, BOB1 positive, and are negative for PAX5 with internal positive control and negative for EBV by Shrifter in situ hybridization and negative for ALK, both with external positive control.

This immunologic test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by Stanford University Immunoperoxidase Laboratory.  Unless indicated otherwise, it has not been cleared or approved by the Iola , although such approval is not required for analyte-specific reagents of this type.  All controls show appropriate reactivity.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Noe Nolen is a previously healthy 27 Year old male referred for treatment of newly diagnosed infradiaphragmatic stage IIIA classical Cappiello lymphoma.



I have reviewed the specimen and agree with the interpretation above. Cristi Ramani M.D.,PhD   Electronically signed 11/01/2017

Call (999-999-9999 option #5 for the following:  · Temperature > 100.4°F  · Uncontrolled nausea or vomiting  · Diarrhea (3 or more loose/watery stools in 1 day)  · If you are constipated and have not had a bowel movement in >3 days   · Episodes of bleeding (blood in urine, blood in stool, bleeding gums, unusual bruising)  · Shortness of breath  · New or worsening symptoms  · Signs and symptoms of infection with or without a fever (burning during urination, mucus associated with cold symptoms etc.)  **During the day 8:00- 5:00 ask for a nurse, after hours, the physician on call will be paged. If unable to reach someone go to the nearest ER and have the ER doctor call Stanford.        Anti Nausea Medications:     Zofran (ondansetron) 8 mg-- Take scheduled as provided on written schedule from clinic. You can take this medication 1 tablet by mouth every 8 hours as needed. This can cause constipation.       Compazine (Prochlorperazine) 10 mg- Take 1 tablet by mouth every 4 hours as needed for nausea and vomiting. This can sometimes cause drowsiness.      Ativan (Lorazepam) 1 mg- Take 1 tablet by mouth every 4 hours as needed for nausea. This can cause drowsiness and you should not drive after taking.       **Do not take Compazine and Ativan at the same time    **You may stagger your anti nausea medications        Optional Medications For Constipation:    Hausner (Docusate Sodium) 100 mg take 1 cap in the AM and PM. This is a stool softener.    MiraLAX -take 1 Dose for constipation    Senna (sennakot) 8.6 mg Take 1-2 tablets daily as needed for constipation.    Call your doctor if you haven't had a bowel movement for 3 days.

Filgrastim, G-CSF injection  What is this medicine?  FILGRASTIM, G-CSF (fil GRA stim) is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor that stimulates the growth of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell (WBC) important in the body's fight against infection. It is used to reduce the incidence of fever and infection in patients with certain types of cancer who are receiving chemotherapy that affects the bone marrow, to stimulate blood cell production for removal of WBCs from the body prior to a bone marrow transplantation, to reduce the incidence of fever and infection in patients who have severe chronic neutropenia, and to improve survival outcomes following high-dose radiation exposure that is toxic to the bone marrow.  This medicine may be used for other purposes; ask your health care provider or pharmacist if you have questions.  COMMON BRAND NAME(S): Neupogen  What should I tell my health care provider before I take this medicine?  They need to know if you have any of these conditions:  -latex allergy  -ongoing radiation therapy  -sickle cell disease  -an unusual or allergic reaction to filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, other medicines, foods, dyes, or preservatives  -pregnant or trying to get pregnant  -breast-feeding  How should I use this medicine?  This medicine is for injection under the skin. If you get this medicine at home, you will be taught how to prepare and give this medicine. Refer to the Instructions for Use that come with your medication packaging. Use exactly as directed. Take your medicine at regular intervals. Do not take your medicine more often than directed.  It is important that you put your used needles and syringes in a special sharps container. Do not put them in a trash can. If you do not have a sharps container, call your pharmacist or healthcare provider to get one.  Talk to your pediatrician regarding the use of this medicine in children. While this drug may be prescribed for children as young  as 7 months for selected conditions, precautions do apply.  Overdosage: If you think you have taken too much of this medicine contact a poison control center or emergency room at once.  NOTE: This medicine is only for you. Do not share this medicine with others.  What if I miss a dose?  It is important not to miss your dose. Call your doctor or health care professional if you miss a dose.  What may interact with this medicine?  This medicine may interact with the following medications:  -medicines that may cause a release of neutrophils, such as lithium  This list may not describe all possible interactions. Give your health care provider a list of all the medicines, herbs, non-prescription drugs, or dietary supplements you use. Also tell them if you smoke, drink alcohol, or use illegal drugs. Some items may interact with your medicine.  What should I watch for while using this medicine?  You may need blood work done while you are taking this medicine.  What side effects may I notice from receiving this medicine?  Side effects that you should report to your doctor or health care professional as soon as possible:  -allergic reactions like skin rash, itching or hives, swelling of the face, lips, or tongue  -dizziness or feeling faint  -fever  -pain, redness, or irritation at site where injected  -pinpoint red spots on the skin  -shortness of breath or breathing problems  -signs and symptoms of kidney injury like trouble passing urine, change in the amount of urine, or red or dark-brown urine  -stomach or side pain, or pain at the shoulder  -swelling  -tiredness  -unusual bleeding or bruising  Side effects that usually do not require medical attention (report to your doctor or health care professional if they continue or are bothersome):  -bone pain  -headache  -muscle pain  This list may not describe all possible side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at  1-800-FDA-1088.  Where should I keep my medicine?  Keep out of the reach of children.  Store in a refrigerator between 2 and 8 degrees C (36 and 46 degrees F). Do not freeze. Keep in carton to protect from light. Throw away this medicine if vials or syringes are left out of the refrigerator for more than 24 hours. Throw away any unused medicine after the expiration date.  NOTE: This sheet is a summary. It may not cover all possible information. If you have questions about this medicine, talk to your doctor, pharmacist, or health care provider.  © 2015, Elsevier/Gold Standard. (08/20/2015)      How and Where to Give Subcutaneous Insulin Injections, Adult  There are many different types of injectable medicines that are meant to be injected into the fat layer under your skin. The type of medicine you take may determine how many injections you give yourself and when to take the injections.   CHOOSING A SITE FOR INJECTION  Neupogen absorption varies from site to site. As with any injectable medication it is best for the Neupogen to be injected within the same body region. However, do not inject the Neupogen in the same spot each time. Rotating the spots you give your injections will prevent inflammation or tissue breakdown. There are four main regions that can be used for injections. The regions include the:  · Abdomen (preferred region).  · Back of upper arm.    USING a pre-filled syringe  1. Wash your hands with soap and water.  2. Use an alcohol wipe to clean the area of the body to be injected.  3. Pinch up 1 inch of skin and hold it.  4. Put the needle at an angle into the skin (45-degree angle) being careful not to aim towards your fingers that are pinching the skin.  5. Depress the plunger slowly  6. Place used needle into approved hard-sided container.  THROWING AWAY SUPPLIES  · Discard used needles in a puncture proof sharps disposal container. Follow disposal regulations for the area where you live  (check your county website for "sharps disposal" information).
