SW received a consult to assist pt with housing resources/options near Stanford. Pt is a 27yo male with Wanetta Mitch. Pt lies in Turlock, currently staying at home since diagnosis. Pt receives chemo, but he may start daily radiation. He hasn't decided if he would come to PA or go locally for radiation at the Stanford Radiation center in Turlock.    Pt's parents accompany him to his chemo appointments. They are able to assist with hotel for one night, but if it is daily, then they wanted to know the options. Pt is currently on SDI making approx $1,500 per month. Pt visited the facility in Turlock once, but not the Stanford side. He has concerns. He would like to visit the Stanford side to make a decision.     Pt has a motor home that he could use if he had hook ups. SW will email him the places that allow for parking and have hookups. It is connected to his truck, so if he needed his car to shop, then he couldn't go in his car due to that it is hooked up to the home. For this reason, he needs to park it in a place that allows for long term use and has hook ups.     Pt has parents and a fiance who are supportive. Pt admits he feels anxious coming to appointments. Pt reports his Dad is having a difficult time coping with his diagnosis. His Dad is frustrated and angry that it isn't him diagnosed instead of his son. Mom is coping WNL. She was appropriately tearful as SW provided support.     Pt's Dad or fiance plan to provide transport or needed assistance during chemo appointments or if he receives radiation at SHC. Pt denies barriers to care.  SW provided information on local housing resources including the ACS. SW suggested accessing the Supportive Oncology Classes including the Lymphoma support group and meditation for helping with anxiety.     SW provided supportive listening and offered ongoing support. Pt and family have my direct contact number and email. Per pt's request, SW will email housing resources to  deidentified@example.com    Arias Mcfadden, LCSW  Lymphoma and Uro Onc  pgr 25163

Impression/Plan   Evelyne Mangat is a 27 Y male with stage IIIA classical Zayas lymphoma, with an IPS score of 1 for male gender. Involved sites of disease include the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. Due to his EF of 47%, we recommended Stanford V in lieu of ABVD given the lower total doxorubicin dose.     1. Worley lymphoma  - Now in CR with recent PET/CT showing Deauville 3 after 6 cycles   - Labs and exam adequate to proceed with treatment today:    Chemotherapy  Week 8, Day 1 = 12/25/2017   Body surface area is 2.29 meters squared.  · Bleomycin 5 units/m2 IV on D1  · Vincristine 2 mg IV on D1  · Prednisone 40 mg/kg PO every other day    Supportive Care  · Bactrim PO BID on Saturday/Sunday  ·  Protonix 40 mg PO daily  · Dreyfuss PO BID daily    - Neupogen for [3] days next week (none on even weeks), advised Claritin to reduce bone pain  - Will continue to give IV Zofran in ITA as well as PO ativan as this mitigates his carsickness following infusions  -  Scheduled to see Dr. Grigorian on 01/04/2018  - If radiation to spleen is planned, will need vaccinations per standard of care   - Switch to Protonix for persistent GERD symptoms  - Continue metoclopramide at home for refractory nausea  - Give dexamethasone equivalent of prednisone in ITA today (patient states forgot to take today)    2. Mild cardiomyopathy  - Repeat echocardiogram at end of treatment; EF stable to improved  - Continue daily lisinopril, monitor for side effects including dizziness  - Per Dr. Rouse, can consider infusional doxorubicin and/or dexrazoxane if EF worsens    3. Anxiety  - Switch to BID clonazepam with gabapentin BID PRN  - Stop lorazepam after today  - Referral to Psych-Onc for further assistance with anxiety managment    RTC in 1 week for consideration prior to week 9 Stanford V chemotherapy with PORT labs (CBCD, CMP). Mild cardiomyopathy  - Repeat echocardiogram at end of treatment; EF stable to improved  - Continue daily lisinopril, monitor for side effects including dizziness  - Per Dr. Tenorio, can consider infusional doxorubicin and/or dexrazoxane if EF worsens    3. New Patient Consultation      Name: Kapur: 05/29/1990  MRN: [000000]   Address:   625 I35 Frontage Rd, Red Oak TX   Phone:   999-999-9999 (home)     Date: 01/23/2018   Attending Physician: Ortman Lirio Winkler, Bitner, Ranjana  Lymphoma Clinic 834 Vdot Way, Charlottesville VA     Abbigail Kuck, MD  Lymphoma Clinic  668 6Yank Ct, Arvada CO     Dear Doctors,     We had the pleasure of seeing your patient, Mr. Petar Ghumman, in consultation today, 01/23/2018, in the Department of Radiation Oncology at Stanford Hospital & Clinics.     Identification: Mr. Izayah Min is a 27 year-old man with a history of zoster in 2015, stage IIIAS classic Hodgkin lymphoma, IPS 1 (male), with involved sites including the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. At presentation, his mediastinal and right iliac disease both measured greater than 5cm at largest dimension. He is undergoing Stanford V chemotherapy due to low EF of 47% and experienced a complete metabolic response on interim PET/CT with Deauville 3. He presents for consideration of adjuvant radiation therapy.    Chronological History of Present Illness:  Initial Presentation  06/29/2017: He initially experienced firmness of his right groin. Over the following weeks he began to develop an enlarging lump of the right groin. The lump became painful.  08/04/2017: He presented to urgent care at outside hospital (in Oregon) with right groin pain and swelling. An Ultra-Sound of the right inguinal region showed right inguinal adenopathy with a 3.7x1.1x2.0cm inguinal node and 3.4x2.1x2.7cm inguinal node. Studies for HIV, hep B/C, gonorrhea, and chlamydia were negative.    Biopsy and Diagnosis  09/22/2017: Underwent core biopsy of enlarged right inguinal node; Stanford review (11/01/2017) showed classic hodgkin lymphoma    Initial Blood-Work  10/04/2017: Outside labs showed WBC 12.9, Hb 15.4, PLT 421. Albumin 4.6, LDH 243,  ESR 11    Initial CT Scan  10/05/2017: CT CAP showed lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm, including a (i) 4.5cm mediastinal mass, (ii) 1.1cm right hilar node, (iii) 1.2cm aortocaval node, (iv) 4.5cm right iliac bifurcation, (v) 6cm right external iliac node, and (vi) 2.5cm right inguinal node    Echo/PFTs  10/10/2017: Echo showed reduced LVEF of 45-50%  10/12/2017: PFTs showed normal diffuse capacity (DLCO 85% of predicted) with no ventilatory defect    Initial PET/CT  10/12/2017: PET/CT showed hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm, including a (i) 5.4cm anterior mediastinal mass SUV 7.5, (ii) 1.1cm right hilar node, (iii) 1.2cm aortocaval node, (iv) 6.1cm right iliac node conglomerate SUV 9.6, and (v) 2.6cm right inguinal node SUV 12.7    Heme/Onc Consult  10/18/2017: Consult with Dr. Steffen. Patient reported several swollen nodes over right grown. No pruritis but new alcohol intolerance with significant pain in right groin after drinking alcohol. Exam notable for 3cm right femoral node and 3cm right inguinal node. Noted atypical presentation with mainly infradiaphragmatic disease. Plan for Stanford V if repeat Echos shows EF <50%. Consider consolidative radiation to right groin.    10/23/2017: CXR showed mildly prominent cardiomediastinal silhouette with a known anterior mediastinal mass    10/25/2017: PET/MR showed mediastinal mass, supra- and infradiaphragmatic nodal disease and focal lesion in the spleen.     Cardiology Consult  10/25/2017: Seen by Dr. Sweet (Cardiology) for evaluation of reduced LV function. Noted unclear etiology. Agreed with Stanford V. Recommended starting lisinopril and repeating Echo halfway through radiation. Repeat echocardiogram mid-treatment.    11/06/2017: Seen by Dr. Mcdowell. Noted EF of 47%. Recommend Stanford V in lieu of ABVD given the lower total doxorubicin dose.     Stanford V  11/06/2017: Week 1 Stanford V  11/13/2017: Week 2 Stanford V  11/20/2017: Week 3 Stanford V  (dose reduced doxorubicin, vinblastine, and etoposide by 35% given ANC 830 and initiated Neupogen x 5 days)  11/27/2017: Week 4 Stanford V  12/04/2017: Week 5 Stanford V  12/11/2017: Week 6 Stanford V    Interim PET/CT  12/15/2017: PET/CT showed complete metabolic resolution of right iliac, inguinal, mediastinal, hilar and right axillary lymph nodes. Deauville 3    12/15/2017: Repeat Echo showed EF 52.9%    Stanford V  12/18/2017: Week 7 Stanford V  12/25/2017: Week 8 Stanford V  01/01/2018: Week 9 Stanford V  01/10/2018: Week 10 Stanford V  01/17/2017: Week 11 Stanford V    Social Work Encounter  01/12/2018: Social work reached out to Mr. Funderburk regarding a psych/onc referral. He believes he might be interested once he starts radiation.    Heme/Onc Follow Up  01/17/2017: Seen by Dr. Rubin. Mr. Funderburk was generally feeling well, although his appetite had decreased from 5 meals per day to 2-3 meals per day. His energy was slightly better and his anxiety symptoms were stable. Exam notable for small (<1cm) right inguinal node.    Today, Mr. Kilburn discussed his initial presentation of his illness. He said that he felt fatigued for about 2 months and he noticed he had decreased energy and started to work less hours. He said over the course of one weekend he noticed growth of a mass on his right groin. He did not experience any fevers or unexplained weigh loss. He said he has experienced night-sweats throughout his life that did not increase in intensity or frequency. He did not experience any generalized itching. He said that shortly after the groin mass appeared, he had 2-3 beers and 15-20 minutes later he had severe pain localized to the site of the right groin mass. He has not had alcohol since. He did not noticed any other lumps or bumps other than the right groin mass.    Mr. Funderburk said that while on chemotherapy his first week he felt very fatigued and could not get out of bed. Over the course of his therapy he had good weeks and bad weeks,  based on the rotation of the chemotherapy he has been receiving. The symptoms he experienced that were problematic for him have been severe nausea and low energy level. He has not experienced any fevers or illnesses while receiving chemotherapy. He feels physically fatigued easily and gets short of breath climbing stairs. He has not experienced any bowel symptoms including no constipation or diarrhea. He said that his right groin mass felt soft after the first week for treatment and resolved after about 4-5 weeks of treatment. Three weeks ago he started to experienced mild neuropathy on the bottoms of his feet. He has not experienced weakness and has not had issues with balance.    He has a history of eczema and he was diagnosed with psoriasis on the hands around 2012 by a Dermatologist - Dr. Nisar in Turlock at Advanced Skin Institute. He was treated with an ointment that he cannot recall. On 01/18/2018, the day after his chemotherapy he started to itch all over (thighs, arm, and back). He had no shortness of breath. He has not seen anyone for this. He said these symptoms are still going on but slowly improving. Mr. Funderburk also explained that he experienced herpes zoster around 2015 that was localized to his right abdomen around the level of the umbilicus and extended laterally towards his back. Laboratory:   Lab Results   Basename Value Date    WBC 9.9 01/17/2018    HGB 11.4 (L) 01/17/2018    HCT 32.9 (L) 01/17/2018    PLT 274 01/17/2018     Lab Results   Basename Value Date    NA 137 01/17/2018    K 3.8 01/17/2018    CL 101 01/17/2018    CO2 29 01/17/2018    BUN 11 01/17/2018    CR 0.81 01/17/2018    GLU 80  01/17/2018    CA 8.8 01/17/2018    AST 35 01/17/2018    ALT 77 (H) 01/17/2018     Pathology:  11/01/2017 Stanford Outside Slide Review  Accession No: 9999-9999  SPECIMEN SUBMITTED: VP17-[000000], 8 SLIDES; VP17-2715, 6 UNSTAINED SLIDES ADDED    DIAGNOSIS:  lymph node, right inguinal, needle core biopsy  --   classical hodgkin lymphoma (see comment)    Nienaber/NATKUNAM/GRATZINGER    COMMENT: Sections of the needle core biopsy show small fragments of lymph node tissue and intervening fibrous tissue. The lymphoid tissue is composed of a mix of small lymphocytes, neutrophils, plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, and histiocytes. Additionally, there are scattered atypical large cells with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, one or multiple large rounded nuclei with vesicular chromatin, and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli with perinuclear clearing; consistent with Pung and Austin  cells. Additionally, there are occasional mummified cells with condensed cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei. Subtyping classical Trott lymphoma on a needle core biopsy is generally not done and the differential includes mixed cellularity and nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma. Given the thick band or fibrosis seen in the specimen, we favor a nodular sclerosing subtype.  On submitted immunostains the Khangura cells show membranous and Golgi pattern CD30 and CD15 staining, and are negative for CD20, CD45, CD5, and CD10 with internal positive control    Additional immunohistochemical studies are performed at Stanford on provided unstained slides as follows: The large cells are OCT2 positive, BOB1 positive, and are negative for PAX5 with internal positive control and negative for EBV by Moore in situ hybridization and negative for ALK, both with external positive control.    Imaging: We personally reviewed the imaging and agree with the impressions as described above. Specifically, we reviewed Mr. Doroshow's initial PET/CT conducted in September  demonstrating his hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm, including his mediastinal disease and large right groin lesion. We also reviewed his mid-treatment PET/CT from December showing a complete metabolic response.    12/15/2017 PET/CT  IMPRESSION  1. Interval complete metabolic resolution of right iliac, inguinal as well as mediastinal, bilateral hilar and right axillary lymph nodes, representing favorable response to treatment.  2. Extensive FDG uptake in cervical, paraspinal, axillary, mediastinal and peritoneal brown fat.    FINDINGS:  Head and neck: Extensive FDG uptake in cervical, paraspinal, axillary, mediastinal and peritoneal brown fat, which limits the evaluation of lymphoma. Interval complete metabolic resolution of bilateral hilar and anterior mediastinal nodes as well as left axillary nodes.  Limited evaluation of the brain demonstrates intense FDG uptake in the visualized cerebral cortex gray matter. This high physiologic background activity reduces the sensitivity of PET for malignant processes. Physiologic FDG uptake is seen in the ocular muscles, salivary glands, oropharynx, and vocal cords There are no pathologically enlarged cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes. The thyroid gland is unremarkable.    Thorax: No hypermetabolic pulmonary nodule.  Lung parenchymal evaluation, including for punctate nodules, is limited by low dose CT and non-breathhold technique. Physiologic FDG uptake is present in the myocardium. There is no pleural or pericardial effusion. The thoracic aorta and main pulmonary artery are grossly normal in caliber. There are no pathologically enlarged or hypermetabolic axillary, mediastinal, or hilar lymph nodes. Right chest port with tip terminating the cavoatrial junction.     Abdomen and pelvis: Physiologic FDG uptake is present in the liver, spleen, and bowel. The adrenal glands and pancreas are unremarkable on the non-contrast CT.  The kidneys, ureters,  and urinary bladder are visualized per clearance of the radiotracer. Intense signal from excreted tracer limits evaluation for malignancy in the urinary tract. The abdominal aorta is grossly normal in caliber. Interval metabolic resolution of right iliac and inguinal lymph nodes to background, see measurements in index lesions.    Musculoskeletal: Physiologic FDG uptake is present in the axial and proximal appendicular skeleton.  No suspicious lytic or sclerotic osseous lesions are visualized on the CT.    Index lesions:  Anterior mediastinal mass adjacent to main pulmonary artery: resolved  Right hilar node: resolved   Aortocaval node: resolved  Right iliac nodal conglomerate (CT image 258): 3.9x2.1cm, SUVmax 2.2, prior 6.1 x 4.2 cm (SUVmax 9.6)      Right inguinal node (CT image 285): 1.9cm, SUVmax 2.4, prior 2.6 cm (SUVmax 12.7)      Deauville: 3    10/25/2017 PET MR  IMPRESSION  Mediastinal mass, supra- and infradiaphragmatic nodal disease and focal lesion in the spleen as described above, consistent with Grove's lymphoma.     FINDINGS:   BRAIN:   The brain is unremarkable.  SINUSES:   The paranasal sinuses are normal.    NECK:  No abnormal cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy identified.     CHEST:  There is an inhomogenous mass in the anterior mediastinum with dimensions of 5.2 cm anteroposterior, 4.6cm mediolateral and 5.1cm anteroposterior, and an SUV 8.61. The lesion shows a central T2-hyperintense area, consistent with a central necrosis.    There are additional hypermetabolic nodes in the anterior-superior mediastinum with a size of 1.1x0.9x0.9cm and at the right hilum with a size of 1.2x1.1x1.1cm, SUV 6.93.    No evidence for pulmonary nodules. Please note that MRI has a limited sensitivity for the detection of pulmonary nodules with a diameter of less than 5 mm.   No pleural effusion. No pericardial effusion. Thoracic aorta and pulmonary artery are of normal diameter.    ABDOMEN/PELVIS:  There  are multiple enlarged and hypermetabolic lymph nodes along the inferior vena cava, the bilateral common iliac vein, the right external and internal iliac vein and the right groin.  The largest lesion in the aortocaval window measures 1.7 x 1.3 x 1.3 cm and an SUV of 5.54  The right external iliac nodal conglomerate measures 5.7 x 3.6 x 4.5 cm and has an SUV 10.66,   the right internal iliac nodal conglomerate measures 5.2 x 2.9 x 4.8 cm, with an SUV 11.5  The largest right inguinal node measures 2.9 x 2.6 x 2.5 cm, and has an SUV 14.5    In addition, there is a mildly hypermetabolic, focal lesion in the lower pole of the spleen (Seq 38/24 and 409/41), which measures 1.5x1.4x1.5cm and has an SUV 4.89.      The liver, gallbladder, bilateral adrenal glands and kidneys, and the pancreas are normal. Abdominal aorta is of normal caliber.    MUSCULOSKELETAL:  There are no abnormal focal lesions in the bones or bone marrow.    10/23/2017 CXR  IMPRESSION  1. Findings consistent with lymphoma within the chest, abdomen and to the greatest degree pelvis as desribed above. The most hypermetabolic focus is extending around the LEFT ventricle with a maximum SUV of 7.5. It is unclear if this is physiologic from the heart itself versus a new lesion although a soft tissue lesion was not seen in this location of prior CT scan obtained one week ago therefore I favor this to be artifact. The most hypermetabolic lymph node is in the RIGHT inguinal chain where there is a 2.6 similar lymph node with a maximum SUV of 12.7.        10/05/2017 CT (Outside)  IMPRESSION  1. 4.5x3.2cm sized heterogenous somewhat low-density mass in the mediastinum adjacent to the main pulmonary artery presumably related to the reported Ruane's disease. Additionally there is a minimally enlarged RIGHT hilar lymph node, numerous mildly enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes, as well as multiple enlarged RIGHT pelvic inguinal lymph nodes.  2. Mild splenomegaly though with no focal splenic abnormality detected    Lymphoma Staging Conference     Impression and Plan:  In summary, Mr. Pierce Kamboj is a 27 year-old man with a history of zotser in 2015, stage IIIAS classic Hodgkin lymphoma, IPS 1 (male), with involved sites including the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. At presentation, his mediastinal and right iliac disease both measured greater than 5cm at largest dimension. He is undergoing Stanford V chemotherapy due to low EF of 47% and experienced a complete metabolic response on interim PET/CT with Deauville 3. He presents for consideration of adjuvant radiation therapy.    Mr. Picard  presented with disease in the following nodal regions: (i) right axilla, (ii) mediastinum, (iii) left hilum, (iv) right hilum, (v) para-aortic, (vi) right iliac, and (vii) right inguinal. Since he has involvement of lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm, he is Stage III. He did not present with any B symptoms (fevers, drenching night sweats, or unintentional weight loss). In addition to the nodal sites listed above, he had splenic involvement based on FDG-avidity on PET imaging, but did not have macroscopic splenic disease on CT evaluation. At presentation. he had two sites that were greater than 5cm at largest dimension, (i) mediastinum (5.4cm), and (ii) right iliac (6.1cm). His International Prognostic Score (IPS) is 1 based on being male (Hasenclever et al., NEJM 1998). Overall, Mr. Funderburk presented with Stage IIIAS, classic Judson's Lymphoma, IPI 1 disease, with mediastinal and right groin disease >5cm at presentation.  Mr. Jost underwent chemotherapy with the Stanford V regiment management of his Hodgkin's Disease. Patients with stage III classic Teng's Disease treated with Stanford V have an excellent overall 5-year failure free rate of 71%, based on data from E2496 (Nolte et al., JCO 2013). Mr. Hinrichsen had an excellent overall response to chemotherapy on his interim PET/CT, with complete metabolic resolution of his initial disease in the right iliac and inguinal, mediastinal, bilateral hilar, and right axillary lymph nodes. Based on these results, we anticipate that Mr. Funderburk will achieve a Deauville 1-4 on his end-of-treatment PET/CT, whereby we typically recommend involved-site radiation therapy to initial sites of disease greater than 5cm. This recommendation is guided by data from E2496 (Osterman et al., JCO 2013) and single-institutional data (Randolph et al., JCO 2012), whereby patients treated with Stanford V received radiation to any pre-treatment region >5cm or for macroscopic splenic  disease on initial CT evaluation with excellent results.   At presentation, Mr. Cepeda's mediastinal mass and right iliac node were both greater than 5cm. While Mr. Maloney had FDG-avid splenic disease on PET imaging, he did not demonstrate macroscopic splenic disease on his initial CT. Therefore, we recommend adjuvant involved-site radiation therapy to his mediastinal mass and right iliac node, but not to his spleen. Regarding dose, we typically recommend treatment with 30Gy to any sites negative on interim PET/CT and up to 36Gy for any sites positive on interim PET/CT. Since all of Mr. Yao's areas of disease appeared negative on his interim PET/CT, we recommend treatment with 30Gy.  For our radiation fields, we will utilize Involved Site Radiation Therapy (ISRT), whereby our target volumes will be based on Mr. Mccormack' pre-chemotherapy FDG-avid disease modified to conform to changes in anatomy and reduction in disease burden after chemotherapy (Specth et al., IJROBP 2013). We will only include the initially regions in his mediastinum and right iliac area that measured greater than 5cm at presentation, and not his other initially involved sites.  With respect to radiation, we recommend treating Mr. Nigro's with involved site radiation therapy (ISRT) to his initial sites of disease (greater than 5cm) in the mediastinum and right iliac region to a total dose of 30Gy in 20 fractions (1.5Gy per fraction) over the course of 4-5 weeks using an intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) or 3D-conformal technique. Radiation treatment will begin ~1-2 weeks following simulation scan, and occur daily, Monday through Friday. Rapid Arc VMAT (volume-modulated arc therapy), a special form of IMRT, will be required in order to conformally treat our target while avoiding nearby organs at risk, principally the heart, lungs, thyroid, spinal cord, and major blood vessels. Prior to commencing treatment, a  CT simulation scan will be  performed in order to accurately delineate our targets of radiation therapy. For his simulation scan, we will obtain a CT with contrast as well as a PET/CT (which will also serve as his end-of-treatment PET/CT) in order to help delineate our targets. The CT scan will be performed with his arms up. We will obtain a scan using a deep inspiratory breath hold to keep his heart away from our treatment field in the mediastinum. We will also obtain a free-breathing CT scan for his treatment of his right groin.In addition, we anticipate the necessity of image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT) techniques including weekly cone beam CT and daily kV imaging for accurate tumor position verification.  We will plan to treat his two targets, the mediastinum and the right groin, concurrently. During treatment we will follow Mr. Nickel blood counts. If he demonstrates bone marrow suppression during our treatments then we will limit treatment to a single field and resume treatment with the second field.  Acute side effects may include but are not limited to fatigue, skin changes, throat irritation, low-grade nausea, bone marrow suppression, loose stools, or skin irritation. Long-term side effects may include but are not limited to thyroid dysfunction, increased risk of cardiac disease, radiation pneumonitis, and a small risk of secondary malignancies. Mr. Funderburk has a history of herpes zoster and we explained that radiation could increase his changes of herpes zoster reactivation but we do not recommend any prophylactic measures.    As a result of his radiation for Hodgkin's lymphoma, Mr. Ghate is at risk for late side effects that will require ongoing monitoring. Due to elevated risk of cardiovascular disease, we recommend a stress echocardiogram 10 years after completing radiation. He should also have CBCs checked at every visit, annual thyroid function tests, and lipid screening.  In addition, we recommend that all patients treated  for Saleem's lymphoma receive an annual flu shot, maintain regular exercise, eat a healthy diet, and refrain from smoking.    Regarding Mr. Just' skin rash, we recommend he follow up with medical oncology, particularly before his next chemotherapy infusion.    We explained all these recommendations in detail, including the rationale, technique, and potential short and long-term side effects of radiation treatment, as discussed above.    Mr. Glynn Deberry asked appropriate questions, which were answered completely to his satisfaction. Written informed consent was obtained. He knows he can contact us at any point with any additional questions or concerns.    Plan  - Informed written consent obtained to proceed with radiation therapy therapy  - We recommendinvolved site radiation therapy (ISRT) to initial sites of disease (greater than 5cm) in the mediastinum and right iliac region to a total dose of 30Gy in 20 fractions (1.5Gy per fraction)  - Simulation will be CT with contrast, with arms above head, with deep inspiratory breath hold and training, along with a same-day PET/CT (that will also serve as his end-of-treatment PET/CT)  - Treatment of mediastinal field to be conducted in deep inspiratory breath hold; treatment of right groin to be conducted free-breathing  - Plan to treat both sites concurrently; we will monitor bloodwork and may change to sequential treatment if there significant marrow suppression  - Follow up with medical oncology regarding skin rash    Future Appointments       Provider Department Dept Phone Address    01/24/2018 WITTELES/PAYNE Cardiovascular Med 999-999-9999 300 Pasteur DriveA21, Heart Clinic 611 1N22 Forest Svc Rd, San Bernardino CA     01/24/2018 LEVEL ONE Infusion Treatment Area 547 Janice Ln, Laplace LA     01/24/2018 Kretzschmar, 26 Vvv Rd, Sentinel Butte ND     01/24/2018 ITA MED ONC Infusion Treatment  Area 664 U29 Rd, Norwood CO         Thank you for allowing us the privilege of participating in the care of Mr. King Mcmurry. Radiation Oncology Consultation    Summary of Your Appointment with Dr. Amidon.    Dr. Shakir recommends radiation treatment for about 4 weeks.      *Planning for Your Treatment:  Our Radiation Therapy Coordinator will be contacting you for a PET/CT simulation appointment in the Radiation Therapy Department.  Please expect to be in the department for 1-2 hours.  A unique treatment plan is created for each patient using information gathered during the simulation.  A return appointment to start radiation treatment will be given to you at the end of your simulation.    *Instructions for Your Simulation Appointment: Our scheduler will review any prep instructions with you prior to your treatment planning session.     PET/CT Scan Preparation Instructions:    Prep Instructions  NON DIABETIC PATIENTS   Food: Nothing to eat 6 hours prior to the scan  Liquids: Drink only water for 6 hours before the scan.   Drink 4-6 glasses of water during the fast time as being well hydrated is recommended.   You may take your other medications with water only.    CT Scan with Contrast Preparation  *Please refrain from eating a minimum of 3  hours prior to your appointment.     *If you are a diabetic and taking medication, please follow the preparation below:  You should stop taking Metformin or any medicine that contains Metformin for 48 hours after the scan and have your kidney function (Creatinine) tested before restarting your Metformin medication.      *Your Daily Treatments:  Usually, patients receive treatment 5 days a week (Monday through Friday) with weekends off treatment to rest and recover. You will spend about 45 minutes in the Radiation Therapy Department during your treatment days. The specific number of treatments you will get will be based on the type of tumor, its location, and your individualized treatment plan.  Your provider will discuss this schedule with you during or after your simulation appointment.    Contact  Information    Call 911 if you experience:  ¿ Chest pain  ¿ Shortness of breath    Please contact your provider if you experience any of the following:  ¿ Increased pain, unrelieved by prescribed pain medication.  ¿ Fever, above 100.3 degrees F or 38.0 degrees C    Clinic Phone:  999-999-9999  After Hours:  999-999-9999    For information about radiology tests (CT, PET-CT, MRI, bone scan) including location of exams or scheduling of these studies, contact:    Stanford Radiology: 999-999-9999    At Stanford Radiation Oncology, we strive to provide an outstanding patient experience, and we value your feedback at any point throughout your journey.  You may also receive a survey in the mail, and we would appreciate your time and willingness to complete this as it will help ensure that we are meeting our goal and let us know of any areas that may need improvement.      Thank you for allowing us to be part of your care. Impression/Plan   Sunshine Yakubov is a 27 Y male with stage IIIA classical Dalla lymphoma, with an IPS score of 1 for male gender. Involved sites of disease include the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. Due to his baseline EF of 47%, we recommended Stanford V in lieu of ABVD given the lower total doxorubicin dose.     1. Clark lymphoma  - Most recent PET/CT demonstrates complete response to treatment  - Labs and exam adequate to proceed with treatment today:    Chemotherapy  Week 12, Day 1 = 01/24/2018   Body surface area is 2.29 meters squared.  · Bleomycin 5 units/m2 IV on D1  · Vincristine 1 mg IV on D1 (50%  reduction given possible neuropathy)  · Prednisone 40 mg/kg PO every other day (now in taper)    Supportive Care  · Bactrim PO BID on Saturday/Sunday (will continue for 2 weeks following completion of prednisone taper along with Protonix)  · Protonix 40 mg PO daily  · Hijaz PO BID daily    - Painful erection may represent neuropathy, though etiology unclear, so will dose-reduce vincristine   - Radiation to spleen planned so will need revaccination with PCV13, PPSV23, meningococcal, and Hib at least 2 weeks prior to radiation    2. Mild cardiomyopathy  - Repeat echocardiogram at end of treatment; EF stable to improved  - Will continue lisinopril and carvedilol for the time being  - F/u with cardiology in 3 months    3. Pruritis  - May be reaction to steroid taper vs underlying eczema  - Rx for hydroxyzine and topical benadryl sent to pharmacy  - Recommended oatmeal bath and calamine lotion  - Referral to supportive derm onc placed today    RTC 3 months after radiation completion with CT scan (Rad Onc to arrange)    Patient seen and examined by Leonard, NP and attending physician Dr. Syniah Workman. "Physician to Physician Radiology Consult Line: (999-999-9999" Signed WHOLE-BODY F18-FDG PET-CT: 02/01/2018 CLINICAL HISTORY: 27 years of age, Male, with history of stage?IIIA classical Abramovitz lymphoma, status post Stanford V chemotherapy x 6 cycles, prior PET/CT demonstrated complete metabolic resolution. This PET/CT scan is requested for surveillance. PET SEQUENCE: Subsequent treatment strategy COMPARISON: PET CT 12/15/2017. PROCEDURE COMMENTS:  Tracer information: Measured (injected) dose: 10.8 mCi. Injection site: Scoggin. Imaging information, imaging parameters, and additional medications: Anatomical region: The area imaged included the vertex to mid thighs. Lasix: None. Oral contrast: None. IV contrast: None. CT dose information: Based on a 32 cm phantom, the estimated radiation dose (CTDIvol [mGy]) for each series in this exam is 16.2. The estimated cumulative dose (DLP [mGy-cm]) is 1584. Scan technique: Following IV administration of the radiopharmaceutical, images were acquired using a Siemens PET-CT scanner. A low-dose CT scan was performed for attenuation correction and anatomic correlation only. If a comprehensive diagnostic CT is required, the Department of Radiology should be consulted for an adjunct CT study. Images were reconstructed using OSEM, and both OSEM and BSREM algorithms when studies were acquired on scanner models MI and 710. On these scanners, future reconstruction will only be with BSREM. Images were reviewed in the axial, coronal, and sagittal planes. For descriptive purposes, the maximum standard uptake value (SUV max) of metabolically active tissues is reported in g/mL, unless stated otherwise.  Baseline measurements: Current mean liver SUV: 2.3 g/mL. Prior mean liver SUV: 1.9 g/mL. FINDINGS: Head and neck: Limited evaluation of the brain demonstrates intense FDG uptake in the visualized cerebral cortex gray matter. This high physiologic background activity reduces the sensitivity of PET for malignant processes. Physiologic FDG uptake is seen in the ocular muscles, salivary glands, oropharynx, and vocal cords There are no pathologically enlarged cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes. The thyroid gland is unremarkable. Thorax: Right chest port in place, terminating near cavoatrial junction. No hypermetabolic pulmonary nodule.  Lung parenchymal evaluation, including for punctate nodules, is limited by low dose CT and non-breathhold technique. Physiologic FDG uptake is present in the myocardium. There is no pleural or pericardial effusion. The thoracic aorta and main pulmonary artery are grossly normal in caliber. Few FDG avid right axillary nodes are visualized, with SUV measuring up to 14.0 (CT image 103). These lymph nodes appear to be morphologically normal on the CT images. There are no pathologically enlarged or hypermetabolic, mediastinal, or hilar lymph nodes. Abdomen and pelvis: Physiologic FDG uptake is present in the liver, spleen, and bowel. The adrenal glands and pancreas are unremarkable on the non-contrast CT.  The kidneys, ureters, and urinary bladder are visualized per clearance of the radiotracer. Intense signal from excreted tracer limits evaluation for malignancy in the urinary tract. The abdominal aorta is grossly normal in caliber. Grossly unchanged right iliac and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Musculoskeletal: Physiologic FDG uptake is present in the axial and proximal appendicular skeleton.  No suspicious lytic or sclerotic osseous lesions are visualized on the CT. Index lesions: Anterior mediastinal mass adjacent to main pulmonary artery: resolved Right hilar node: resolved  Aortocaval node: resolved Right iliac nodal conglomerate (CT image 359): 3.9x2.1 cm, SUVmax 2.9, prior 3.9 x 2.1 cm (SUVmax 2.2) Right inguinal node (CT image 393): 1.8 cm, SUVmax 2.5, prior 1.9 cm (SUVmax 2.4) Right axillary lymph nodes as detailed above Deauville: X

PRIMARY/REFERRING ONCOLOGIST: Zissy Juarez, MD    ONCOLOGIC HISTORY:   History of stage IIIA classical Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 09/29/2017  - s/p 12 cycles of Stanford V chemotherapy (11/06/2017 -01/24/2018) (doxorubicin/vinblastine/etoposide/prednisone alternating weeks with Bleomycin/vincristine/prednisone, with supportive care with Bactrim PO BID on Saturday/Sunday, protonix, Ranker)  - planning to start XRT (plan for 30 Gy) to mediastinum and right iliac region on 02/13/2018    HPI/SKIN EXAM/ASSESSMENT&PLAN:   1. Generalized pruritus with minimal skin findings in setting of chemotherapy, appears to be improving. Patient received his last dose of Stanford V chemo on 01/24/2018. His last dose of PO prednisone (10 mg dose) was on 01/30/2018. He reports that, during the time that his prednisone started to be tapered during week 11 of chemo, he started noticing itching from his neck to his knees. The itching was initially constant and severe. He also developed a rash on his arms and abdomen, which has gotten much better. Today, the patient reports that he has been applying a topical benadryl cream to areas of rash and taking hydroxyzine 25 mg QID. Now, itching is not constant, however he has "random itch attacks" periodically throughout the day and usually for a few hours at night. Reports that itching was never a problem for his before his diagnosis or when he was diagnosed.   Examination with faint pink eczematous papules with minimal scale on the bilateral lower abdomen and upper arms.  -- recommend optimizing antihistamine tx: start Zyrtec 10 mg Q AM, increase hydroxyzine dose from 25 mg QIDto 75 mg nightly. Slow up-titration discussed; take 50 mg tonight, if no somnolence and still itchy, may increase to 75 mg  tomorrow night and continue at this dose.   -- start triamcinolone 0.1% cream BID to active areas on arms and abdomen. SE reviewed, including but not limited to atrophy, striae, dyspigmentation, acneiform eruption, bruising. Patient understands.  -- re-evaluate next week; IF continued pruritus despite above measures, will check generalized pruritus labs including thyroid studies     2. Melanocytic nevus, L lateral chest. Patient reports mole on left chest that has been present "all his life." Denies any changes including growth, itching, or bleeding. At one point in the past he "scratched part of it off." No personal history of skin cancer. Family history unknown as he was adopted.   Examination with 6 mm round uniform brown papule on left lateral chest  -- discussed warning signs of skin cancer, including the ABCDEs of melanoma   -- encouraged monthly self skin exams and annual total body skin examinations  -- monitor; will plan to biopsy if any changes/evolution    RETURN TO CLINIC: next week     Review of Systems  ROS reviewed: fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, SOB, constipation, diarrhea, change in appetite, cough, unintended weight loss, headache, chest pain, vision change, dizziness, painful urination, anxiety, depression, joint pain, numbness, easy bruising/bleeding. PRIMARY/REFERRING ONCOLOGIST: Vicki Celentano, MD    ONCOLOGIC HISTORY:   History of stage IIIA classical Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 09/29/2017  - s/p 12 cycles of Stanford V chemotherapy (11/06/2017 -01/24/2018) (doxorubicin/vinblastine/etoposide/prednisone alternating weeks with Bleomycin/vincristine/prednisone, with supportive care with Bactrim PO BID on Saturday/Sunday, protonix, Sasse)  - planning to start XRT (plan for 30 Gy) to mediastinum and right iliac region on 02/13/2018    HPI/SKIN EXAM/ASSESSMENT&PLAN:   1. Generalized pruritus with minimal skin findings in setting of chemotherapy, appears to be improving. Patient received his last dose of Stanford V chemo on 01/24/2018. His last dose of PO prednisone (10 mg dose) was on 01/30/2018. He reports that, during the time that his prednisone started to be tapered during week 11 of chemo, he started noticing itching from his neck to his knees. The itching was initially constant and severe. He also developed a rash on his arms and abdomen, which has gotten much better. Today, the patient reports that he has been applying a topical benadryl cream to areas of rash and taking  hydroxyzine 25 mg QID. Now, itching is not constant, however he has "random itch attacks" periodically throughout the day and usually for a few hours at night. Reports that itching was never a problem for his before his diagnosis or when he was diagnosed.   Examination with faint pink eczematous papules with minimal scale on the bilateral lower abdomen and upper arms.  -- recommend optimizing antihistamine tx: start Zyrtec 10 mg Q AM, increase hydroxyzine dose from 25 mg QIDto 75 mg nightly. SE reviewed, including but not limited to atrophy, striae, dyspigmentation, acneiform eruption, bruising. Patient understands.  -- re-evaluate next week; IF continued pruritus despite above measures, will check generalized pruritus labs including thyroid studies     2. Melanocytic nevus, L lateral chest. No personal history of skin cancer. Family history unknown as he was adopted. Stanford Healthcare    RADIATION ONCOLOGY TREATMENT SUMMARY    Izel Babovic, MD    Dear Doctor(s) ,     Your patient Lon Lowy was treated here in the Stanford Radiation Oncology Department from 02/13/2018 to 03/12/2018 and the following is a concise summary of the treatment administered.     DIAGNOSIS: Advanced classic Hodgkin lymphoma     IDENTIFICATION and INDICATIONS:   Mr. Ronnie Wile is a 27 year-old man with a history of zoster in 2015, stage IIIAS classic Hodgkin lymphoma, IPS 1 (male), with involved sites including the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. At presentation, his mediastinal and right iliac disease both measured greater than 5cm at largest dimension. He is undergoing Stanford V chemotherapy due to low EF of 47% and experienced a complete metabolic response on interim PET/CT with Deauville 3.     Mr. Lowy underwent consolidative radiotherapy for disease control. Mr. Prine was initially seen for consultation and after he indicated an understanding of the rationale, risks, and potential benefits of radiation therapy, informed consent was obtained and placed in the medical record.     COURSE: A CT simulation was performed with Mr. Lowy in the supine position. A customized immobilization device was created to minimize inter-fraction variability in patient positioning. Target volumes were delineated using computerized software and special care was taken to limit the radiation dose to surrounding critical structures. Mr. Lowy was seen weekly on treatment for side effect management and supportive care. The treatment was tolerated without unexpected side effects. He had moderate nausea managed with Zofran, mild dysphagia, otherwise no toxicities. It was a pleasure to see Mr Thomas today in the cardiomyopathy clinic for routine follow up. We were of course disappointed with the decrease in LV function on today's repeat echocardiogram as detailed above. This is certainly related to the self-discontinuation of carvedilol and entresto and much of the visit today was spent discussing the importance of restarting these medications without interruption. We also asked that he contact our clinic with any side effects and certainly prior to adjusting/discontinuing the medications. We will see him back in 3 months time with a repeat echocardiogram but will attempt to increase the medications via telephone in the interim. Follow Up Visit      Name: Finnley Parikh  DOB: 05/29/1990  MRN: [000000]   Address:   23 1742nd Dr, Espanola NM   Phone:   999-999-9999 (home)     Date: 05/15/2018   Attending Physician: Nelson Clair Oser, MD    Blythe Solberg, MD  Lymphoma Clinic  116 D650 Rd, Jay OK     Dear Doctors,     We had the pleasure of seeing our mutual patient, Mr. Finnley Parikh, in routine follow up today, 05/15/2018, in the Department of Radiation Oncology at Stanford Hospital & Clinics.     Identification: Mr. Finnley Parikh is a 27 Year-old male with Stage IIIAS classic Hodgkin lymphoma, IPS 1 (male), with involvement of 7 Clatskanie  sites at presentation (mainly infradiaphragmatic). He was treated with Stanford V chemotherapy due to low EF of 47% with a complete metabolic response on interim PET/CT (Deauville 3), followed by consolidative RT to initial sites of bulky disease in the mediastinum and right groin to a dose of 30 Gy in 20 fractions, completed 03/12/2018. He returns for follow up visit with 2 weeks of cough and superficial back pain.    Interval Since Completion of Radiation Therapy: 2 months.    Last Clinic Visit: 04/30/2018 at which time he was doing well overall with mild groin pain that was resolving.    Interval History: He tolerated RT well, with moderate nausea managed with Zofran, and mild dysphagia.    Today, he reports 2 week of dry cough (initially with some phlegm coming up), with some wheezing. He believes the cough began after he was cleaning the house with excess dust exposure. He has not had a similar cough prior. He has tried over the counter cough medications without relief. He has mild associated shortness of breath, stable, no progressive. No pleuritic chest pain. He has seasonal allergies but never a cough. He had self discontinued carvedilol and entresto and was seen by Dr. Zahn on 4/11. He started coreg the day after that appointment and has the prior light  headedness, worse with exertion that occurred when he was taking the medication. He is hydrating very well.      Secondly, he also reports a shingles-like sensation, paresthesia which has spread to both sides of the back. He is having severe itching on his thighs but not prior to his diagnosis. No other environmental exposures, changes in soap, moisturizers, or detergents. He had shingles in 12/29/2015 on right flank. He saw a local doctor and was prescribed He had 4 months of pain and resolved.     Review of Systems: As per chronological history of present illness. Impression and Plan:  In summary, Mr. Finnley Parikh is a 27 Year-old male with Stage IIIAS classic Hodgkin lymphoma, IPS 1 (male), with involvement of 7 Dallas  sites at presentation (mainly infradiaphragmatic). He was treated with Stanford V chemotherapy due to low EF of 47% with a complete metabolic response on interim PET/CT (Deauville 3), followed by consolidative  RT to initial sites of bulky disease in the mediastinum and right groin to a dose of 30 Gy in 20 fractions, completed 03/12/2018. He returns today with 2 symptoms concerning him. First, regarding his cough, the differential is broad and includes reactive airways, seasonal allergies, Seavey, and less likely given his normal CXR and low lung dose, radiation pneumonitis. We do not favor pneumonitis without fever, normal CBC from today, and CXR without evidence of inflammatory reaction within or near the radiation treatment volume. We recommend trial of over the counter dextromethorphan cough syrup and establishment of care with a primary care physician for further evaluation of other possible etiologies. We also counseled him to avoid dust, pollen and other allergens that seem to possibly have triggered the cough. For his back skin pain and thigh itching, it is very superficial and reproducible diffusely on exam (not consistent with zoster, which he did have in 2015). He is going to follow with his dermatologist here, Dr. Suprenant who's team has contacted Mr. Parikh. Regarding his Wingo lymphoma, he remains clinically and serologically without recurrent disease and our recommendation for surveillance PET in 2 months remains given mild nodal uptake on his last PET in 01/29/2018. We will see him for follow up visit shortly after for review of his imaging.     Mr. Finnley Parikh asked appropriate questions, which were answered completely to his satisfaction. He knows he can contact us at any point with any additional questions or concerns.    Plan  - We ordered a CXR which is stable from prior, and we verbally communicated this with him. CBC without neutropenia or leukocytosis. Metabolic panel within normal limits. For his cough, we recommend dextromethorphan cough syrup and establishment of care with a primary care doctor for further evaluation and management.   - For his thigh itching and superficial back pain, we recommend  further evaluation with his dermatologist Dr. Plyler.   - Return in 2 months with PET/CT    Thank you for allowing us the privilege of participating in the care of Mr. Sylvan Mcclung. Please feel free to contact us with any questions or concerns. HPI:   Yitzchak Puckett is a pleasant 27 Y male with a past medical history of Merino lymphoma (diagnosed 09/29/2017) s/p chemotherapy and radiation c/b nonischemic cardiomyopathy who presents to clinic today alone for routine follow up.     We last saw him on 04/25/2018, at which time he exhibited NYHA Class II symptoms. At that visit we restarted carvedilol, started entresto after patient had self-discontinued lisinopril with decrease in EF, and asked that he return for follow up in 2 months with repeat echocardiogram.     He returns today feeling essentially unchanged from his previous visit. He continues to endorse decreased energy, which he believes is directly related to his cardiac medications. Fortunately, he continues to exercise at the gym 3-4 days per week where he walks on the treadmill for 35-40 minutes. Previously he was able to jog with the treadmill at an incline, in addition to lifting weights, but he is no longer able to exert himself to such an extent. Aside from symptoms of fatigue and difficulty sleeping, Mr Perales denies any additional complaints including recent shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, lightheadedness, edema, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea or syncope. Sadly, he continues to struggle financially as he does not currently qualify for disability despite the past 2 years of treatment for lymphoma and cardiomyopathy. He is optimistic about reapplying in December at which point he will have been out of work for 14 months which, he tells me, is the federal disability requirement. Mediport Removal  Patient Education     MEDIPORT REMOVAL      What to do after the procedure.  Please attempt the following if you are experience PAIN at procedure site:  -Place an ice pack on site for 20 minutes and then remove for a period of 20 minutes. May repeat as many times as needed.   -Tylenol or Advil over the counter is the first line of pain relief medication. Please follow labels instructions on dosing.   -If you have attempted the above for pain relief and they are not controlling the pain, please contact us during working hours at 999-999-9999 and after hours at 999-999-9999 or Page Operator and ask for IR MD pager number 27237.     Please follow the WOUND CARE instructions:  -The procedure site incision located on the neck area is closed via derma bond, and covered with steri-strips. The derma bond is absorbed and no care is needed after procedure.   -The steri-strips should remain in place for a period of seven days. After a week, the steri-strips can be removed. The catheter site is covered with a bio-patch and an opsite clear dressing. Please follow the class care instructions on how to take care of catheter. If you have not had a class on the care of catheter, please call your primary care provider or us at the number above.   -If you notice any of the following at the procedure site please inform us at the above phone number:     Oozing of liquid at site.     Pain.     Redness (not bruising).     Increased warmth.     Or any other concerns     Please follow the guidelines for ACTIVITY.    -For line removal, there are not any activity limitations.       For Patients Who Have Received Moderate Sedation      You must have someone drive you home when you leave the hospital.   We encourage you to have a responsible adult stay with you the first night.   For 24 hours after your procedure, do not do anything where you need                         to be mentally alert. This includes making important  decisions,                          operating machinery, signing important paperwork, etc.   Eat light for the first 24 hours and slowly increase as tolerated     Drink plenty of fluids.   If you are taking pain medications:   ?them as directed   ?not drink alcohol while taking narcotic pain medication   ?not drive   ?you are constipated, increase your fluid intake. You may take an over-the-counter stool softener. Call your primary care doctor if you have had no bowel movement after 3 days.

Previously a body builder and shares, "I used to have 4% body fat and now on prednisone I am trying to work out and fit in my wedding tux- cancer really messed with my self image". Currently attending college as full time student. Lives at home with parents.     Resources: Patient is not eligible for SDI/SSDI and he is worried about depending on his parents for finances and housing. His fiance, Allam, is completing her masters in accounting. He reports significant debt "I had to sell my 5-wheeler and truck and might have to file for bankruptcy". His insurance will be ending in the next few months and he was provided education on eligibility for Medi-Cal and options for covered california. Debt and financial stress are significant for him.     Mental Health and Substance Use: Patient initially denied any history of depression then stated, "we have been together since 2009 and the only time I felt like this before [referring to SI] was when we split up- I was drinking a lot". Patient reports age 22 maladaptive coping and excessive alcohol use but denies any other drug use. Patient reports first noticing return of depressed mood when diagnosed  with lymphoma and he had to move in with his parents and then reports worsening mood in past month. Feels burdensome to his family and reports the loss of income, loss of his previous occupation, physical health and changes in appearance contribute towards depressed mood. Additionally he reports persistent insomnia sleeping 2 hours per night. He reports owning 2 pistols which are locked in his bedroom, understanding of recommendation to store these elsewhere.     Clinical Impressions and Recommendations    Patient was understanding of social work recommendation for psychiatry evaluation and aware that psychiatric admission was not guaranteed and would be assessed during ER evaluation. Patient agreeable to voluntarily present to Stanford ER for evaluation stating, "I cannot go on like this" and reports readiness for engaging in regular psychotherapy and consideration of psychotropic medications if recommended by MD. Patient reports feeling burdensome to his family and fiance, states, "before this I used to support my parents and fiance I earned a lot and I was capable- I feel really emasculated after treatment". He reports that his fiance is his reason for living and persevering and he has a close friend Rein who lives 3 miles away whom he would reach out to if he feels depressed or suicidal. Patient endorses feelings of grief and loss around the life he previously enjoyed before his cancer diagnosis.     Outpatient oncology social worker will remain available to support psychosocial needs. MSW breifly provided overview of PHP, counseling, and voluntary psych admission. Patient requests psychiatry evaluation for possible admission to manage his depressed mood. Fuerst, Philip Lawrence, MD     11/08/2018 Stanford Hospital and Clinics ED Psychiatry Initial Evaluation and Consultation Date:  11/05/2018 Patient's Name: Rylee Ordway Medical Record Number: [000000] ID and Chief Complaint: Patient is a 28 Y,male Caucasian male  with a chief complaint of depression and suicidal ideation Brief description of patient's experience leading up to admission  Patient was encountered by Aditya Howe MSW at the Stanford  Cancer Center and accompanied to the ED for further assessment Legal Status: Voluntary History of Present Illness 28M with a psat medical history of stage IIIA Hodgkin Lymphoma  diagnosed in 09/29/2017, treated with CTX, completed in  01/29/2018, RXT to mediastinum and right groin with remission  of disease. Patient is now almost 8 months out of active  treatment. He was presenting as a routine visit and endorsed  suicidal ideation to the MSW as documented elsewhere. On approach in the ED by this writer patient speaks at length  about the multiple stressors related to his cancer illness  experience, including losing his job, financial toxicity,  burdening his fiancee, burdening his family, "not having purpose  or a plan," and experiencing feelings of hopelessness and  helplessness. He admits to feeling a low self worth and stating  that he feels a better option would be for him to not go on  living instead of burdening his loved ones. He admits to  suffering from this for months and more recently feeling "I have  run out of options." He describes a need to reach out to others  when he does not want to compromise his relationship with his  wife yet feels that it is hard for others to related to him. He  describes feeling like he has a compromised sense of self right  now. He shares that previously he had had low mood and wishes  preceding the cancer illness as documented elsewhere but at this  time relates much of his distress to the consequences of  treatment and cancer. He admits to having access to guns at home.  He denies any plans to actively harm himself or hurt himself. He  denies any death wishes at this time and states, "I just wanted  to come here to get help, I don't know what else I can do." He  admits to poor sleep, worsening his mood and cognition. He  relates variable appetite. He is enrolled in school now "which  will take 3.5 years to finish, I need to borrow money to file for  bankruptcy." He denies a history of manic symptoms. He denies a  history of psychotic symptoms. He denies currently using any  substances. He denies any history of PTSD symptoms. He denies any  history of obsessions or compulsions. Brief description of patient's experience leading up to admission: Presentation Upon Admission: You were depressed and having thoughts of wanting to end your life    Chief Complaint:   "wanting to end it all"    History of Present Illness:   Lessie Parkins is a 28 Y male with a past medical history of stage IIIA Hodgkin Lymphoma diagnosed in 09/29/2017, treated with CTX, completed in 01/29/2018, RXT to mediastinum and right groin with remission of disease. Patient is now almost 8 months out of active treatment. He was presenting as a routine visit and endorsed suicidal ideation.    ------------------Extracted from psych SW note --------------  Patient was brought from the cancer center after he disclosed to the SW that he has been contemplating suicide and he is plan to get access to his gun and end his life. Patient is  is a 28 Y with previous hx of psychiatric tx or condition in the past engaged caucasian male who resides in Turlock and was diagnosed with stage IIIA classical Akusoba lymphoma in 09/29/2017 who was treated with 12 cycles of Stanford V completed in 01/29/2018 followed by 30 Gy in 20 fractions of Radiation Therapy to the mediastinum and right groin completed 03/12/2018. He presents today in the lymphoma clinic for follow up and he is also followed by  Stanford Cardiology for nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Patient has been experiencing depression with  due to his medical conditions , patient with multiple psychosocial stressors, loss of job, loss of financial stability and loss of health, with no financial resources and unable to cope with his losses and his medical conditions.     Patient at the interview, very tearful, expressing hopelessness and helplessness, insomnia, sleeping 2 hours during the night, unable to manage his responsibilities and duties, Unable to perform at work due to his new cardiac diagnosis and cancer. Patient is dependent on parents who exhausted all their financial assests to help patient. Patient is feeling guilty and ashame about that " I become a burden on everyone, my parents, my fiance, I has a wedding  Planned, and have no financial assets to meet that deadline, I live with my parents now, with no job, I lost the job that I loved so much due to my cardiac condition" Patient doesn't feel safe outside of the hospital and feeling desperate for any help he can get, patient is motivated for TX and he would like to treat his depression and get recs for psych outpatient resources as well Financial resources. Patient with active SI and plan but not intent in acting on it at the hospital. " I need help, before my insurance expires in December" patient's fiancee is very supportive of patient and would like to be involved in his Tx . Patient will benefit from inpatient psych Tx, PHP and Outpatient psych TX after discharge.   -------------------------------------------------------------------------  -------------Extracted from Psych ED note with edits ------------------  On approach in the ED by this writer patient speaks at length about the multiple stressors related to his cancer illness experience, including losing his job, financial toxicity, burdening his fiancee, burdening his family, "not having purpose or a plan," and experiencing feelings  of hopelessness and helplessness. He admits to feeling a low self worth and stating that he feels a better option would be for him to not go on living instead of burdening his loved ones. He admits to suffering from this for months and more recently feeling "I have run out of options." He describes a need to reach out to others when he does not want to compromise his relationship with his wife yet feels that it is hard for others to related to him. He describes feeling like he has a compromised sense of self right now. He shares that previously he had had low mood and wishes preceding the cancer illness as documented elsewhere but at this time relates much of his distress to the consequences of treatment and cancer. He admits to having access to guns at home. He denies any plans to actively harm himself or hurt himself. FOr hte past several weeks he has been having thoughts of wanting to end his life, that it would be better if he were not here to be a burden on his family. "I just wanted to come here to get help, I don't know what else I can do." He admits to poor sleep, worsening his mood and cognition. He relates variable appetite. He is enrolled in school now "which will take 3.5 years to finish, I need to borrow money to file for bankruptcy." He denies a history of manic symptoms. He denies a history of psychotic symptoms. Coordinated Care Assessment   Vernon Treece is a 28 Y male and presented on 11/05/2018 for UNSPECIFIED MOOD (AFFECTIVE) DISORDER. The expected discharge date is to be determined       This psych CCM reviewed the charts and met with patient 1 to 1, Patient was brought from the cancer center after he disclosed to the SW that he has been contemplating suicide and he is plan to get access to his gun and end his life. Patient is  is a 28 Y with previous hx of psychiatric tx or condition in the past engaged caucasian male who resides in Turlock and was diagnosed with stage IIIA classical Dibble lymphoma in 09/29/2017 who was treated with 12 cycles of Stanford V completed in 01/29/2018 followed by 30 Gy in 20 fractions of Radiation Therapy to the mediastinum and right groin completed 03/12/2018. He presents today in the lymphoma clinic for follow up and he is also followed by Stanford Cardiology for nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Patient has been experiencing depression with  due to his medical conditions , patient with multiple psychosocial stressors, loss of job, loss of financial stability and loss of health, with no financial resources and unable to cope with his losses and his medical conditions.    Patient at the interview, very tearful, expressing hopelessness and helplessness, insomnia, sleeping 2 hours during the night, unable to manage his responsibilities and duties, Unable to perform at work due to his new cardiac diagnosis and cancer. Patient is dependent on parents who exhausted all their financial assests to help patient. Patient is feeling guilty and ashame about that " I become a burden on everyone, my parents, my fiance, I has a wedding  Planned, and have no financial assets to meet that deadline, I live with my parents now, with no job, I lost the job that I loved so much due to my cardiac condition" Patient doesn't feel safe outside of the hospital and feeling desperate for any help he can get, patient  is motivated for TX and he would like to treat his depression and get recs for psych outpatient resources as well Financial resources. Patient with active SI and plan but not intent in acting on it at the hospital. " I need help, before my insurance expires in December" patient's fiancee is very supportive of patient and would like to be involved in his Tx . Patient will benefit from inpatient psych Tx, PHP and Outpatient psych TX after discharge.     Patient will benefit from a referral to psych oncology psych Clinic, since he receives , his onc and cardiac care at Stanford health and clinics. Stanford Hospital and Clinics  ED Psychiatry Initial Evaluation and Consultation      Date:  11/05/2018  Patient's Name: Porche Neff  Medical Record Number: [000000]    ID and Chief Complaint: Patient is a 28 Y,male Caucasian male with a chief complaint of depression and suicidal ideation    Brief description of patient's experience leading up to admission   Patient was encountered by Faustino Mawhinney MSW at the Stanford Cancer Center and accompanied to the ED for further assessment    Legal Status: Voluntary    History of Present Illness  28M with a psat medical history of stage IIIA Hodgkin Lymphoma diagnosed in 09/29/2017, treated with CTX, completed in 01/29/2018, RXT to mediastinum and right groin with remission of disease. Patient is now almost 8 months out of active treatment. He was presenting as a routine visit and endorsed suicidal ideation to the MSW as documented elsewhere.  On approach in the ED by this writer patient speaks at length about the multiple stressors related to his cancer illness experience, including losing his job, financial toxicity, burdening his fiancee, burdening his family, "not having purpose or a plan," and experiencing feelings of hopelessness and helplessness. He admits to feeling a low self worth and stating that he feels a better option would be for him to not go on living instead of burdening his loved ones. He admits to suffering from this for months and more recently feeling "I have run out of options." He describes a need to reach out to others when he does not want to compromise his relationship with his wife yet feels that it is hard for others to related to him. He describes feeling like he has a compromised sense of self right now. He shares that previously he had had low mood and wishes preceding the cancer illness as documented elsewhere but at this time relates much of his distress to the consequences of treatment and cancer. He admits to having access to guns  at home. He denies any plans to actively harm himself or hurt himself. He denies any death wishes at this time and states, "I just wanted to come here to get help, I don't know what else I can do." He admits to poor sleep, worsening his mood and cognition. He relates variable appetite. He is enrolled in school now "which will take 3.5 years to finish, I need to borrow money to file for bankruptcy." He denies a history of manic symptoms. He denies a history of psychotic symptoms. He denies currently using any substances. He denies any history of PTSD symptoms. He denies any history of obsessions or compulsions. Relevant Imaging/Studies:  EKG (QTc): 410    Narrative Assessment:   28M with a past medical history of stage IIIA Hodgkin Lymphoma diagnosed 9/17, in remission s/p CTX,  RXT, now with chemo-induced cardiomyopathy, unemployed, bankrupt, with two weeks of suicidal ideation without a plan.  Patient endorses low mood, low self worth, helplessness, hopelessness, periods of passive death wishes, limited future orientation that are suggestive of a major depressive episode vs adjustment disorder given its duration of at least 2 weeks in the context of medical illness, financial toxicity and psychosocial stressors.       Given the patient's acute psychiatric decompensation and inability to safely discharge patient from SHC, the patient warrants inpatient psychiatric admission for stabilization, psychiatric workup, treatment adjustment, and transitional care  planning. Since the patient is willing to come into the hospital on a voluntary basis, we will defer LPS hold for now with the understanding that the patient will require urgent psychiatric evaluation for 5150 placement if the patient were to attempt to leave AMA.      Diagnostic Assessment:  Adjustment disorder     Update 11/06/2018: Patient already appears slightly improved since admission. The process of recognizing the symptoms and sharing them appears to have set him on a new track. Still burned out, tired, poor concentration, depressed, intermittent hopelessness, but wants to get into treatment. Starting zoloft today. Will arrange outpatient follow-up psychiatry and psychotherapy. Pt presents with broad affect, "better" mood, good eye contact and linear, goal-directed thought process.     Pt provides medical history and explains how it has impacted his life (loss of job and need for new career path, depleted finances and being more dependent on his family).  Pt is currently living with his parents who he reports have had to delay their retirement plans in order to help him financially. Pt has enrolled in Junior College and is pursuing a degree in business.  Pt has been with his fiance since 2009 and shares she is hugely supportive.     Pt is highly motivated to pursue out-patient mental health treatment but would like to continue attending school. CCM discussed PHP/IOP, therapy and psychiatry. Learning About Mood Disorders  What are mood disorders?    Mood disorders are medical problems that affect how you feel. They can impact your moods, thoughts, and actions. Mood disorders include:  · Depression. This causes you to feel sad or hopeless for much of the time.  · Bipolar disorder. This causes extreme mood changes from manic episodes of very high energy to extreme lows of depression.  · Seasonal affective disorder (SAD). This is a type of depression that affects you during the same season each year. Most often people experience SAD during the fall and winter months when days are shorter and there is less light.  What are the symptoms?  Depression  You may:  · Feel sad or hopeless nearly every day.  · Lose interest in or not get pleasure from most daily activities. You feel this way nearly every day.  · Have low energy, changes in your appetite, or changes in how well you sleep.  · Have trouble concentrating.  · Think about death and suicide. Keep the numbers for these national suicide hotlines: 1-800-273-TALK (1-999-999-9999) and 1-800-SUICIDE (1-999-999-9999). If you or someone you know talks about suicide or feeling hopeless, get help right away.  Bipolar disorder  Symptoms depend on your mood swings. You may:  · Feel very happy, energetic, or on edge.  · Feel like you need very little sleep.  · Feel overly self-confident.  · Do impulsive things, such as spending a lot of money.  · Feel sad or hopeless.  · Have racing thoughts or trouble thinking and making decisions.  · Lose interest in things you have enjoyed in the past.  · Think about death and suicide. Keep the numbers for these national suicide hotlines: 1-800-273-TALK (1-999-999-9999) and 1-800-SUICIDE (1-999-999-9999). If you or someone you know talks about suicide or feeling hopeless, get help right away.  Seasonal affective disorder (SAD)  Symptoms come and go at about the same time each year. For most people with SAD, symptoms come  during the winter when there is less daylight. You may:  · Feel sad, grumpy, moody, or anxious.  · Lose interest in your usual activities.  · Eat more and crave carbohydrates, such as bread and pasta.  · Gain weight.  · Sleep more and feel drowsy during the daytime.  How are mood disorders treated?  Mood disorders can be treated with medicines or counseling, or a combination of both.  Medicines for depression and SAD may include antidepressants.  Medicines for bipolar disorder may include:  · Mood stabilizers.  · Antipsychotics.  · Benzodiazepines.  Counseling may involve cognitive-behavioral therapy. It teaches you how to change the ways you think and behave. This can help you stop thinking bad thoughts about yourself and your life.  Light therapy is the main treatment for SAD. This therapy uses a special kind of lamp. You let the lamp shine on you at certain times, usually in the morning. This may help your symptoms during the months when there is less sunlight.  Healthy lifestyle  Healthy lifestyle changes may help you feel better.  · Get at least 30 minutes of exercise on most days of the week. Walking is a good choice.  · Eat a healthy diet. Include fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains in your diet each day.  · Keep a regular sleep schedule. Try for 8 hours of sleep a night.  · Find ways to manage stress, such as relaxation exercises.  · Avoid alcohol and illegal drugs.  Follow-up care is a key part of your treatment and safety. Be sure to make and go to all appointments, and call your doctor if you are having problems. It's also a good idea to know your test results and keep a list of the medicines you take.  Where can you learn more?  Go to www.example.com  Enter Z126 in the search box to learn more about "Learning About Mood Disorders."    Dr. Elias Aboujaoude   Stanford Psychiatry Clinic     RE: Dombek, Nisa   MRN: [000000]  DOB: 05/29/1990     Dear Colleagues,      We had the pleasure today of seeing Mr. Nisa Dewald at the Stanford Heart Failure and Cardiomyopathy Clinic with Dr. Nickolas Thai. Mr. Dewald, of course, is a very pleasant 28-year-old gentleman with a past medical history of Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in  09/29/2017, status post chemotherapy and radiation, was complicated by nonischemic cardiomyopathy likely secondary to anthracycline, who presented in clinic today in followup. Since Mr. Glowacki was seen in 06/29/2018, he continued to exhibit New York Heart Association class 2 symptoms, though he felt that his activity tolerance might be a little worse now than it was a little prior. He, overall, has been feeling rather down, and unfortunately was hospitalized in late October for suicidal ideations under the care of Dr. Olin. Fortunately, Mr. Koo is now feeling better, and is currently trying to maintain a more positive outlook in life. Mr. Fetter states that he continues to go to the gym several times a week, and tries to do as much of weightlifting and cardio as he could. He is very upset by the fact that he could not return back to his previous exercise tolerance no matter how hard he tries. He is able to spend some amount of time on the treadmill, but is unable to go at a faster pace that he would like, and feels that he tired out a lot easier. He is no longer able to jog up an incline, which troubles him significantly, and he attributed this partially to his "lack of motivation". Beyond that, he otherwise denied any chest pain, orthopnea, palpitation, PND, lower extremity edema, or any concerning findings. He continues to struggle with getting disability coverage, is working with primary care physician to obtain that, but beyond that, the review of systems was performed and is otherwise noncontributory.     Medication Reconciliation: Medication reconciliation was performed and included in note below.     Vitals And Physical Exam: Vitals and physical exam were performed, included in note.     Echocardiogram: Mr. Nery' echocardiogram was reviewed in clinic today, was notable for moderately reduced LV systolic function of a normal size LV, that appears slightly worse than the previous echocardiogram  from 6 months ago on side-to-side comparison.     Assessment And Plan: Overall, Mr. Kody Ghani is a very pleasant 28-year-old gentleman with history of Bukhari lymphoma status post chemoradiation, complicated by a nonischemic cardiomyopathy, who presented in clinic in followup. As a whole, Mr. Quraishi' activity tolerance remains stable to slightly worse, which is reflected on his left ventricular systolic function on echocardiogram as well. We spent a significant amount of time reassuring Mr. Dewald that his exercise tolerance is likely not due to his lack of motivation, but in fact, due to his limited left ventricular systolic function. To help him achieve better exercise tolerance as well as possible long-term benefit, we asked Mr. Dewald to increase his afterload reduction agents by increasing Entresto followed by increasing his carvedilol as long as he can tolerate without any side effects. We also, in addition, asked him to have his basic metabolic panel checked again in about 1 week's time after he increased the dose of his Entresto.
