12/09/2018        Dr. Abby Keogh   Stanford Oncology Clinic     Dr. Elias Aboujaoude   Stanford Psychiatry Clinic    RE: Perrin, Mairead   MRN: [000000]  DOB: 05/29/1990    Dear Colleagues,     We had the pleasure today of seeing Mr. Mairead Osborn at the Stanford Heart Failure and Cardiomyopathy Clinic with Dr. Izaiah Kutz. Mr. Osborn, of course, is a very pleasant 28-year-old gentleman with a past medical history of Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 09/29/2017, status post chemotherapy and radiation, was complicated by nonischemic cardiomyopathy likely secondary to anthracycline, who presented in clinic today in followup. Since Mr. Osborn was seen in 06/29/2018, he continued to exhibit New York Heart Association class 2 symptoms, though he felt that his activity tolerance might be a little worse now than it was a little prior. He, overall, has been feeling rather down, and unfortunately was hospitalized in late October for suicidal ideations under the care of Dr. Quick. Fortunately, Mr. Osborn is now feeling better, and is currently trying to maintain a more positive outlook in life. Mr. Plyler states that he continues to go to the gym several times a week, and tries to do as much of weightlifting and cardio as he could. He is very upset by the fact that he could not return back to his previous exercise tolerance no matter how hard he tries. He is able to spend some amount of time on the treadmill, but is unable to go at a faster pace that he would like, and feels that he tired out a lot easier. He is no longer able to jog up an incline, which troubles him significantly, and he attributed this partially to his "lack of motivation". Beyond that, he otherwise denied any chest pain, orthopnea, palpitation, PND, lower extremity edema, or any concerning findings. He continues to struggle with getting disability coverage, is working with primary care physician to obtain that, but beyond that, the  review of systems was performed and is otherwise noncontributory.    Medication Reconciliation: Medication reconciliation was performed and included in note below.    Vitals And Physical Exam: Vitals and physical exam were performed, included in note.    Echocardiogram: Mr. Osborn' echocardiogram was reviewed in clinic today, was notable for moderately reduced LV systolic function of a normal size LV, that appears slightly worse than the previous echocardiogram from 6 months ago on side-to-side comparison.    Assessment And Plan: Overall, Mr. Thaddeus Wiese is a very pleasant 28-year-old gentleman with history of Lemke lymphoma status post chemoradiation, complicated by a nonischemic cardiomyopathy, who presented in clinic in followup. As a whole, Mr. Osborn' activity tolerance remains stable to slightly worse, which is reflected on his left ventricular systolic function on echocardiogram as well. We spent a significant amount of time reassuring Mr. Rios that his exercise tolerance is likely not due to his lack of motivation, but in fact, due to his limited left ventricular systolic function. To help him achieve better exercise tolerance as well as possible long-term benefit, we asked Mr. Osborn to increase his afterload reduction agents by increasing Entresto followed by increasing his carvedilol as long as he can tolerate without any side effects. We also, in addition, asked him to have his basic metabolic panel checked again in about 1 week's time after he increased the dose of his Entresto. We asked Mr. Osborn to contact us should he start to experience any symptoms that can be attributed to the increased dose of medication.     Given the relative clinical stability, will ask Mr. Rigby to see us back in about 6 months' time, or certainly sooner should he experience any new symptoms that would indicate that his heart failure may be worsening. Thank you very much for allowing us to participate in the care of  this very nice gentleman.  Please do not hesitate to contact us with any additional questions or concerns. Scan technique: Following IV administration of the radiopharmaceutical, images were acquired using a MI PET-CT scanner. A low-dose CT scan was performed for attenuation correction and anatomic correlation only. CTAC dose information: Based on a 32 cm phantom, the estimated radiation dose (CTDIvol [mGy]) for each series in this exam is 6.7. The estimated cumulative dose (DLP [mGy-cm]) is 680.13. Images were reviewed in the axial, coronal, and sagittal planes. For descriptive purposes, the maximum standard uptake value (SUV max) of metabolically active tissues is reported in g/mL, unless stated otherwise. The image number corresponding to the CT series is provided in reference to findings. Outpatient Social Work Note:    Outpatient MSW briefly met with patient during his return to clinic visit to provide psychosocial support. Mr. Kropf returns to clinic with his supportive parents, Jeganathan and Yazdani and fiance Lucchesi. He reports that he felt anxious before having the results of his scan read and very relieved hearing positive news during this visit. Overall he reports stable mood at baseline and plan to continue seeing Dr. Azariah Po (psychiatrist) in Tulsa  and when he transitions to a new health care plan in the new year she has agreed to speak to his plan case manager to create a payment/coverage plan that will enable him to return for future visits. Patient does not require new psychiatry referrals at this time.     Additionally patient reports that he is hopeful that he will find a new job that will accommodate his cardiac health needs. He is considering a position as a military plane inspector and SW provided education on benefits/insurance eligibility with new employment advising that potentially he might lose eligibility for Covered California Health Plan and SSDI (which he is applying for using Pianka) and he is understanding. SW also provided education that he should contact the Stanford financial counselors to ensure his new plan is accepted at Stanford (provided referral). SW spent time providing active listening and emotional support as both patient and family shared some of the challenges they have encountered in this survivorship stage of illness (financial toxicity, patient will be filing for bankruptcy, need for career change). SW offered validation, encouragement and spent time identifying patient and family system strengths. Patient's family was appropriately tearful and shared they are committed to supporting patient until he is able to regain employment and support himself financially. SW agreed to remain available to assist with referrals and paperwork coordination needs.      Frei Thomson, MSW  Lymphoma & GU Oncology Social Worker  Phone: 999-999-9999  Pager: 25163

Involved sites of disease include the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. Due to his baseline EF of 47%, we recommended Stanford V in lieu of ABVD given the lower total doxorubicin dose. He completed 12 cycles of Stanford V in 01/29/2018 followed by 30 Gy in 20 fractions of RT to the mediastinum and right groin completed on 03/12/2018. He presents today 1 year and 4 months after all treatment for follow up.     # Hodgkin lymphoma  He is doing well from a lymphoma perspective with no significant cytopenias, constitutional symptoms, or lymphadenopathy. His recent CT NCAP showed no pathologic cervical lymphadenopathy; slightly decreased size of a subcentimeter prepulmonic node (0.9 cm); unchanged size of R pelvic sidewall/external iliac node conglomerate (1.5 x 2.0 cm, prior 1.7 x 2.4 cm) and R inguinal node (0.9 cm); and no new or enlarging lymphnodes in the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. We will continue to monitor him with surveillance CT imaging unless there is concern for new or enlarging nodes or suspicious findings.   - Plan to continue with routine surveillance:    Medical Oncology Follow Up Visits:  Every 3 months in the first two years following treatment   From year 2-5, every 6 months  From year 5 and beyond, annually    Testing schedule: (we will order all  of these test in medical oncology with the exception of the fasting lipid panel)  - lab work at 6, 12, 20, 24 and 36 months  1. CBC with differential  2. Chemistry profile  3. ESR (ESR was elevated at diagnosis to 29)  4. Beginning at 36 months, we also recommend an annual fasting lipid panel. This should be ordered by patient's primary doctor.  5. TSH (for hx of mediastinal radiation)    Imaging guidelines:   - CT scan of neck and chest 3 months from completion of radiation and CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis at the end of years 1 and 2 (PET completed 12/28/2018 as 1 year scan, next CT due in 02/29/2020)  - Chest X ray at 6, 36 and 60 months from treatment and again at the end of year 10 (next due 03/01/2021)   - Stress echo per cardiology schedule, given history of mild cardiomyopathy    # Mild cardiomyopathy  He is being followed by Dr. Ashe from the Heart Failure Clinic to manage his nonischemic cardiomyopathy (baseline EF: 45%). Most recent echo on 06/05/2019 showed an improved EF (45.3%) with an RVSP now estimated. Changed to annual follow-up visits.  - Continue carvedilol and sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto) per cardiology  - Continue to follow with cardiology (next visit: 05/29/2020 with ECHO on the same day)    # Dribbling of urine  He reports dribbling of urine and taking longer to urinate since the end of RT. He has no infectious symptoms or medications that could cause urinary retention.   - Advised to monitor for an increased frequency of symptoms and symptoms of UTI.    # Depression/anxiety  He recently discontinued zoloft and has not re-established care with a mental health provider due to scheduling difficulties. Once he is married in October, he plans to enroll in his spouse's benefit plan and may seek psychotherapy offered through this plan as his current Medi-cal plan has limited options  - Not eligible for SSDI for financial assistance. Plans to work for cousin's catering company.  - Provided  validation of stressors and reassurance during visit, discussed current and potential coping mechanisms  - ED if SI/HI    RTC in 3 months with labs (CBCD, CMP, ESR) with NP.     As usual, we encourage the patient to contact us should they develop any new symptoms or have any questions or concerns. Impression/Plan   Holli Yadlapati is a 29 Y male with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and stage IIIA nodular sclerosis classical Hodgkin lymphoma, with an IPS score of 1 for male gender. Involved sites of disease include the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. Due to his baseline EF of 47%, we recommended Stanford V in lieu of ABVD given the lower total doxorubicin dose. He completed 12 cycles of Stanford V in 01/29/2018 followed by 30 Gy in 20 fractions of RT to the mediastinum and right groin completed on 03/12/2018. He presents today 1 year and 8 months after all treatment for follow up.     # Hodgkin lymphoma  -  Labs and exam today are adequate to proceed with ongoing surveillance:    Medical Oncology Follow Up Visits:  Every 3 months in the first two years following treatment   From year 2-5, every 6 months  From year 5 and beyond, annually    Testing schedule: (we will order all of these test in medical oncology with the exception of the fasting lipid panel)  - lab work at 6, 12, 20, 24 and 36 months  1. CBC with differential  2. Chemistry profile  3. ESR (ESR was elevated at diagnosis to 29)  4. Beginning at 36 months, we also recommend an annual fasting lipid panel. This should be ordered by patient's primary doctor.  5. TSH (for hx of mediastinal radiation)    Imaging guidelines:   - CT scan of neck and chest 3 months from completion of radiation and CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis at the end of years 1 and 2 (PET completed 12/28/2018 as 1 year scan, next CT due in 02/29/2020)  - Chest X ray at 6, 36 and 60 months from treatment and again at the end of year 10 (next due 03/01/2021)   - Stress echo per cardiology schedule, given history of mild cardiomyopathy    # Mild cardiomyopathy  He is being followed by Dr. Bohn from the Heart Failure Clinic to manage his nonischemic cardiomyopathy (baseline EF: 45%). Most recent echo on 06/05/2019 showed an improved EF (45.3%) with an RVSP now estimated. Changed to annual follow-up visits.  - Continue carvedilol and sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto) per cardiology  - Continue to follow with cardiology (next visit: 05/29/2020 with ECHO on the same day)    # Depression/anxiety  - 10/22 -10/29/2019: admitted for suicidal ideation related to multiple stressors related to his "cancer illness experience, including losing his job, financial toxicity, burdening his fiancee, burdening his family"  - Mood is stable today without SI/HI  - Established good relationship with SW and will continue follow up    RTC in 4 months with labs (CBCD, CMP, ESR) with interval CT NCAP to review (ordered  in Epic)    Patient and father expressed understanding and agree with the plan as outlined above. They were encouraged to call sooner with any questions, concerns, or new symptoms in the interim.     Patient was seen and examined by Viviano, NP. Discussed plan with Dr. Guida Trent as attending physician who agrees with the above plan. Dr. Trent not physically present at this visit.         I reviewed the note and agree with the documented findings and plan of care.    Guida Trent M.D.  Professor of Medicine/Oncology

Involved sites of disease include the right groin/pelvis, infradiaphragmatic, and chest. Due to his baseline EF of 47%, we recommended Stanford V in lieu of ABVD given the lower total doxorubicin dose. He completed 12 cycles of Stanford V in 01/29/2018 followed by 30 Gy in 20 fractions of RT to the mediastinum and right groin completed on 03/12/2018. He presents today 3 years and 6 months after all treatment for follow up.     # Hodgkin lymphoma  Recent chest XR today showed no acute cardiopulmonary changes. Recent TTE with Dr. Read in 04/29/2021 demonstrated slightly worsened LVEF of 45% compared to TTE from 11/29/2018. Labs and exam today are adequate to proceed with ongoing surveillance:    Medical Oncology Follow Up Visits:     From year 2-5, every 6 months  From year 5 and beyond, annually    Testing schedule: (we will order all of these test in medical oncology with the exception of the fasting lipid panel)  - lab work at 6, 12, 20, 24 and 36 months  1. CBC with differential  2. Chemistry profile  3. ESR (ESR was elevated at diagnosis to 29)  4. Beginning at 36 months, we also recommend an annual fasting lipid panel. This should be ordered by patient's primary doctor.  5. TSH (for hx of mediastinal radiation)    Imaging guidelines:   2   - Chest X ray at 6, 36 and 60 months from treatment and again at the end of year 10 (next due 03/01/2023)   - Stress echo per cardiology schedule, given history of mild cardiomyopathy (due 10/29/2021)    # Mild cardiomyopathy  He is being followed by Dr. Kimple from the Heart Failure Clinic to manage his nonischemic cardiomyopathy (baseline EF: 45%). Most recent echo on 06/05/2019 showed an improved EF (45.3%) with an RVSP now estimated. Changed to annual  follow-up visits (next due 05/29/2020)  - Continue carvedilol, spironolactone and sacubitril-valsartan (Entresto) per cardiology  - Follow up in 10/29/2021 with TTE    # Depression/anxiety  - 10/22 -10/29/2019: admitted for suicidal ideation related to multiple stressors related to his "cancer illness experience, including losing his job, financial toxicity, burdening his fiancee, burdening his family"  - Mood is stable today without SI/HI  - Established good relationship with SW and will continue follow up    # R medial rib pain  In 06/29/2021, he developed intermittent, 1-2/10, cramp pain to his R medial rib cage below his R nipple that became increasingly persistent over the last month. He denies trauma, injury, rash, inspiratory pain, R sidelying pain, or pain that wakes him from sleep. He does not require use of medications or supportive care measures. His pain is likely related to a musculoskeletal injury given his recent increase in exercise.   - Continue to monitor for worsening pain  - Encouraged to notify our clinic if he develops a rash    RTC 6 months for video visit with labs done prior (CBCD, CMP, ESR, TFTs)    Patient and father expressed understanding and agree with the plan as outlined above.    For therapy:   Www.theshrinkspace.com        Guided relaxations calm the nervous system by decreasing blood pressure, heart rate and muscle tension while increasing blood flow. Setting your phone alarm or work calendar for reminders to do this during lunch or before bed are also great ways to schedule it into your day.       Mind Shift     Mind Shift is one of the best mental health apps designed specifically for teens and young adults with anxiety. Rather than trying to avoid anxious feelings, Mind Shift stresses the importance of changing how you think about anxiety. Think of this app as the cheerleader in your pocket, encouraging you to take charge of your life, ride out intense emotions, and face challenging situations.          Smiling Mind   Free meditation app with age-group specific content that teaches mindfulness to improve overall emotional well-being and decrease stress.          UCLA Mindful   With this easy-to-use app, you can practice mindfulness meditation anywhere, anytime with the guidance of the UCLA  Mindful Awareness Research Center. Scientific research shows mindfulness can help manage stress-related physical conditions, reduce anxiety and depression, cultivate positive emotions, and help improve overall physical health and well-being.     Calm introduces you to mindfulness with 5 minute instructions. It also has relaxation scenes and sounds to support self-guided meditation. Available for Apple or Android.     Headspace teaches you the basics of meditation and mindfulness in just 10 minutes a day. Available for Apple or Android. There is no evidence of free fluid in her left upper quadrant scan of her abdomen and no trauma or timeline to suggest this was the case. CPSP:  Phone intake completed via phone due to Covid-19 Pandemic  Patient is not set up for My Chart      1. 11/14/2017 Stanford records show POSITIVE for mutation Factor 5 Leiden See Media for documentation. PLEASE SEE CARE EVERYWHERE for records:    Assessment/Plan:     Remington Franson is a 25 y.o. female who had 2 early unexplained SABs following a healthy term pregnancy. She is still breastfeeding but has had regular menses for some months now. Workup above is unremarkable except for FVL heterozygous with no personal or FHx of TED.    - I discussed the common causes of SABs and the background rate. Roughly 15% of clinically recognized pregnancies ends in SAB. After 1 SAB there is no increased risk of recurrence, still about 15%. After 2 consecutive SAB the rate increases to about 20%. After 3 consecutive SAB the rate increases to about 30%. However, this means that most of the time subsequent pregnancies do well without SAB.    - We discussed the pros and cons of an extensive workup after 2 SABs. One risk is finding something that isn't "normal" that either cannot be treated or is not actually the cause. She and her partner seemed to understand this well in terms of pursuing rare causes with further workup.    - We discussed FVL heterozygous state in detail. She's also had a Hem consult who recommended that she not have anticoagulation in her situation. Here is what we understand about FVL mutation as it relates to pregnancy:  - There may be an increased rate of SAB (2X higher in one large study but not in others).   - Treatment with LDASA or Heparin has NOT been shown to improve obstetrical outcomes.  - FVL does increase risk of TED some but in the absence of a personal or FHx most hems do not recommend treatment - c/w her understanding from the hematologist she saw.  - Pregnancy also increases risk of TED. I do not recommend tx in her situation if she becomes pregnant UNLESS there is another additive risk for TED.  She should receive prophylactic dose lovenox if she is incapacitated in pregnancy (hospitalized, for instance) or if she has a c/section.    If she has another SAB, I would recommend the following 2 tests  - Either HSG or saline ultrasound to better define any uterine cavity irregularities that have been associated ith SAB. These can be fixed and are worth pursuing.  - Parental karyotyping. If the saline ultrasound is normal I would get this next. While they do have a healthy child that does NOT eliminate the possibility of a balanced translocation which can be associated with rec SAB.    Overall, I think this couple has a good prognosis for successful and healthy pregnancy. I also discussed stress reduction with mediation, biofeedback, yoga or therapy.    Thank you for the opportunity to help with Wendy and I wish her and her husband the best. As she will soon be changing insurances a copy of this consult will also be mailed to her for her records.    More than 62 minutes were spent face to face with Wendy during her visit. More than 50% of the visit was spent providing education to and/or counseling Wendy (and the family if present) regarding the issues documented in this note. TEST PARAMETERS AND METHODOLOGY Methodology: Transcription-Mediated Amplification (TMA) This qualitative nucleic acid amplification test detects and differentiates Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae ribosomal RNA (rRNA).  This test is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for Male and Female Urine, Endocervical Swabs, PreservCyt ThinPrep Pap Specimens, Male Urethral Swabs, Vaginal Swabs, Throat and Rectum Specimens. Sensitivity and specificity are unknown for other specimen types and collection devices.  NOTE:  Negative results do not preclude infection. Detection is dependent on adequate specimen collection, the absence of inhibitors, and the presence of a sufficient number of rRNA targets. Furthermore, positive results do not infer organism viability and/or infectivity.  All positive results are reported to the California Department of Health Services as required by law.

Disclaimer: Molecular diagnostic test results should be interpreted in the context of standard clinical, laboratory and pathological findings. Molecular genetic test results impart a probabilistic risk of disease. In order to derive the most meaningful benefit from this testing, it is recommended that the results and subsequent options from these complex tests be discussed with patients by a trained medical/genetics professional. False negative results may be due to sampling error or errors in sample handling, as well as clonal/signal density below the level of detection. Genotyping errors can result from trace contamination of PCR reactions and from rare genetic variants that interfere with analysis, including deletions or polymorphisms in primer binding sites which prevent allele amplification. Perinatal Genetic Counseling Summary Report    Patient Name Quamir Farley   DOB 02/15/1992   Referring Provider Lobo, Zechariah Spearman*   Date of Service 07/13/2020   Site of Visit LPCH Stanford     Indication Options                       Maternal age at EDC 28   Maternal age risk of   chromosome abnormality 1/434   EDC 11/15/2020   Plurality singleton   Gravida / Para / SAB / TAB 4 / 1 / 2 / 0   Gestational age at date of service 22+1   Medical History Factor V Leiden    Family History 1st degree relative to fetus with "anemia"   Exposures None reported         Testing offered (if applicable) Elected/Declined  Date test ordered Results (if applicable)   NIPT Declined     Amniocentesis Declined       Ms. Pickering was accompanied today in her genetic counseling appointment by her partner, Razavi. Prior to the start of the counseling session, we obtained Ms. Peach's verbal consent to proceed with the discussion in the presence of this individual.     Description of Testing Offered:    Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT):  NIPT is a maternal blood test drawn after 10 weeks 0 days gestation that screens for trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), trisomy 18, trisomy 13, triploidy, and sex chromosome aneuploidies. There is an option to add screening to predict fetal sex. There are data that suggest a higher false positive rate for sex chromosome aneuploidy and, rarely, there are errors in fetal sex screening.  A normal result on NIPT cannot completely rule out trisomy 21, 18, 13, triploidy, or sex chromosome aneuploidy. If the results of testing indicate a high risk for aneuploidy, then diagnostic testing through CVS or amniocentesis is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.     Amniocentesis:  Amniocentesis is a procedure that involves taking a sample of amniotic fluid.  It is usually performed between 16 and 20 weeks gestation.  The risk of miscarriage associated with amniocentesis is  1/300-1/500. Diagnostic testing including karyotype or array based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) can be performed.    Karyotype:  A karyotype can be performed on cultured cells obtained from either a CVS or amniocentesis sample.  It is a visual representation of the chromosomes that analyzes their number and structure.  It is used to diagnose aneuploidy and can also detect some rearrangements and structural abnormalities.       Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), also known as chromosomal microarray (CMA):  This technique is able to detect submicroscopic genomic copy number variants (CNVs), that is, small missing or extra pieces of genetic material that are not identified by standard chromosome analysis (karyotype).      The limitations of these tests performed individually or in combination were discussed with the patient.      Discussion:    Prenatal testing options were discussed.  Depending on the gestational age, screening options may include NIPT and State of California Prenatal Screening (1st trimester, serum only, quad only or sequential integrated).  We discussed the possibility that the fetus may have a chromosome abnormality or other genetic problem that cannot be detected by these screening methods.  Thus, the option of diagnostic testing through amniocentesis was discussed.  Ms. Nadal declined an invasive procedure.       Ms. Dicharry-Juan had quad screening through the California Prenatal Screening Program which was screen negative.  The Down syndrome risk was 1/220, trisomy 18 risk was less than 1/10,000, SCD risk (Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, congential abnormalities, and fetal demise) was less than 1/10,000, and risk for neural tube defects was negative. Ms. Dicharry-Juan had declined first trimester risk assessment through the California Screening Program.     The limitations of screening were reviewed. We discussed that Ms. Dicharry-Juan's risk for Down syndrome is  greater than her age-related risk, but is still less than 1%. We discussed the advantages and disadvantages of proceeding with NIPT for further risk assessment, as NIPT is a more accurate screening test. Ms. Purohit declined additional testing.    A review of the family history reveals that Ms. Dicharry-Juan was found to have factor V Leiden after experiencing 2 miscarriages. She reports she is heterozygous. Records were not available for review today. Factor V Leiden is a mutation that occurs in 3-8% of the general US and European populations.  Carriers of this mutation face an increased risk for thromboembolism.  Individuals who have two factor V Leiden mutations are at greater risk for thrombotic complications.  However, those who only have one factor V Leiden mutation can have variable presentation due to interaction with other genes in the clotting pathway and environmental factors.  Children of an individual with one factor V Leiden mutation have a 50% risk of inheriting the factor V Leiden mutation.  If the other parent is a carrier, then the children are at risk to be homozygous for this gene.    Ms. Zaidi's partner reports that he may have "borderline anemia" or iron deficiency of unknown etiology. Records were not available for review. Without a specific diagnosis or additional information, we are unable to evaluate the possible genetic etiology or determine recurrence risks. We are available to review medical records if provided.    The patient questionnaire and family history were reviewed.  Based on the information gathered, no additional increased reproductive risk was identified.  The patient was reminded, however, that every pregnancy has a 3-4% risk of a problem detectable at birth.  Many of these problems are not detectable prenatally.     Screening Recommendations:    MCV: We recommend that the patient have an MCV performed, if not already done, to determine her thalassemia carrier  status.    Cystic fibrosis (CF):  The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends offering CF carrier screening to all patients, regardless of ethnicity.    Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA): The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends offering SMA carrier screening to all patients, regardless of ethnicity.     Sickle cell disease: This patient’s partner is of African descent.  Based on national practice guidelines, we recommend offering carrier screening for sickle cell disease. Ms. Osman's partner declined screening for sickle cell disease today. We discussed the availability of newborn screening for hemoglobinopathies.        Sincerely,    Corbett, CGC, CGCL  Genetic Counselor    Ponti, MD  Clinical Geneticist

It is used to diagnose aneuploidy and can also detect some rearrangements and structural abnormalities.       Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), also known as chromosomal microarray (CMA):  This technique is able to detect submicroscopic genomic copy number variants (CNVs), that is, small missing or extra pieces of genetic material that are not identified by standard chromosome analysis (karyotype).      The limitations of these tests performed individually or in combination were discussed with the patient.      Discussion:    Prenatal testing options were discussed.  Depending on the gestational age, screening options may include NIPT and State of California Prenatal Screening (1st trimester, serum only, quad only or sequential integrated).  We discussed the possibility that the fetus may have a chromosome abnormality or other genetic problem that cannot be detected by these screening methods.  Thus, the option of diagnostic testing through amniocentesis was discussed.  Ms. Towle-Singh declined an invasive procedure.       Ms. Towle-Singh had quad screening through the California Prenatal Screening Program which was screen negative.  The Down syndrome risk was 1/220, trisomy 18 risk was less than 1/10,000, SCD risk (Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, congential abnormalities, and fetal demise) was less than 1/10,000, and risk for neural tube defects was negative.  Ms. Vanheukelom had declined first trimester risk assessment through the California Screening Program.     The limitations of screening were reviewed. We discussed that Ms. Towle-Singh's risk for Down syndrome is greater than her age-related risk, but is still less than 1%. We discussed the advantages and disadvantages of proceeding with NIPT for further risk assessment, as NIPT is a more accurate screening test. Ms. Towle-Singh declined additional testing.    A review of the family history reveals that Ms. Towle-Singh was found to have factor V Leiden after experiencing 2 miscarriages. She reports she is heterozygous. Records were not available for review today. Factor V Leiden is a mutation that occurs in 3-8% of the general US and European populations.  Carriers of this mutation face an increased risk for thromboembolism.  Individuals who have two factor V Leiden mutations are at greater risk for thrombotic complications.  However, those who only have one factor V Leiden mutation can have variable presentation due to interaction with other genes in the clotting pathway and environmental factors.  Children of an individual with one factor V Leiden mutation have a 50% risk of inheriting the factor V Leiden mutation.  If the other parent is a carrier, then the children are at risk to be homozygous for this gene.    Ms. Towle-Singh's partner reports that he may have "borderline anemia" or iron deficiency of unknown etiology. Records were not available for review. Without a specific diagnosis or additional information, we are unable to evaluate the possible genetic etiology or determine recurrence risks. We are available to review medical records if provided.    The patient questionnaire and family history were reviewed.  Based on the information gathered, no additional increased reproductive risk was identified.  The patient was reminded, however, that every pregnancy has a 3-4% risk of a problem detectable at birth.   Many of these problems are not detectable prenatally.     Screening Recommendations:    MCV: We recommend that the patient have an MCV performed, if not already done, to determine her thalassemia carrier status.    Cystic fibrosis (CF):  The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends offering CF carrier screening to all patients, regardless of ethnicity.    Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA): The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends offering SMA carrier screening to all patients, regardless of ethnicity.     Sickle cell disease: This patient’s partner is of African descent.  Based on national practice guidelines, we recommend offering carrier screening for sickle cell disease. Ms. Towle-Singh's partner declined screening for sickle cell disease today. We discussed the availability of newborn screening for hemoglobinopathies.        Sincerely,    Leggett, CGC, CGCL  Genetic Counselor    Sousa, MD  Clinical Geneticist

Clinical Notes:
Chest X-ray (CXR) is an imaging test that takes pictures of the heart and lungs. It is used to detect and diagnose various conditions such as pneumonia, lung cancer, and heart failure. The test is typically done on an outpatient basis and is usually quick and painless. A chest X-ray can be performed in a doctor's office, hospital, or imaging center. A chest X-ray is performed by a healthcare professional who places the patient on an X-ray table and positions the X-ray machine to take pictures of the chest. The patient may be asked to stand up or sit up to get the best image. The X-ray machine emits a small amount of radiation, which passes through the body and creates an image of the chest on a film or digital screen. The image is then reviewed by a radiologist, who interprets the results and reports them to the patient's doctor. In some cases, a chest X-ray may be performed to monitor the progression of a disease or to check the effectiveness of treatment. It is an important diagnostic tool that can help healthcare providers diagnose and manage various conditions.
```

Clinical Note:
HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was a 78-year-old female admitted for hook-wire excision and sentinel lymph node biopsy for breast cancer. She had a history of cardiopulmonary resuscitation due to stress-induced cardiomyopathy secondary to pneumonia, congestive heart failure, controlled hypertension, and chronic obstructive lung disease. Surgery was performed under regional anesthesia, which was achieved through a single injection of ropivacaine into the inter-fascial plane between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles. Standard monitoring was initiated, and the patient was administered dexmedetomidine and remifentanil for anesthetic management. The operation proceeded uneventfully and lasted for one hour and twenty minutes. No intraoperative complications were reported. The patient was observed in the post-anesthesia care unit for a brief period and subsequently discharged.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:
The patient was a 78-year-old female admitted for breast cancer treatment. The surgical intervention was performed without any complications under regional anesthesia, and adequate anesthetic coverage was achieved through the administration of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil. The patient was monitored appropriately and recovered without any perioperative complications. She has since been discharged.

A CT scan of his abdomen revealed a hypodense, well-defined, multilocular cystic lesion measuring 20.0 × 15.0 cm, located in the right lobe of his liver. It was associated with compression over the porta hepatis with mildly prominent intrahepatic ducts in both lobes of his liver.

Hospital Course:
A radiological diagnosis of giant hydatid cyst resulting in obstructive jaundice secondary to compression effect was made. Surgical excision was performed in December 2015. The specimen comprised a single, tan brown, irregular, flattened tissue piece measuring 7.5 × 6.5 cm. The wall thickness was 0.4 cm. The outer surface was smooth while the inner surface was irregular and hemorrhagic. Multiple cystic spaces were seen. Histopathologic examination showed a cyst wall lined by a single layer of tall columnar epithelium with basally placed nuclei and apical mucin. Dysplasia was not seen. Underlying stroma was fibroconnective and did not look like ovarian-type stroma. Fibrinopurulent exudate was also seen. A diagnosis of intrahepatic biliary cystadenoma was made. Surgical excision was incomplete as the cyst was 7.5 × 6.0 cm while radiologically the complete cyst measured 20.0 × 15.0 cm. The patient has so far not undergone a repeat resection for removal of residual tumor.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Intrahepatic biliary cystadenoma

Recommendations:
The patient requires a repeat resection for removal of residual tumor. It is recommended that the patient schedule an appointment with their primary care physician for further evaluation and management of their condition. The patient should undergo regular follow-up with their physician to monitor their condition and ensure that any necessary treatment is administered promptly.

After initial treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and immobilization, the patient was reevaluated 24 hours later due to an increase in CRP. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed suspected osteomyelitis of the patella, and a puncture aspiration yielded a sanguine-purulent liquid, confirming the diagnosis of osteomyelitis.

At six months post-diagnosis, the patient's knee function was normal with scores remaining at the maximum. There were no complications reported during the hospital course.

Osteomyelitis

Procedure:
Puncture aspiration

Treatment:
Empiric antibiotics, NSAIDs, immobilization

Follow-up Care:
Oral antibiotics, full-extension brace for 15 days
